title: The Emancipation Proclamation takes effect
headline: In 1863, the Emancipation Proclamation declared the enslaved people of the Confederate states to be free.
story:
On January 1, 1863, in the middle of the American Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln signed the final version of the Emancipation Proclamation. The decree declared free all enslaved people in the territories still in rebellion against the Union — some three and a half million people.

Its practical reach was limited: it did not touch the slave states that had stayed in the Union, and it could not be enforced where the Confederacy still ruled. But it changed the meaning of the war, which became a war for abolition as well, and it opened the ranks of the Union Army to Black soldiers, who would eventually number nearly 200,000. Full and permanent abolition came in December 1865 with the Thirteenth Amendment.

title: The fall of Granada
headline: In 1492, Boabdil handed Granada over to the Catholic Monarchs, ending the Reconquista.
story:
On January 2, 1492, the armies of Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon entered Granada after months of siege. Muhammad XII, known as Boabdil, the last Nasrid emir, surrendered the keys of the Alhambra and went into exile. With that, the last Muslim state on the Iberian Peninsula disappeared, almost eight centuries after Tariq's landing in 711.

The surrender terms promised the Muslim population that it could keep its religion, language and customs, but those guarantees were broken within a few years, through forced conversions and, later, the expulsion of the Moriscos. 1492 also brought two other events of enormous weight: the decree expelling the Jews and Columbus's first voyage.

title: Leo X excommunicates Luther
headline: In 1521, the bull 'Decet Romanum Pontificem' formally excommunicated Martin Luther.
story:
On January 3, 1521, Pope Leo X issued the bull 'Decet Romanum Pontificem', which made the excommunication of Martin Luther effective. The Augustinian friar had been challenging the sale of indulgences and papal authority since 1517, and had already publicly burned the earlier bull that gave him a deadline to recant.

Weeks later, Luther appeared before the Diet of Worms and again refused to take back his words. The break was complete. Protected by the Prince-Elector of Saxony, he translated the Bible into German and laid the foundations of the Protestant churches. The Reformation split Western Christianity and fed more than a century of religious wars in Europe.

title: Louis Braille is born
headline: In 1809, Louis Braille was born — creator of the tactile reading system for blind people.
story:
Louis Braille was born on January 4, 1809, in Coupvray, near Paris. At the age of three he injured one eye with a tool from his father's workshop; the infection spread to the other eye and he lost his sight completely.

On a scholarship at the Royal Institute for Blind Youth in Paris, he came across a military code of raised dots designed for reading at night without light. By around 1824, still only fifteen, he had simplified it into a six-dot cell able to represent letters, numbers and musical notation. The system was barely used in Braille's lifetime — he died of tuberculosis in 1852 — but today it is the standard for tactile reading and writing in almost every language.

title: The degradation of Alfred Dreyfus
headline: In 1895, Captain Dreyfus was publicly stripped of his rank for a treason he did not commit.
story:
On January 5, 1895, in the courtyard of the École Militaire in Paris, Captain Alfred Dreyfus was stripped of his insignia and his sword in front of the assembled troops. A court-martial had convicted him of spying for Germany on the basis of flimsy evidence and the fact that he was Jewish. He was deported to Devil's Island.

The real spy, Major Esterhazy, was uncovered soon afterwards and acquitted in order to cover up the mistake. In 1898 Émile Zola published 'J'accuse…!', and the "Dreyfus affair" split France in two for years. Dreyfus was finally exonerated in 1906 and reinstated in the Army.

title: Montessori opens the first Casa dei Bambini
headline: In 1907, Maria Montessori opened the Rome school that gave her method its name.
story:
On January 6, 1907, the physician Maria Montessori opened the first Casa dei Bambini in the San Lorenzo district of Rome, to care for the young children of poor families while their parents worked.

Montessori designed a classroom with child-height furniture and hands-on materials that let children learn by discovery and at their own pace, with the adult as a guide rather than an instructor. The results drew international attention and the method spread around the world. Today there are tens of thousands of Montessori schools, and many of its ideas about independence and the prepared environment have passed into mainstream education.

title: Galileo sees the moons of Jupiter
headline: In 1610, Galileo observed three of Jupiter's large satellites for the first time.
story:
On the night of January 7, 1610, Galileo Galilei pointed his telescope at Jupiter and noted three bright points lined up beside the planet. Over the following nights he saw that they shifted position and that there were four of them: not background stars, but bodies orbiting Jupiter.

The discovery, published in March in the 'Sidereus Nuncius', was devastating for the idea that everything revolved around the Earth. If Jupiter had its own moons, the Earth was not the only center of motion in the cosmos. The four satellites — Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto — have been known ever since as the Galilean moons.

title: The Battle of New Orleans
headline: In 1815 a major battle was fought over a war that, unknown to the men fighting it, was already over.
story:
On January 8, 1815, American troops under Andrew Jackson repelled a British assault on the outskirts of New Orleans. Protected behind earthworks and backed by good artillery, they inflicted hundreds of casualties on the enemy while suffering very few of their own.

The paradox is that the Treaty of Ghent, which ended the War of 1812 between the United States and Britain, had been signed in Belgium two weeks earlier. The news had not yet crossed the Atlantic. The victory, militarily pointless, made Jackson a national hero and set him on the road to the presidency.

title: Steve Jobs unveils the iPhone
headline: In 2007, Apple showed the first iPhone and redefined what a phone was.
story:
On January 9, 2007, at the Macworld expo in San Francisco, Steve Jobs introduced the iPhone as "an iPod, a phone and an internet communicator" in a single device. The touchscreen took up almost the entire front face, and there was no physical keyboard or stylus.

The phone went on sale in the United States in June. It was not the first smartphone, but its direct interface, its full web browser and, a year later, the App Store changed the whole industry. Within a decade, touchscreen phones had become the main device for accessing the internet worldwide.

title: Caesar crosses the Rubicon
headline: Around 49 BC, Julius Caesar led his army across the river Rubicon and touched off a civil war.
story:
By tradition, around January 10, 49 BC, Julius Caesar crossed the river Rubicon at the head of one of his legions. That river marked the boundary of his province: entering Italy with troops was, by law, an act of war against the Republic.

The phrase attributed to him, "alea iacta est" ("the die is cast"), sums up the point of no return. Caesar marched on Rome, defeated Pompey and the senators who opposed him, and made himself master of the state. His dictatorship and his assassination in 44 BC opened the way for his great-nephew Octavian to become the first emperor. "Crossing the Rubicon" still means making an irreversible decision.

title: The first injection of insulin
headline: In 1922, a teenager with diabetes received the first dose of insulin in history, in Toronto.
story:
On January 11, 1922, Leonard Thompson, a fourteen-year-old boy dying of type 1 diabetes in a Toronto hospital, was given a pancreatic extract prepared by Frederick Banting and Charles Best. The first attempt barely worked and caused an allergic reaction.

A more purified version, injected twelve days later, brought his blood sugar down dramatically and Thompson recovered. Until then, type 1 diabetes was a death sentence within months. The discovery was handed to the University of Toronto for a token one pound so that insulin could reach the whole world, and it earned the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1923.

title: The Haiti earthquake
headline: In 2010, a magnitude 7 quake devastated Port-au-Prince and killed hundreds of thousands.
story:
On January 12, 2010, at 4:53 p.m. local time, an earthquake of magnitude 7.0 with its epicenter very close to the capital, Port-au-Prince, shook Haiti for a few seconds. Flimsy construction and enormous population density turned the tremor into a catastrophe: estimates run between 200,000 and 300,000 dead — a figure hard to pin down — and more than a million people left homeless.

The presidential palace, the cathedral, hospitals and the UN headquarters were destroyed. The international response was massive but disorganized, and months later a cholera outbreak introduced by UN peacekeepers made the emergency worse. Haiti, the poorest country in the Americas, took years just to clear the rubble.

title: Zola publishes 'J'accuse…!'
headline: In 1898, Émile Zola used a newspaper's front page to accuse the French state of covering up the Dreyfus affair.
story:
On January 13, 1898, the newspaper 'L'Aurore' filled its entire front page with an open letter from the writer Émile Zola to the President of the Republic, under the headline "J'accuse…!". In it he accused military officers and handwriting experts by name of having convicted Alfred Dreyfus while knowing he was innocent, and of shielding the real spy.

The paper sold 300,000 copies in a day. Zola was prosecuted for libel and had to flee to England, but his gesture revived the case and mobilized intellectuals across Europe. It is often cited as the birth of the modern figure of the "intellectual" who intervenes in public life.

title: The Casablanca Conference
headline: In 1943, Roosevelt and Churchill met in Morocco to plan the rest of the war.
story:
On January 14, 1943, a ten-day meeting began in Casablanca, in Allied-controlled Morocco, between US President Franklin D. Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, with their military staffs. Stalin, invited, did not attend because of the Battle of Stalingrad.

There it was decided to invade Sicily before northern Europe, to intensify the bombing of Germany, and to give priority to the war in the Atlantic. Roosevelt also announced that only the "unconditional surrender" of Germany, Italy and Japan would be accepted — a contested formula that shaped the rest of the conflict.

title: Wikipedia is founded
headline: In 2001, Wikipedia went live: a free encyclopedia that anyone could edit.
story:
On January 15, 2001, Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger launched Wikipedia as a side experiment of Nupedia, an online encyclopedia written by experts that was progressing very slowly. The idea was to use a "wiki", a website anyone can edit directly in the browser.

Growth was explosive: within a year it had 20,000 articles and soon spread to dozens of languages. Run by a non-profit foundation and carrying no advertising, it has become one of the most visited websites in the world. Its reliability, uneven and always debated, depends on thousands of volunteers and on claims being backed by sources.

title: Octavian is given the title Augustus
headline: In 27 BC, the Senate granted Octavian the name Augustus and the Roman Empire was effectively born.
story:
On January 16, 27 BC, the Senate of Rome granted Gaius Octavius the honorary title "Augustus" ("the venerable") and confirmed the extraordinary powers he had already accumulated. Formally, Octavian had "restored the Republic"; in practice, he held command of the army, control of the key provinces and the final word in politics.

That arrangement, known as the Principate, gave Rome two centuries of relative internal stability, the 'Pax Romana'. Augustus reformed the administration, the army and public finances, and boasted of having found a city of brick and left it in marble. The month of August is named after him.

title: Scott reaches the South Pole
headline: In 1912, Scott's expedition reached the South Pole and found that Amundsen had beaten them to it.
story:
On January 17, 1912, the Briton Robert Falcon Scott and his four companions reached the South Pole after weeks of hauling sledges on foot. There they found a tent and a Norwegian flag: Roald Amundsen had arrived 34 days earlier, with dogs and skis, and had returned safely.

Scott's journey back was a tragedy. Exhausted, underfed and trapped by bad weather, the men died one after another. The bodies of Scott and the last two were found in November inside the tent, barely 18 km from a supply depot. His diary, published afterwards, turned the failure into a British national myth.

title: The German Empire is proclaimed
headline: In 1871, the German princes proclaimed William I emperor in the Palace of Versailles.
story:
On January 18, 1871, in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles, while the Prussian army was still besieging Paris, the princes of the German states proclaimed King William I of Prussia emperor of a unified Germany. The political architect was Chancellor Otto von Bismarck.

Unification capped three wars in seven years. Choosing Versailles for the ceremony humiliated France, which also lost Alsace and Lorraine, and sowed a resentment that would weigh on Europe until 1945. The new empire quickly became the leading industrial and military power on the continent.

title: Edgar Allan Poe is born
headline: In 1809, Edgar Allan Poe was born — master of the horror tale and pioneer of detective fiction.
story:
Edgar Allan Poe was born on January 19, 1809, in Boston, the son of traveling actors. Orphaned early, he had a life marked by poverty, alcohol and the early death of his young wife.

In barely two decades of work he shaped several genres: the tale of psychological horror ('The Tell-Tale Heart', 'The Fall of the House of Usher'), the detective story with 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue' — which would inspire Sherlock Holmes — and a musical, obsessive poetry such as 'The Raven'. He died in Baltimore in 1849, at the age of 40, in circumstances never explained. His influence on modern literature is enormous.

title: Simon de Montfort's first Parliament
headline: In 1265, an assembly met in London that, for the first time, included representatives of the towns.
story:
On January 20, 1265, an assembly convened by Simon de Montfort opened at Westminster. Montfort was the baron who had defeated and captured King Henry III of England. Needing support against the nobility that was hostile to him, he summoned not only barons and bishops but also two knights per county and two burgesses from each town.

That presence of representatives of the "commons" is why it is regarded as a direct forerunner of the English Parliament and, through it, of modern parliaments. Montfort was killed in battle a few months later, but the practice of summoning the commons endured.

title: The execution of Louis XVI
headline: In 1793, King Louis XVI was guillotined in Paris after being tried by the Convention.
story:
On January 21, 1793, Louis XVI mounted the scaffold set up in what is now the Place de la Concorde in Paris. The Convention, the revolutionary parliament, had tried him for conspiring against the nation and had sentenced him to death by a narrow majority. He tried to address the crowd, but a drum roll drowned out his voice.

The execution of a king by decision of an assembly shocked the monarchies of Europe and hastened France's war against much of the continent. In October, Queen Marie Antoinette would also be guillotined. The country was entering the harshest phase of the Revolution, the Terror.

title: Queen Victoria dies
headline: In 1901, Queen Victoria died after 63 years on the throne, closing an entire age.
story:
Queen Victoria of the United Kingdom died on January 22, 1901, on the Isle of Wight, at the age of 81, surrounded by her large family, among them the German Kaiser Wilhelm II. She had reigned since 1837: 63 years, the longest reign in British history up to that point.

Her name became linked with an era of industrial and colonial expansion — the British Empire came to cover a quarter of the planet — and with a strict public morality. Related to almost every royal house on the continent, she was called "the grandmother of Europe". She was succeeded by her son Edward VII, already 59.

title: The Trieste descends into the Mariana Trench
headline: In 1960, two men descended in a bathyscaphe to the deepest point of the ocean.
story:
On January 23, 1960, the bathyscaphe Trieste, crewed by the Swiss Jacques Piccard and the American Don Walsh, settled on the floor of the Challenger Deep, in the Pacific's Mariana Trench, at almost 11 kilometers down. The descent took about five hours.

The pressure down there is more than a thousand times that at the surface. A window cracked during the dive, but the capsule held. Piccard and Walsh said they had seen a flatfish, a claim disputed today. There was no other crewed visit to the bottom of the Mariana Trench until 2012, with the filmmaker James Cameron.

title: Gold in California
headline: In 1848, gold was found at a California sawmill and the Gold Rush began.
story:
On January 24, 1848, a carpenter named James Marshall spotted shiny flakes in the tailrace of a sawmill he was building for John Sutter, beside the American River in California. The attempt to keep it secret failed almost at once.

In 1849 some 300,000 prospectors arrived from all over the United States and from China, Chile, Europe and Australia: the "forty-niners". San Francisco went from village to city in months, and California entered the Union in 1850. The rush transformed the economy of the Pacific, ruined Sutter, and was devastating for the region's Indigenous peoples.

title: The first transcontinental telephone call
headline: In 1915, people spoke by telephone from one US coast to the other for the first time.
story:
On January 25, 1915, Alexander Graham Bell, in New York, telephoned his former assistant Thomas Watson, who was in San Francisco, and repeated the line they had used for the first telephone test 39 years earlier: "Mr. Watson, come here, I want you." Watson replied that it would now take him a week to get there.

The line, more than 5,000 kilometers long, was made possible by vacuum-tube repeaters that amplified the signal along the way. The call officially opened coast-to-coast telephone service and coincided with the World's Fair in San Francisco.

title: The First Fleet reaches Australia
headline: In 1788, eleven British ships founded the first European colony in Australia, at Sydney.
story:
On January 26, 1788, Captain Arthur Phillip moved the settlers of the so-called First Fleet to Sydney Cove, a better anchorage than Botany Bay, where they had arrived days earlier. On board were some 1,400 people, most of them convicts transported from Britain, which had lost its American colonies as a penal destination.

That day is now Australia's national holiday, but for the Aboriginal peoples, who had been on the continent for tens of thousands of years, it marked the start of the dispossession of their lands and of a demographic collapse. Many call it "Invasion Day" or "Day of Mourning".

title: The liberation of Auschwitz
headline: In 1945, the Red Army entered the Auschwitz camp and found a few thousand survivors.
story:
On January 27, 1945, Soviet soldiers reached the Auschwitz-Birkenau complex in occupied Poland. Days earlier the Nazis had evacuated tens of thousands of prisoners in "death marches" and had left behind about 7,000, most of them too sick to walk.

Around 1.1 million people were murdered at Auschwitz, the vast majority of them Jews, along with Polish, Roma and Soviet prisoners. The gas chambers and crematoria had been dynamited to destroy the evidence. Since 2005, this day has been International Holocaust Remembrance Day.

title: The Challenger disaster
headline: In 1986, the shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff.
story:
On January 28, 1986, the Space Shuttle Challenger lifted off from Florida on an unusually cold morning. Seventy-three seconds into the flight it broke apart and fell into the Atlantic. All seven crew members died, among them Christa McAuliffe, a teacher who was to give lessons from space — which had led millions of schoolchildren to watch the launch live.

The investigation, with the physicist Richard Feynman as a leading voice, found that rubber O-ring seals in the booster rockets had lost their elasticity in the cold and let burning gases escape. NASA had received warnings from engineers the night before. The shuttle program was grounded for almost three years.

title: Karl Benz patents the automobile
headline: In 1886, Karl Benz filed the patent for the first vehicle driven by a gasoline engine.
story:
On January 29, 1886, the German engineer Karl Benz filed patent number 37435 for a "gas-powered vehicle", the Benz Patent-Motorwagen. It was a light three-wheeler with a single-cylinder four-stroke engine, electric ignition and water cooling, capable of about 16 km/h.

The car barely sold until, in 1888, Benz's wife Bertha took their sons on a journey of more than 100 km without telling her husband, to prove it was good for something. The adventure, with stops to buy fuel at a pharmacy, was a brilliant advertising campaign and marks the practical birth of the automobile.

title: The assassination of Gandhi
headline: In 1948, Mahatma Gandhi was shot in New Delhi, five months after India's independence.
story:
On January 30, 1948, as he walked to a public prayer meeting in the gardens of Birla House in New Delhi, Mohandas "Mahatma" Gandhi was shot three times at point-blank range by Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist who accused him of being too conciliatory toward Muslims and the new Pakistan.

Gandhi, 78, had led the non-violent struggle against British rule for three decades. His death, only months after an independence accompanied by a bloody partition, caused worldwide shock. Godse was tried and executed in 1949.

title: The United States launches Explorer 1
headline: In 1958, the first American satellite discovered the Earth's radiation belts.
story:
On January 31, 1958, the United States placed Explorer 1, its first satellite, into orbit, almost four months after the Soviet Sputnik and after the public failure of the Vanguard rocket. The launch was led by Wernher von Braun's team on a Juno I rocket.

The small satellite carried a cosmic-ray detector designed by James Van Allen. Its readings, strange at first, revealed that the Earth is surrounded by zones of charged particles trapped by the magnetic field: the Van Allen belts. It was the first major scientific discovery of the space age.

title: The Greensboro sit-in
headline: In 1960, four Black students sat down at a "whites only" lunch counter and would not move.
story:
On February 1, 1960, four students from a Black college in Greensboro, North Carolina, sat down at the lunch counter of a Woolworth's store, reserved for white customers, ordered coffee and, when refused, stayed seated until closing time.

The next day they came back with more classmates. Within a week, sit-ins had spread to other Southern cities; within months, to tens of thousands of people. The tactic of peaceful resistance forced segregation to be dropped in many establishments and gave momentum to the civil rights movement that would culminate in the laws of 1964 and 1965.

title: German surrender at Stalingrad
headline: In 1943, the last remnants of the German 6th Army surrendered after months of siege.
story:
On February 2, 1943, the last soldiers of the German 6th Army encircled at Stalingrad laid down their arms. The battle for the city on the Volga had lasted more than five months and combined house-to-house fighting with a double Soviet encirclement that trapped some 250,000 men.

Hitler had forbidden any retreat or surrender and had promoted the commander, Paulus, to field marshal, expecting him to take his own life; Paulus surrendered instead. Of the German prisoners, very few made it home years later. Stalingrad is regarded as the turning point of the war in Europe: from then on, the initiative passed to the Soviet Union.

title: The day the music died
headline: In 1959, a small-plane crash killed Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens and The Big Bopper.
story:
In the early hours of February 3, 1959, a small plane crashed into an Iowa cornfield shortly after taking off in bad weather. The pilot and the three musicians on board were killed: Buddy Holly, 22, one of the great pioneers of rock and roll; Ritchie Valens, 17, who wrote 'La Bamba'; and J. P. Richardson, 'The Big Bopper'.

They were on tour in unheated buses, and Holly had chartered the plane to go ahead and do some laundry. Years later, Don McLean's song 'American Pie' called that date "the day the music died", and it has been known that way ever since.

title: Facebook is founded
headline: In 2004, a Harvard student launched a social network for his university.
story:
On February 4, 2004, Mark Zuckerberg launched 'TheFacebook' from his dorm room at Harvard, with the help of several classmates. At first only students with an email address from that university could sign up; within weeks it opened to other colleges, and in 2006 to the general public.

The network grew past 2 billion users and transformed advertising, journalism and social life online. It also brought controversy: privacy, content moderation, disinformation and the role of its algorithms in politics. The parent company was renamed Meta in 2021.

title: Bakelite, the first synthetic plastic
headline: In 1909, Leo Baekeland presented Bakelite, the first entirely artificial plastic.
story:
On February 5, 1909, the Belgian-American chemist Leo Baekeland announced to the American Chemical Society a new material made by reacting phenol and formaldehyde under heat and pressure: Bakelite.

Unlike treated materials such as celluloid, it derived from no natural substance. It was hard, insulating, resistant to heat and solvents, and could be mass-molded. It was used in telephones, plugs, radios, pan handles and a thousand other objects. It opened the age of plastics, with everything that brought: cheap, light goods, and also a waste problem we still carry.

title: The Treaty of Waitangi
headline: In 1840, Māori chiefs and the British Crown signed New Zealand's founding agreement.
story:
On February 6, 1840, some 40 Māori chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi with British representatives; in time more than 500 would sign. The text ceded sovereignty to the Crown in exchange for guaranteeing the Māori possession of their lands and the rights of British subjects.

The problem is that the English and Māori versions did not say the same thing: where one spoke of "sovereignty", the other spoke of "governance". From that ambiguity came wars, land confiscations and disputes that continue. Today the treaty is regarded as the country's founding document, and February 6 is a national holiday.

title: The Maastricht Treaty is signed
headline: In 1992, twelve European countries signed the treaty that created the European Union.
story:
On February 7, 1992, the ministers of the twelve states of the European Community signed the Treaty on European Union in the Dutch city of Maastricht. The agreement turned a mostly economic community into a political union: it created European citizenship, strengthened the Parliament and set the path toward a common currency.

That currency, the euro, would begin circulating as notes and coins ten years later. Ratification was not easy: Denmark rejected it in a referendum and it had to be renegotiated, and in France it passed by the narrowest of margins. Maastricht defined the Europe of the following decades, with its achievements and its tensions.

title: The execution of Mary, Queen of Scots
headline: In 1587, Mary, Queen of Scots, was beheaded after nearly twenty years as a prisoner of her cousin Elizabeth I.
story:
On February 8, 1587, Mary Stuart was beheaded at Fotheringhay Castle in England. Queen of Scots since infancy and the widow of a king of France, she had been overthrown by the Scottish nobility and had fled to England seeking the protection of her cousin Elizabeth I.

There she spent 19 years under arrest. As a Catholic and a great-granddaughter of Henry VII, she was the focus of every plot to unseat the Protestant Elizabeth. When one such scheme implicated her by letter, she was tried and condemned. Elizabeth signed the sentence reluctantly. Mary's son James would inherit the English throne in 1603 and unite the two crowns.

title: The Beatles on The Ed Sullivan Show
headline: In 1964, some 73 million Americans watched the Beatles live on television.
story:
On February 9, 1964, the Beatles performed live on 'The Ed Sullivan Show', the most-watched variety program in the United States. They played five songs before an audience of teenagers screaming so loudly that the music could barely be heard.

Around 73 million people watched, a record figure for the time. The performance set off Beatlemania in North America and opened the door to the so-called "British Invasion": by April, the top five spots on the US singles chart were all theirs. It is often marked as the moment British pop conquered the world's largest market.

title: Deep Blue wins a game against Kasparov
headline: In 1996, a computer beat a reigning world chess champion in a serious game for the first time.
story:
On February 10, 1996, IBM's computer Deep Blue defeated Garry Kasparov in the first game of a six-game match. It was the first time a machine had beaten a reigning world champion at tournament time controls.

Kasparov recovered and won the overall match 4–2. But in the 1997 rematch, against an improved version of Deep Blue, the champion lost the whole contest and alleged, without proof, human intervention. That duel marked a before and after: in chess, the superiority of machines is now total, and today they are used to train the grandmasters themselves.

title: Mandela walks free
headline: In 1990, Nelson Mandela was released after 27 years imprisoned by the apartheid regime.
story:
On February 11, 1990, Nelson Mandela walked out of the gate of Victor Verster Prison, near Cape Town, with his fist raised and before the cameras of the world. He was 71 and had spent 27 years in prison, most of them on Robben Island, serving a life sentence for his armed struggle against apartheid.

Days earlier, President F. W. de Klerk had legalized the African National Congress and other banned parties. A difficult negotiation began that led in 1994 to the first elections with universal suffrage, which Mandela won. He and De Klerk shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993.

title: Charles Darwin is born
headline: In 1809, Charles Darwin was born — the naturalist who explained evolution by natural selection.
story:
Charles Darwin was born on February 12, 1809, in Shrewsbury, England — the same day as Abraham Lincoln on the other side of the Atlantic. As a young man he dropped out of medicine and nearly became a clergyman before setting sail as a naturalist on HMS Beagle for almost five years.

What he saw on that voyage — fossils, islands, the variety of Galápagos finches — led him to an idea he mulled over for twenty years before daring to publish it. In 1859, pushed in part by a parallel paper from Alfred Russel Wallace, he brought out 'On the Origin of Species'. His thesis — that all forms of life descend from common ancestors and change through natural selection — is the foundation of modern biology.

title: The bombing of Dresden
headline: In 1945, Allied aircraft razed Dresden with incendiary bombs in the final months of the war.
story:
On the night of February 13–14, 1945, hundreds of British and American bombers dropped thousands of tons of explosives and incendiaries on Dresden. The historic center of the city, nicknamed "the Florence of the Elbe", was destroyed by a firestorm. Around 25,000 people died, according to the most recent historical studies, many of them refugees fleeing the eastern front.

The attack — on a city of little military value and when German defeat was certain — became a symbol of the debate over the bombing of civilian areas. Nazi propaganda and, later, that of East Germany greatly inflated the death toll.

title: The Pale Blue Dot
headline: In 1990, the Voyager 1 probe photographed the Earth from more than 6 billion kilometers away.
story:
On February 14, 1990, as Voyager 1 was leaving the Solar System, NASA turned the camera back toward the inner planets and took a family portrait. In one of the images, the Earth appeared as a point less than a pixel across, suspended in a scattered ray of sunlight.

The idea had come from the astronomer Carl Sagan, who years later wrote a famous passage about that photo: on that "pale blue dot" all of human history has taken place, every war and every empire, on "a mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam". It is one of the most influential images in the history of science.

title: The explosion of the Maine
headline: In 1898, the US battleship Maine blew up in Havana harbor and lit the war with Spain.
story:
On the night of February 15, 1898, the USS Maine, anchored in Havana to "protect American interests" during the Cuban war of independence, exploded and sank with more than 250 sailors aboard. The cause was never fully established; today it is thought to have been an internal explosion in a coal bunker rather than a mine.

New York's sensationalist press blamed Spain without evidence, with the slogan "Remember the Maine!". In April, the United States declared war. Within a few months Spain lost Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines. In Spain, that "Disaster of '98" caused a deep moral and intellectual crisis.

title: The tomb of Tutankhamun is opened
headline: In 1923, Howard Carter entered the burial chamber of the boy pharaoh, almost intact after 3,000 years.
story:
On February 16, 1923, the British archaeologist Howard Carter, before a small group of guests, broke through the wall separating the antechamber from the burial chamber of Tutankhamun, in the Valley of the Kings. Inside was the huge gilded sarcophagus and, around it, gilded shrines nested one inside another.

Carter had discovered the entrance to the tomb in November 1922, after years of excavations funded by Lord Carnarvon. It was the best-preserved Egyptian royal burial ever found: more than 5,000 objects, including the gold mask. Carnarvon's death a few weeks later fed the legend of the "mummy's curse".

title: Giordano Bruno, burned in Rome
headline: In 1600, the Inquisition executed the philosopher Giordano Bruno at the stake for heresy.
story:
On February 17, 1600, the Dominican friar and philosopher Giordano Bruno was burned alive in the Campo de' Fiori in Rome after an eight-year Inquisition trial and his refusal to recant. He was led to the stake gagged.

Bruno argued for an infinite universe, with no center, containing countless inhabited worlds, and with the stars as distant suns; he also held theological positions the Church considered grave heresies. For centuries he has been portrayed as a martyr of science, though historians note that he was condemned mainly on religious grounds. In 1889 a statue was raised in his memory on that same spot.

title: The discovery of Pluto
headline: In 1930, Clyde Tombaugh spotted Pluto by comparing photographs of the night sky.
story:
On February 18, 1930, Clyde Tombaugh, a young assistant at the Lowell Observatory in Arizona with no university degree, found Pluto while comparing photographic plates of the sky taken days apart, looking for an object that moved against the stars.

It was called the ninth planet, and the name was proposed by an eleven-year-old British girl. Decades later, many similar bodies were discovered beyond Neptune, and in 2006 the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a "dwarf planet". The decision was controversial and some still do not accept it.

title: Edison patents the phonograph
headline: In 1878, Thomas Edison registered the machine that first recorded and played back sound.
story:
On February 19, 1878, Thomas Edison obtained the patent for the phonograph, a device that recorded the vibrations of sound as grooves in a sheet of tinfoil wrapped around a cylinder, then played them back by running a needle along those same grooves. The first phrase recorded was, according to Edison, a nursery rhyme.

No one had ever preserved a human voice before. The invention astonished people so much that he was nicknamed "the Wizard of Menlo Park". Tinfoil was soon replaced by wax and, later, cylinders by flat discs. From that idea come the record industry and the whole culture of recorded music.

title: John Glenn orbits the Earth
headline: In 1962, John Glenn became the first American to circle the planet in orbit.
story:
On February 20, 1962, the Friendship 7 capsule, with John Glenn aboard, lifted off from Cape Canaveral and circled the Earth three times in just under five hours. The United States was behind: the Soviets had already put Gagarin and Titov into orbit the year before.

The flight had a scare: a sensor indicated that the heat shield might be loose, and ground control decided that Glenn should not jettison the retrorocket pack during reentry, to hold it in place. The alarm turned out to be false. Glenn returned a national hero; decades later, in 1998 and at the age of 77, he flew again on a shuttle.

title: The Communist Manifesto is published
headline: In 1848, the pamphlet by Marx and Engels appeared in London, opening: 'A spectre is haunting Europe'.
story:
On February 21, 1848, a pamphlet of about 23 pages came off a London press, commissioned by the Communist League and written by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels: the 'Manifesto of the Communist Party'. It was published in German and had almost no immediate impact.

A few days later revolution broke out in Paris and spread across half of Europe. The text — with its analysis of class struggle and its closing call, "Workers of the world, unite!" — became over the years one of the most influential political writings in history, the basis of parties and of states throughout the 20th century.

title: The world meets Dolly the sheep
headline: In 1997, a Scottish institute announced it had cloned a sheep from an adult cell.
story:
On February 22, 1997, the Roslin Institute, near Edinburgh, made public that it had cloned a mammal from an adult cell. The sheep, born in July 1996, was named Dolly and was genetically identical to the ewe that had donated the cell, taken from a mammary gland.

Until then it was believed that a specialized cell could not behave like an embryo again. Dolly proved otherwise and opened huge debates about cloning, including human cloning. She lived six and a half years, had lambs, and died after developing a lung disease. She is on display, taxidermied, at the National Museum of Scotland.

title: The 23-F coup attempt
headline: In 1981, a Civil Guard lieutenant colonel stormed the Spanish Congress at gunpoint.
story:
On the afternoon of February 23, 1981, as the Congress of Deputies was voting to install Leopoldo Calvo-Sotelo as prime minister, Lieutenant Colonel Antonio Tejero entered the chamber at the head of a group of armed Civil Guards, fired at the ceiling and held the entire government and parliament hostage. In Valencia, General Milans del Bosch sent tanks into the streets.

The coup failed that same night, above all after King Juan Carlos I's televised message rejecting it. It is the gravest episode Spain's young democracy faced after the Franco dictatorship. The main figures were tried and convicted.

title: The monarchy falls in France
headline: In 1848, a revolution in Paris brought down King Louis Philippe and proclaimed the Second Republic.
story:
On February 24, 1848, after three days of barricades and gunfire in Paris, King Louis Philippe of Orléans abdicated and fled to England in disguise. That same day, a crowd invaded the Chamber and a provisional government proclaimed the French Second Republic.

The new Republic introduced universal male suffrage, abolished slavery in the colonies and the death penalty for political offenses. The spark from Paris caught across Europe: within weeks there were revolutions in Vienna, Berlin, Milan, Budapest. The "Spring of Nations" of 1848 was mostly crushed, but it changed the political map of the continent.

title: Khrushchev's "Secret Speech"
headline: In 1956, the Soviet leader denounced Stalin's crimes before the Communist Party congress.
story:
In the early hours of February 25, 1956, at the close of the 20th Congress of the Communist Party of the USSR, Nikita Khrushchev read a speech of several hours behind closed doors, accusing Stalin — dead three years earlier — of a criminal "cult of personality": mass purges, torture, deportations and blunders during the war.

The text was not published in the USSR, but it leaked to the West within months. It opened the so-called "Thaw": the release of Gulag prisoners and a degree of cultural openness. It also shook the communist bloc: that year there were revolts in Poland and a revolution in Hungary, crushed by Soviet tanks.

title: The first demonstration of radar
headline: In 1935, an experiment in England proved that an aircraft could be detected by radio waves.
story:
On February 26, 1935, in a field near Daventry, England, the physicist Robert Watson-Watt set up a demonstration for the Air Ministry: an RAF bomber flew several times over a shortwave radio transmitter while a nearby receiver recorded on a screen the echo reflected by the aircraft.

The experiment worked and unlocked funding to build a chain of detection stations along Britain's south and east coasts. That system, ready in 1939, was decisive in winning the Battle of Britain in 1940, by allowing fighters to be concentrated where and when they were needed.

title: The Reichstag fire
headline: In 1933, a fire at the German parliament served as a pretext to suspend civil liberties.
story:
On the night of February 27, 1933, barely four weeks after Hitler became chancellor, the Reichstag building, seat of the German parliament in Berlin, burned to the ground. Police arrested a young Dutch communist at the scene, Marinus van der Lubbe, who declared himself the sole culprit.

The next day, the government pushed through an emergency decree suspending freedom of the press, assembly and expression and allowing detention without trial. It was the legal instrument with which the Nazis decapitated the opposition and won the March elections. It is still debated whether the fire was Van der Lubbe's work alone or whether more hands were behind it.

title: The double helix of DNA
headline: In 1953, Watson and Crick worked out the double-helix structure of the molecule of heredity.
story:
On February 28, 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick, in the Cavendish Laboratory at Cambridge, built a model of wire and cardboard that fit all the data: DNA was a double helix, two coiled strands whose rungs always paired adenine with thymine and guanine with cytosine.

That pairing rule explained at a stroke how genetic information is copied when a cell divides. The model rested decisively on the X-ray diffraction images obtained by Rosalind Franklin, whose role was recognized late. Watson, Crick and Wilkins received the Nobel Prize in 1962; Franklin had died in 1958.

title: The day that exists only every four years
headline: February 29 corrects the mismatch between the calendar and the real time the Earth takes to circle the Sun.
story:
The Earth takes about 365 days and almost 6 hours to circle the Sun. If the calendar always had 365 days, those nearly 6 hours a year would make the seasons drift: within a few centuries, summer would fall in December. That is why the Julian calendar (46 BC) already added a day every four years.

That correction was slightly too much and the drift built up again. In 1582, Pope Gregory XIII adjusted the rule: there is a leap year every 4 years, except century years not divisible by 400. So 1900 was not a leap year and 2000 was. That Gregorian calendar is the one almost the whole world uses today, and anyone born on February 29 only "officially" has a birthday once every four years.

title: Yellowstone, the first national park, is born
headline: In 1872, the United States protected Yellowstone and created the idea of the national park.
story:
On March 1, 1872, President Ulysses S. Grant signed the law that set aside some 9,000 km² of mountains, geysers and forests in the territories of Wyoming, Montana and Idaho "as a public park for the benefit and enjoyment of the people". It was the first national park in the world.

The idea of shielding a great landscape from the advance of mining, logging and the railroad, and managing it for the public, was later copied by dozens of countries. It also had a dark side: creating the park expelled the Indigenous peoples who had used that land for millennia. Today Yellowstone receives more than four million visitors a year.

title: First flight of Concorde
headline: In 1969, the Franco-British supersonic airliner flew for the first time.
story:
On March 2, 1969, the Concorde prototype took off from Toulouse for a test flight of less than half an hour, without breaking the sound barrier. It was the fruit of an agreement between France and Britain to build a commercial aircraft able to fly at more than twice the speed of sound.

It entered service in 1976 and crossed the Atlantic in about three and a half hours, half the time of a normal plane, but only Air France and British Airways bought it: it was noisy, burned enormous amounts of fuel and carried only about a hundred passengers at very high prices. After the Paris crash of 2000 and the fall in traffic, it was retired in 2003. There is still no successor.

title: 'Carmen' premieres
headline: In 1875, Bizet's opera premiered in Paris — a failure that is now one of the most performed in the world.
story:
On March 3, 1875, the Opéra-Comique in Paris premiered 'Carmen', by Georges Bizet, about a free and defiant Andalusian cigarette-factory worker who is finally murdered by a jealous lover. The bourgeois audience was scandalized to see smugglers, women fighting and such a violent ending on stage.

The reviews were harsh, and Bizet, 36, died three months later convinced he had failed. He did not see how, within a few years, 'Carmen' triumphed in Vienna, London and New York and became one of the most popular operas in history, with melodies — the habanera, the toreador's march — that almost everyone recognizes.

title: Roosevelt: "the only thing we have to fear is fear itself"
headline: In 1933, Franklin D. Roosevelt took office in the depths of the Great Depression and launched the New Deal.
story:
On March 4, 1933, Franklin Delano Roosevelt was sworn in as President of the United States with the country in ruins: a quarter of the workforce out of a job and thousands of banks closed. In his inaugural address he delivered the line that stuck to him: "The only thing we have to fear is fear itself."

In his first "hundred days" he pushed through an avalanche of laws: a bank rescue, public works to create jobs, farm relief, stock-market regulation. It was the New Deal, a turn toward a state that intervenes in the economy. Roosevelt would win four elections in a row, something no other president has done.

title: The "Iron Curtain" speech
headline: In 1946, Churchill described a Europe split in two by Soviet influence.
story:
On March 5, 1946, at a small college in Fulton, Missouri, with President Truman beside him, former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill said that "from Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent".

Behind that line, he argued, the countries of the east lay under Moscow's control. The USSR took it as a hostile declaration. The phrase "iron curtain" passed into common language, and the speech is often cited as one of the opening acts of the Cold War, which divided the world for more than four decades.

title: Mendeleev presents the periodic table
headline: In 1869, a Russian chemist ordered the elements and left gaps for those not yet known.
story:
On March 6, 1869, a paper by Dmitri Mendeleev was read before the Russian Chemical Society, placing the 63 known elements in a table, ordered by atomic weight and grouped by similar properties.

The brilliant part was that, when an element did not fit, Mendeleev left a gap and predicted what the missing one would be like. In the following years gallium, scandium and germanium were discovered, almost exactly as he had described them. The periodic table is today the basic map of chemistry and has grown to the more than 118 elements known now.

title: Bell patents the telephone
headline: In 1876, Alexander Graham Bell obtained the patent for a device to transmit the voice over a wire.
story:
On March 7, 1876, the US Patent Office granted Alexander Graham Bell patent number 174,465 for an "apparatus for transmitting vocal sounds telegraphically". Three days later he achieved the first clear transmission, with the line to his assistant: "Mr. Watson, come here, I want you."

Bell had filed his application just hours before Elisha Gray, who was working on something very similar; the lawsuit over priority lasted years. The telephone transformed business, journalism and everyday life, and the company Bell founded eventually became the giant AT&T.

title: The women of Petrograd and International Women's Day
headline: In 1917, a strike by women workers in Russia lit the fuse of the February Revolution.
story:
On March 8, 1917 (February 23 in the Russian calendar of the time), thousands of women textile workers in Petrograd went on strike demanding "bread and peace", fed up with the queues, the hunger and a war that was consuming their sons and husbands. The protest grew day by day until it became uncontrollable.

In less than a week, with the army refusing to fire on the crowd, Tsar Nicholas II abdicated. That "February Revolution" opened the year that would end with the Bolsheviks seizing power. The date, already linked to women's labor struggles, became International Women's Day.

title: The firebombing of Tokyo
headline: In 1945, a US incendiary air raid on Tokyo killed about 100,000 people in a single night.
story:
On the night of March 9–10, 1945, more than 300 US B-29 bombers dropped some 1,700 tons of incendiary bombs on Tokyo. The city, built largely of wood and paper, burned in a firestorm that leveled about 40 km² and destroyed close to a million homes.

Around 100,000 people died, most of them civilians, and more than a million were left homeless. "Operation Meetinghouse" is considered the deadliest air raid in history, above even the atomic bombs of August. It was the model for a campaign that razed dozens of Japanese cities before the surrender.

title: The Courrières mining disaster
headline: In 1906, a coal-dust explosion killed more than a thousand miners in northern France.
story:
On the morning of March 10, 1906, an explosion of firedamp and coal dust swept through tens of kilometers of galleries at the Courrières mine, in the Pas-de-Calais. It killed 1,099 people, many of them teenagers. It is the worst mining disaster in the history of Europe.

The rescue teams soon abandoned the search, but twenty days later thirteen survivors walked out on their own, having stayed alive by eating a dead horse's oats and even the bark from the timbers. The outrage triggered a strike by 60,000 miners and sped up workplace safety laws.

title: The 11-M attacks in Madrid
headline: In 2004, ten bombs on Madrid commuter trains killed 193 people.
story:
On the morning of March 11, 2004, at rush hour, ten devices went off on four commuter trains approaching Atocha station in Madrid. 193 people died and nearly 2,000 were injured. It was the deadliest jihadist attack carried out in Europe.

It happened three days before a general election. The government first attributed it to ETA, despite the signs pointing to a jihadist-inspired cell, and the handling of that information marked the electoral swing on March 14. Some of the perpetrators blew themselves up weeks later when cornered by police in Leganés.

title: Gandhi sets out on the Salt March
headline: In 1930, Gandhi walked 385 km to the sea to gather salt and defy the British Empire.
story:
On March 12, 1930, Mohandas Gandhi set out on foot from his ashram with a few dozen followers toward the coast at Dandi, 385 kilometers away. The aim was symbolic: to gather salt from the sea and evaporate it, an act that was forbidden because the British salt monopoly forced people to buy it with a tax that hit the poorest hardest.

The march lasted 24 days and, when Gandhi lifted a fistful of salt on April 6, millions of people across India imitated him. The authorities arrested tens of thousands, Gandhi among them. The civil-disobedience campaign traveled the world and marked a turning point in the struggle for independence.

title: Herschel discovers Uranus
headline: In 1781, William Herschel found the first planet ever discovered with a telescope.
story:
On the night of March 13, 1781, the amateur astronomer William Herschel, a musician by profession, was observing the sky from the garden of his house in Bath, England, with a telescope he had built himself. He saw an object that did not look like a star and that, night after night, moved among them.

At first he thought it was a comet, but it soon became clear that it was a new planet, the first discovered since antiquity. It doubled the known size of the Solar System at a stroke. Herschel wanted to call it "Georgium Sidus" in honor of King George III; the mythological name Uranus prevailed.

title: Albert Einstein is born
headline: In 1879, Albert Einstein was born — the man who changed our idea of space, time and gravity.
story:
Albert Einstein was born on March 14, 1879, in Ulm, Germany. Far from the myth of the poor student, he was brilliant in mathematics and physics, though he clashed with school discipline. In 1905, working as an examiner at the patent office in Bern, he published four papers within a few months that revolutionized physics, including the one on special relativity and the equivalence of mass and energy, E=mc².

In 1915 he completed general relativity, which describes gravity as a curvature of spacetime. He received the Nobel Prize in 1921, fled Nazism to the United States in 1933, and devoted his last years to pacifist politics and to a unified theory he never achieved.

title: The assassination of Julius Caesar
headline: In 44 BC, a group of senators stabbed Caesar in mid-session: the Ides of March.
story:
On March 15, 44 BC — the "Ides of March" — Julius Caesar went to a meeting of the Senate in the Curia of Pompey. A group of about sixty senators, led by Brutus and Cassius, surrounded him and stabbed him; he received 23 wounds. It was said that a soothsayer had warned him of that date.

The conspirators believed that by removing the dictator they were saving the Republic. They achieved the opposite: a civil war broke out, won by Caesar's heirs, and it ended with his great-nephew Octavian becoming Augustus, the first emperor. The Roman Republic did not return.

title: The first liquid-fuel rocket
headline: In 1926, Robert Goddard launched from a cabbage field a rocket that opened the road to space.
story:
On March 16, 1926, at an aunt's farm in Auburn, Massachusetts, the physicist Robert Goddard fired a small rocket fueled by gasoline and liquid oxygen. It flew for 2.5 seconds, reached 12 meters in height and landed 56 meters away. It seemed like little.

But it was the first time a rocket used liquid fuel, the technique that allows thrust to be regulated and that every space launcher uses today. The press had mocked Goddard for suggesting that a rocket could work in a vacuum. Decades later, NASA gave his name to one of its major centers.

title: The Kingdom of Italy is proclaimed
headline: In 1861, the first Italian parliament declared Victor Emmanuel II king of an Italy united at last — except for Rome and Venetia.
story:
On March 17, 1861, the parliament meeting in Turin passed the law proclaiming the Kingdom of Italy and granting Victor Emmanuel II, king of Sardinia-Piedmont, the title of king of Italy 'by the grace of God and the will of the nation'. It capped a decade of wars, plebiscites and Garibaldi's campaign, which in 1860 had conquered the south with his 'Thousand' volunteers.

Unification was not complete: Venetia was still in Austrian hands and Rome under the pope, protected by France. Italy would take them in 1866 and 1870. The new state was also born with vast inequalities between an industrial north and an agrarian south that would shape its history.

title: The first spacewalk
headline: In 1965, the cosmonaut Alexei Leonov left his craft and floated in the vacuum for twelve minutes.
story:
On March 18, 1965, from the Soviet spacecraft Voskhod 2, Alexei Leonov opened an airlock and became the first person to venture into open space, tethered to the capsule only by a five-meter cable. He was outside for about twelve minutes.

It nearly became a tragedy: the suit swelled so much in the vacuum that Leonov could not fit back through the hatch and had to let air out, at the risk of decompression sickness. Then the automatic reentry system failed and the craft landed in a snowy forest in the Urals, where the crew spent two nights surrounded by wolves until they were rescued.

title: The Constitution of Cádiz, "la Pepa"
headline: In 1812, the parliament meeting in Cádiz approved Spain's first constitution.
story:
On March 19, 1812, while most of Spain was occupied by Napoleon's troops, the deputies gathered in Cádiz proclaimed a constitution. As it fell on the feast of Saint Joseph (San José), it was nicknamed "la Pepa".

It established national sovereignty, the separation of powers, a suffrage broad for the time, freedom of the press and equality before the law, though it kept Catholicism as the only religion. Ferdinand VII repealed it on returning to the throne in 1814, and its history was a seesaw of restorations and abolitions. Even so, it marked the birth of constitutionalism in Spain and served as a model in Europe and Spanish America.

title: 'Uncle Tom's Cabin' is published
headline: In 1852, Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel appeared and stirred the conscience against slavery.
story:
On March 20, 1852, 'Uncle Tom's Cabin', by Harriet Beecher Stowe, was published in book form, after appearing in installments in an abolitionist newspaper. It told, in stark terms, the suffering of enslaved people in the American South.

It was a huge success: hundreds of thousands of copies in a year and translations into dozens of languages. It strengthened the abolitionist movement in the North and outraged the South, which accused it of slander. It is said that Abraham Lincoln, on receiving the author during the war, told her half in jest that she was "the little woman who started this great war".

title: The Sharpeville massacre
headline: In 1960, South African police fired on a peaceful protest and killed 69 people.
story:
On March 21, 1960, in the town of Sharpeville, near Johannesburg, thousands of Black people gathered without their passbooks outside a police station to protest the "pass laws", which restricted their movement under the apartheid regime. The police opened fire on the crowd: 69 dead, many shot in the back, and about 180 wounded.

The massacre triggered a wave of international condemnation, the banning of the African National Congress and its shift to armed struggle. Decades later, the United Nations declared March 21 the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination.

title: The Lumières project film for the first time
headline: In 1895, the Lumière brothers showed a film projected onto a screen, in private.
story:
On March 22, 1895, at a session before the Society for the Encouragement of National Industry in Paris, Louis and Auguste Lumière projected 'Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory', about 46 seconds of workers coming out of a gate. Others had already recorded moving images, but to be viewed one at a time through a peephole; the Lumières projected them for an audience.

The first paying screening, at the Salon Indien of the Grand Café, came on December 28 of that year and is usually taken as the birth of cinema as a spectacle. Within a few years there were theaters all over the world.

title: The Enabling Act of 1933
headline: In 1933, the Reichstag passed the law that gave Hitler power to govern without parliament: the end of German democracy.
story:
On March 23, 1933, with the SA surrounding the building and the communist deputies already arrested or in flight, the Reichstag passed the Enabling Act. It allowed Hitler's government to enact laws — even ones contrary to the constitution — without going through parliament or the president.

Only the Social Democrats voted against it. The law, meant to last four years, was renewed again and again and became the legal basis of the Nazi dictatorship: within months the other parties and the trade unions were banned. It was, on paper, a legal end to the Weimar Republic.

title: Koch identifies the tuberculosis bacillus
headline: In 1882, Robert Koch announced that he had found the microbe causing the disease that killed the most people.
story:
On March 24, 1882, before the Berlin Physiological Society, the physician Robert Koch presented the evidence that a bacillus, now called 'Mycobacterium tuberculosis', was the cause of tuberculosis. The disease was then killing one in seven people in Europe.

Koch had developed methods to stain, culture and photograph bacteria that became the standard of microbiology. Identifying the germ opened the door to diagnosis, hygiene measures and, decades later, to a vaccine and antibiotics. March 24 is now World Tuberculosis Day.

title: The Treaty of Rome is signed
headline: In 1957, six countries created the European Economic Community, the seed of the European Union.
story:
On March 25, 1957, on the Capitoline Hill in Rome, the representatives of France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg signed the treaties creating the European Economic Community and the European Atomic Energy Community.

The immediate aim was a common market with no internal tariffs and free movement of goods, people, services and capital. The deeper one was to tie the European economies together — above all France and Germany — so tightly that another war between them would be unthinkable. Those six countries have grown into a Union of 27, with a single currency in most of them.

title: Peace between Egypt and Israel
headline: In 1979, Egypt became the first Arab country to sign peace with Israel.
story:
On March 26, 1979, in the gardens of the White House, Egyptian President Anwar Sadat and Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin signed a peace treaty, with US President Jimmy Carter as mediator. It ended the state of war that had lasted since 1948 and returned to Egypt the Sinai Peninsula, occupied by Israel since 1967.

Sadat and Begin had already shared the Nobel Peace Prize. But the agreement isolated Egypt in the Arab world for years, and in 1981 Sadat was assassinated by Islamist soldiers who blamed him precisely for that peace.

title: The Los Rodeos disaster, in Tenerife
headline: In 1977, two Boeing 747s collided on the runway at Tenerife: 583 dead, the worst disaster in aviation.
story:
On March 27, 1977, a bomb at Gran Canaria airport diverted many flights to the small airfield of Los Rodeos, in Tenerife, which became saturated. In thick fog and with no ground radar, a KLM 747 began its takeoff run while a Pan Am 747 was still taxiing on the same runway in the opposite direction.

The planes collided at high speed. 583 people died; only 61 survived, all from the Pan Am aircraft. The investigation identified a chain of communication failures and the pressure of schedules. The accident changed radio and cockpit-coordination procedures worldwide.

title: The Three Mile Island nuclear accident
headline: In 1979, a Pennsylvania plant suffered a partial reactor meltdown with almost no casualties, but an enormous impact.
story:
In the early hours of March 28, 1979, at the Three Mile Island plant near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, a failure in the cooling system, made worse by operators who misread the indicators, left the core of reactor 2 exposed, and it partially melted.

The containment held and the releases of radioactivity outside were small; no clear effects on the health of the population have been shown. But the confusion, the evacuations and the image of the accident brought nuclear power in the United States to a halt: for decades no new plant was ordered.

title: The Mariner 10 probe flies past Mercury
headline: In 1974, a spacecraft visited Mercury for the first time, the planet closest to the Sun.
story:
On March 29, 1974, the US probe Mariner 10 passed about 700 km from the surface of Mercury and sent back the first close-up photos of a world full of craters, similar to the Moon. It had used the gravity of Venus to get there, the first time that "gravity assist" technique was used, now routine.

Mariner 10 flew past Mercury three times in 1974 and 1975, but could map less than half the planet. There was no other visit until the MESSENGER probe, which entered orbit in 2011.

title: The United States buys Alaska
headline: In 1867, Washington bought Alaska from Russia for $7.2 million; the press called it madness.
story:
On March 30, 1867, US Secretary of State William Seward signed with the Russian ambassador the purchase of Alaska: 1.5 million km² for $7.2 million, about two cents per hectare. Russia wanted to sell a distant territory that was hard to defend; the United States hesitated, and many newspapers spoke of "Seward's folly" or "Seward's icebox".

The joke did not last long. In the following decades gold was discovered and, later, enormous reserves of oil and gas, along with a key strategic value facing Russia. Alaska has been a state of the Union since 1959.

title: The Eiffel Tower is inaugurated
headline: In 1889, Paris's iron tower opened — attacked by many artists and now the symbol of the city.
story:
On March 31, 1889, Gustave Eiffel climbed the 1,710 steps of his tower to place the French flag at the top: 300 meters of iron, the tallest structure in the world for 41 years. It had been built in a little over two years as a monumental gateway to the World's Fair marking the centenary of the Revolution.

A group of writers and artists signed a protest against that "useless and monstrous" column of metal. It was due to be dismantled in 1909, but its usefulness as a radio antenna saved it. Today about seven million people visit it a year.

title: The Royal Air Force is born
headline: In 1918, Britain created the world's first air force independent of the army and navy.
story:
On April 1, 1918, in the middle of the First World War, Britain merged the army's air corps and the navy's into a new, separate service: the Royal Air Force. It was born with more than 20,000 aircraft and 300,000 personnel, the largest air force of the time.

The idea that military aviation deserved its own command, rather than being an appendage of the other services, later spread to almost every country. The RAF had its decisive moment in 1940, when its fighters held off the Luftwaffe in the Battle of Britain and prevented a German invasion.

title: Argentina lands in the Falklands
headline: In 1982, the Argentine occupation of the Falkland Islands set off a war with Britain.
story:
On April 2, 1982, Argentine troops landed in the Falkland Islands and took the capital, Stanley, against light resistance from the small British garrison. The military junta ruling Argentina, worn down and with the economy in ruins, was seeking a patriotic coup over an archipelago it has claimed since 1833.

Britain, with Margaret Thatcher in charge, sent a fleet 13,000 km away. The war lasted 74 days and ended with the Argentine surrender on June 14. About 650 Argentines, 255 Britons and 3 islanders died. The defeat hastened the fall of the Argentine dictatorship.

title: The first call from a mobile phone
headline: In 1973, a Motorola engineer made a call on the street from a phone weighing over a kilo.
story:
On April 3, 1973, on a New York sidewalk, Martin Cooper, an engineer at Motorola, pulled out a prototype portable telephone — about 25 centimeters, more than a kilo, half an hour of battery — and called a rival at Bell Labs to tell him he was doing it from a real handheld phone, not from a car.

It took a decade for a very expensive commercial model to reach the market, and another for mobiles to become pocket-sized objects. Today there are more mobile lines than people on the planet, and the phone has become a camera, a computer and the key to almost everything.

title: The North Atlantic Treaty is signed
headline: In 1949, NATO was born, the military alliance that defined the Western bloc in the Cold War.
story:
On April 4, 1949, twelve countries of North America and Western Europe signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington and created NATO. The central clause, Article 5, states that an armed attack against one member will be considered an attack against all.

The aim was to deter the Soviet Union from expanding across Europe after the Second World War. In response, the Eastern bloc formed the Warsaw Pact in 1955. NATO survived the end of the Cold War, expanded eastward, and has invoked Article 5 only once: after the attacks of September 11, 2001.

title: The eruption of Tambora
headline: In 1815, the largest volcanic eruption in recent history cooled the planet and ruined harvests.
story:
On April 5, 1815, the volcano Tambora, on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa, began an eruption that peaked a few days later with the most powerful explosion recorded in historical times. It was heard 2,000 km away. About 70,000 people died from the eruption itself, the tsunamis and the ensuing famine.

The volcano threw so much ash and sulfur into the atmosphere that the global temperature fell, and 1816 became "the year without a summer": frosts in July in Europe and North America, poor harvests, hunger and epidemics. That gloomy weather is believed to have inspired Mary Shelley's 'Frankenstein'.

title: The first modern Olympic Games
headline: In 1896, Games opened in Athens that revived the Olympic idea after 1,500 years.
story:
On April 6, 1896, in a marble stadium rebuilt in Athens, before some 60,000 spectators, the first Olympic Games of the modern era opened. They were the project of the French educator Pierre de Coubertin, convinced that sport could educate and bring nations together.

About 240 athletes took part, all men, from fourteen countries, in events such as athletics, gymnastics, fencing and swimming. The local hero was Spyridon Louis, a Greek water carrier who won the marathon, a race invented for the occasion in homage to the legend of the soldier of Marathon. Since then the Games have been held every four years, except during the world wars.

title: The Rwandan genocide begins
headline: In 1994, in a hundred days about 800,000 people were killed, most of them ethnic Tutsi.
story:
On April 6, 1994, the plane of the Rwandan president was shot down over the capital, Kigali. From the next day on, Hutu militias and part of the army and administration set in motion a plan of extermination against the Tutsi minority and moderate Hutus.

Over about a hundred days, with machetes and house-by-house lists, around 800,000 people were killed, according to the most cited estimates. The UN had troops in the country but received no mandate or means to intervene. The killing ended only when a Tutsi rebel army took power. It is one of the fastest and most documented genocides in history.

title: The finding of the Venus de Milo
headline: In 1820, a Greek peasant dug up on the island of Milos one of the most famous sculptures in the world.
story:
On April 8, 1820, a farmer named Yorgos Kentrotas found, while moving a wall on his land on the island of Milos, a marble statue broken in two: a female figure almost two meters tall, without arms, identified with the goddess Aphrodite (Venus to the Romans).

French officers bought it and took it to Paris, where the Louvre has displayed it since 1821. It is estimated to have been carved around 130–100 BC. The arms have never been found, and it is not known for certain what it held. Its fame today owes much to the Louvre's campaign to present it as the summit of Greek art just after it had lost other pieces.

title: Lee surrenders at Appomattox
headline: In 1865, the surrender of General Lee effectively ended the American Civil War.
story:
On April 9, 1865, in a house in the village of Appomattox Court House, Virginia, the Confederate general Robert E. Lee met the Union general Ulysses S. Grant and signed the surrender of his army, surrounded and out of supplies. Although other Confederate forces remained, that surrender marked the real end of the war.

Grant offered generous terms: the soldiers could go home with their horses and would not be tried for treason. Four years of war had left about 620,000 dead. Five days later, Abraham Lincoln was assassinated.

title: The Titanic sails from Southampton
headline: In 1912, the largest ocean liner in the world set out on a maiden voyage it would never finish.
story:
On April 10, 1912, the RMS Titanic left the English port of Southampton bound for New York on its maiden voyage, with about 2,200 people aboard. It was 269 meters long, had a swimming pool and a gym, and the press called it "practically unsinkable".

Four nights later it struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic and sank in less than three hours. About 1,500 people died, largely because the lifeboats could carry only half the passengers. The disaster forced changes to international rules: boats for everyone, a permanent radio watch and an iceberg patrol.

title: The liberation of Buchenwald
headline: In 1945, American troops entered one of the largest Nazi concentration camps.
story:
On April 11, 1945, units of the US army reached Buchenwald, near Weimar, Germany. Days earlier, as the Allies advanced, the prisoners had partly taken control of the camp. The soldiers found about 21,000 survivors in extreme conditions.

More than 250,000 people passed through Buchenwald from 1937 — political prisoners, Jews, Roma, Soviet prisoners of war — and about 56,000 died there. General Eisenhower ordered that soldiers, journalists and politicians visit it, and that the population of the neighboring towns be made to walk through it, so that no one could deny what had happened.

title: Gagarin, the first human in space
headline: In 1961, the Soviet Yuri Gagarin circled the Earth in 108 minutes.
story:
On April 12, 1961, the spacecraft Vostok 1, with Yuri Gagarin aboard, lifted off from Baikonur, completed one orbit of the Earth and returned after 108 minutes. Gagarin, a 27-year-old pilot and the son of peasants, became the first human being to go into space.

The flight was automatic — it was feared that weightlessness would incapacitate the pilot — and Gagarin ejected at 7 km up to land by parachute, a fact the USSR hid for a time because of the rules for certifying records. The success was a blow to the United States in the middle of the space race and pushed Kennedy to set the goal of the Moon. April 12 is celebrated as Cosmonautics Day.

title: "Houston, we've had a problem"
headline: In 1970, an explosion aboard Apollo 13 turned a trip to the Moon into a fight to get back alive.
story:
On April 13, 1970, when Apollo 13 was 320,000 km from Earth, an oxygen tank exploded and damaged the service module. The three astronauts — Lovell, Swigert and Haise — had to abandon the Moon landing and use the lunar module as a lifeboat.

For four days, with little power, rationed water, cold and dangerous levels of carbon dioxide, the crew and ground control improvised solutions, such as an air filter made of cardboard and tape. The capsule splashed down safely on April 17. NASA called it "a successful failure".

title: The Spanish Second Republic is proclaimed
headline: In 1931, after local elections, King Alfonso XIII left Spain and the Republic was established.
story:
On April 12, 1931, municipal elections were held that republican candidates won clearly in the big cities. The reading was political: if the capitals rejected the monarchy, the regime was finished. On April 14 the Republic was proclaimed in several town halls and, that same night, Alfonso XIII left the country without abdicating.

The Second Republic undertook deep reforms — women's suffrage, public schooling, land reform, statutes of autonomy — in a deeply divided country hit by the economic crisis. It lasted until the Civil War of 1936–1939 and the Franco dictatorship.

title: The Titanic sinks
headline: In the early hours of April 15, 1912, the Titanic vanished beneath the Atlantic with about 1,500 people.
story:
At 11:40 p.m. on April 14, 1912, the Titanic grazed an iceberg that opened a leak along several compartments. In two hours and forty minutes, the ship broke apart and sank. It was 2:20 a.m. on April 15.

Of the roughly 2,200 people aboard, about 700 survived. There were not enough boats, many were launched half full, and the water was below two degrees. The nearest ship took hours to arrive. The wreck became a cultural symbol of technological hubris and class inequality. The remains were not located until 1985, at almost 4,000 meters down.

title: Hofmann discovers the effects of LSD
headline: In 1943, a Swiss chemist was accidentally poisoned and described an LSD trip for the first time.
story:
On April 16, 1943, in the Sandoz laboratories in Basel, the chemist Albert Hofmann was resynthesizing a substance he had made five years earlier, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD-25). He apparently absorbed a tiny amount through his skin and had to go home, dizzy, seeing shapes and colors with his eyes closed.

Three days later he tried a controlled dose and had a far more intense episode; he rode home on his bicycle, a day remembered as "Bicycle Day". LSD was studied for years in psychiatry before being banned in the 1960s as recreational use spread. Today it is being researched again to treat depression and addiction.

title: The Bay of Pigs invasion
headline: In 1961, a force of Cuban exiles backed by the CIA failed in an attempt to overthrow Castro.
story:
On April 17, 1961, about 1,400 Cuban exiles, trained and armed by the CIA, landed at the Bay of Pigs, on the south coast of Cuba, hoping to spark an uprising against Fidel Castro's government. President Kennedy had inherited the plan and authorized it while cutting back US air support.
