The Cuban army defeated them in three days: more than a hundred dead and about 1,200 prisoners, whom Cuba later exchanged for food and medicine. The fiasco humiliated Washington, drew Cuba closer to the Soviet Union, and was one of the direct precursors of the 1962 missile crisis.

title: The San Francisco earthquake
headline: In 1906, a quake and the fire that followed destroyed much of the city of San Francisco.
story:
At 5:12 a.m. on April 18, 1906, an earthquake with an estimated magnitude of around 7.9 shook the California coast along the San Andreas Fault. In San Francisco, entire buildings collapsed, but the greatest damage was caused by fires: broken water mains left firefighters without resources for days.

The fire razed about 500 blocks of the center. Official figures of the time spoke of about 700 dead, but historians estimate more than 3,000. Close to half the population was left homeless. The city was rebuilt quickly, and the disaster spurred the modern study of seismology.

title: Lexington and Concord: the American Revolution begins
headline: In 1775, the first shots between militiamen and British troops began the US war of independence.
story:
In the early hours of April 19, 1775, a British column left Boston to seize weapons from the rebel colonists at Concord, Massachusetts. Warned by riders such as Paul Revere, militiamen stood on the green at Lexington. Someone fired — it was never known who — and eight colonists fell.

At Concord and during the British retreat toward Boston, the militiamen harassed the troops from behind walls and trees and inflicted hundreds of casualties. That day, with no formal declaration, began the war that would lead to the independence of the Thirteen Colonies in 1783.

title: The Curies isolate radium
headline: In 1902, Marie and Pierre Curie obtained a pure sample of radium after years of processing tons of ore.
story:
On April 20, 1902, Marie Curie managed to isolate a decigram of pure radium chloride and measure the element's atomic weight for the first time. To get there, she and her husband Pierre had processed several tons of pitchblende for four years in an unheated shed in Paris, stirring cauldrons with an iron rod.

Radium glowed in the dark and gave off heat: tangible proof of radioactivity, a new phenomenon. Marie Curie received two Nobel Prizes, in Physics and in Chemistry, the only person honored in two different sciences. She died in 1934 from a bone-marrow disease linked to her long exposure to radiation.

title: The legendary founding of Rome
headline: On April 21, the Romans celebrated the birth of their city, set by tradition in 753 BC.
story:
Legend has it that on April 21, 753 BC, Romulus traced with a plow the sacred perimeter of a city on the Palatine Hill and killed his twin brother Remus for mocking that boundary. Romulus and Remus, according to the myth, were sons of the god Mars, had been abandoned in the Tiber and had been suckled by a she-wolf.

Archaeology does confirm settlements on the hills of the Tiber around the 8th century BC. Rome celebrated the festival of the Parilia on that day, and even today the city commemorates its "Natale di Roma" every April 21 with historical reenactment parades.

title: The first Earth Day
headline: In 1970, twenty million Americans demonstrated for the environment on the same day.
story:
On April 22, 1970, some twenty million people in the United States took part in marches, talks and clean-ups to demand clean air and water. It had been called by Senator Gaylord Nelson after seeing the outrage over a large oil spill off the coast of California.

That mobilization, one of the largest in the country's history, pushed through that same year the creation of the Environmental Protection Agency and laws on air and water. Earth Day went global in 1990 and is now marked in nearly 200 countries.

title: Cervantes and Shakespeare die
headline: April 23, 1616, is the date tradition links to the deaths of literature's two giants.
story:
Miguel de Cervantes, author of 'Don Quixote', was buried in Madrid on April 23, 1616 (he had probably died on the 22nd). William Shakespeare died in Stratford on that same April 23, though by the Julian calendar England still used, so the dates do not actually coincide.

The coincidence, real or not, has turned April 23 into World Book Day, declared by UNESCO in 1995. It was rounded out that day as a tribute also to the Peruvian Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, who likewise died in 1616.

title: The Hubble telescope is launched
headline: In 1990, an observatory the size of a bus went into space to see the universe with no atmosphere in the way.
story:
On April 24, 1990, the shuttle Discovery placed the Hubble Space Telescope into orbit, about 540 km up. Being above the atmosphere, which distorts and blocks part of the light, it promised sharper images than ever.

The start was a disaster: the main mirror was badly polished and the photos came out blurry. In 1993, astronauts fitted corrective "glasses" on a repair mission, and Hubble began delivering historic images: the depth of the universe, the age of the cosmos, black holes, the atmospheres of other planets. It is still working more than three decades later.

title: The Carnation Revolution
headline: In 1974, an almost bloodless military coup ended nearly half a century of dictatorship in Portugal.
story:
In the early hours of April 25, 1974, young officers of the Portuguese army, fed up with an endless colonial war in Africa and with the Estado Novo dictatorship, rose up and seized the key points of Lisbon. The population took to the streets to support them, and a florist handed out red carnations that the soldiers put in their rifle barrels.

The regime gave up almost without a shot. In the following months Portugal became a democracy and granted independence to its colonies. April 25 is a national holiday, "Freedom Day".

title: The Chernobyl disaster
headline: In 1986, the explosion of a reactor in Ukraine caused the worst nuclear accident in history.
story:
In the early hours of April 26, 1986, during a poorly planned safety test, reactor number 4 at the Chernobyl plant, in Soviet Ukraine, suffered an uncontrollable power surge and exploded. The graphite burned for days and threw up a large radioactive cloud that reached half of Europe.

The USSR was slow to acknowledge the accident and to evacuate the city of Pripyat. Dozens of people died immediately, and it is estimated that thousands more died from long-term cancers. An exclusion zone of about 30 km was created and is still in force. The reactor is now covered by an enormous metal structure.

title: South Africa votes without distinction of race
headline: In 1994, millions of Black South Africans voted for the first time and carried Mandela to the presidency.
story:
On April 27, 1994, South Africa held its first general elections with universal suffrage, without the racial restrictions of apartheid. At many polling stations the queues lasted hours; for much of the population it was the first time they had ever voted.

The African National Congress won, and Nelson Mandela, who four years earlier had still been in prison, became president. The country adopted a constitution with broad guarantees and a Truth and Reconciliation Commission to address the crimes of the past without falling into revenge. April 27 is South Africa's Freedom Day.

title: The death of Mussolini
headline: In 1945, Italian partisans captured and shot Benito Mussolini as he tried to flee to Switzerland.
story:
On April 27, 1945, with the Allies about to take northern Italy, partisans stopped Benito Mussolini near Lake Como. He was fleeing in disguise in a German military coat, along with his mistress, Clara Petacci. The next day, April 28, they were shot.

The bodies were taken to Milan and hung upside down in the Piazzale Loreto, where months earlier executed partisans had been displayed. The scene, photographed and spread around the world, marked the end of Italian fascism. Two days later, Hitler took his own life in Berlin.

title: Joan of Arc reaches Orléans
headline: In 1429, a seventeen-year-old peasant girl entered the besieged city and changed the course of the Hundred Years' War.
story:
On April 29, 1429, Joan of Arc entered Orléans, besieged by the English, with a supply convoy. She said she heard the voices of saints ordering her to drive the English out of France and crown the Dauphin, Charles. Against all odds, she had convinced the court to put her at the head of the troops.

In nine days, the French army lifted the siege of Orléans. More victories followed, and the coronation of Charles VII at Reims. A year later, Joan was captured, sold to the English, tried for heresy and burned at Rouen in 1431, at the age of nineteen. The Church declared her a saint in 1920.

title: The fall of Saigon
headline: In 1975, tanks from the North rolled into Saigon and ended the Vietnam War.
story:
On April 30, 1975, North Vietnamese troops took Saigon, the capital of the South, and its government surrendered. Hours earlier, American helicopters had hastily evacuated the last embassy staff and thousands of South Vietnamese from rooftops, in chaotic scenes that traveled the world.

So ended a war of almost twenty years that had cost more than a million Vietnamese lives and about 58,000 American soldiers, and that had divided US society like few others. Vietnam was reunified under a communist regime, and Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City.

title: The origin of May Day
headline: In 1886, a strike in the United States for the eight-hour day gave rise to International Workers' Day.
story:
On May 1, 1886, some 350,000 workers in the United States joined a general strike demanding the eight-hour day. In Chicago, the epicenter of the protest, tension exploded days later in Haymarket Square: a bomb killed several police officers, and the crackdown that followed sent four anarchist labor organizers to the gallows after a heavily criticized trial.

In memory of those events, the international labor congress of 1889 set May 1 as a day of struggle for workers' rights. Today it is a holiday in most of the world. Curiously, in the United States itself Labor Day is celebrated in September.

title: The Dos de Mayo uprising
headline: In 1808, the people of Madrid rose against Napoleon's troops and began the Peninsular War.
story:
On May 2, 1808, seeing French troops taking the last members of the royal family out of Madrid, a crowd gathered outside the Royal Palace shouting "they're taking him away!". The revolt spread through the city and street fighting broke out, with a famous stand at the Monteleón artillery park, where the captains Daoíz and Velarde held out.

The reprisals were immediate and bloody: that night and the following dawn there were mass executions, which Goya immortalized in 'The Third of May 1808'. The uprising spread across Spain and began six years of war against the Napoleonic occupation.

title: The Polish Constitution of 1791
headline: In 1791, Poland-Lithuania adopted the first codified national constitution in Europe.
story:
On May 3, 1791, the parliament of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth adopted a constitution that separated powers, strengthened the monarchy against noble anarchy and extended rights to the middle class. It was the first written constitution in Europe and the second in the world after that of the United States.

It lasted little more than a year: the neighboring powers — Russia, Prussia and Austria — fearing a strong, reformed Polish state, invaded the country and divided it among themselves. Poland vanished from the map until 1918. May 3 is now a Polish national holiday.

title: Thatcher, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom
headline: In 1979, Margaret Thatcher became the first woman to head the British government.
story:
On May 4, 1979, after the Conservative Party won the election, Margaret Thatcher moved into Downing Street. She was the first woman to lead the government of a major Western country and would end up serving the longest continuous term of any British prime minister in the 20th century: eleven years.

Her program — privatizations, curbing union power, tax cuts, controlling inflation — transformed the British economy and marked, together with Ronald Reagan, a conservative turn across the West. She was as admired as she was hated; she was nicknamed "the Iron Lady".

title: Napoleon dies on Saint Helena
headline: In 1821, Napoleon Bonaparte died in exile on a remote island in the South Atlantic.
story:
On May 5, 1821, Napoleon Bonaparte died at the age of 51 at Longwood House, a damp house on the island of Saint Helena, where the British had exiled him after the defeat at Waterloo in 1815. He had spent six years under guard in one of the most isolated places on the planet.

The autopsy attributed the death to stomach cancer, like his father's, though for decades a theory of arsenic poisoning circulated. In 1840, France repatriated his remains and buried them with honors at Les Invalides in Paris, where they still lie.

title: The Hindenburg fire
headline: In 1937, the world's largest airship burned as it landed in the United States, before cameras and microphones.
story:
On May 6, 1937, the German airship Hindenburg, 245 meters long and filled with hydrogen, was maneuvering to moor at the Lakehurst base in New Jersey after crossing the Atlantic. In seconds it caught fire at the tail and fell wrapped in flames. Thirty-six of the 97 people aboard died.

A radio reporter narrated the scene live through sobs — "Oh, the humanity!" — and the footage traveled the world. The spark that started it was never fully explained, but the disaster ended the era of the great passenger airships at a stroke: the future belonged to the airplane.

title: Beethoven's Ninth premieres
headline: In 1824, an already deaf Beethoven conducted the premiere of his Ninth Symphony, with the 'Ode to Joy'.
story:
On May 7, 1824, in Vienna, Ludwig van Beethoven's Symphony No. 9 in D minor premiered, the first great symphony to include a choir and soloists singing, set to Schiller's 'Ode to Joy'. Beethoven, completely deaf, beat time alongside the conductor.

It is said that when it ended he was still facing away from the audience, unable to hear the ovation, and a singer had to turn him around to see the applause. The main theme of the final movement is today the anthem of the European Union, and the score is inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World register.

title: The end of the war in Europe
headline: In 1945, Victory in Europe Day was celebrated: Nazi Germany had signed its unconditional surrender.
story:
On May 8, 1945, the unconditional surrender of Germany took effect, signed the day before in Reims and ratified that night in Berlin. Nearly six years of war in Europe were ending, war that had left tens of millions dead and a continent in ruins.

There were scenes of euphoria in London, Paris and New York. In the Soviet Union, because of the time difference, the official date is May 9, which is still Russia's great military holiday. The war would continue in the Pacific until Japan's surrender in September.

title: The Schuman Declaration
headline: In 1950, France proposed placing coal and steel under a common authority: the seed of the European Union.
story:
On May 9, 1950, the French foreign minister, Robert Schuman, read a brief declaration proposing that France and Germany pool their production of coal and steel — the raw materials of war — under a supranational authority open to other countries.

The idea, mainly the work of Jean Monnet, aimed to make war between Europeans "not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible". In 1951 the European Coal and Steel Community was born, the first step of the integration that would lead to the European Union. May 9 is celebrated as Europe Day.

title: The railroad that joined the United States
headline: In 1869, a golden spike completed the first train line to cross North America coast to coast.
story:
On May 10, 1869, at Promontory Summit, Utah, the tracks of two companies — one advancing from the east, the other from the west — met. A ceremonial golden spike was driven, and the news was sent by telegraph to the whole country, which celebrated with gun salutes and bells.

The journey between New York and California went from months to less than a week. The work was done mostly by Chinese and Irish immigrants in brutal conditions. The transcontinental railroad accelerated the settlement of the West and was devastating for the Indigenous peoples of the Great Plains.

title: The Indian Rebellion of 1857 breaks out
headline: In 1857, a mutiny of Indian troops against the British Company reached Delhi and shook the Empire.
story:
On May 10, 1857, at Meerut, the sepoys — Indian soldiers in the service of the British East India Company — mutinied. The spark was a rumor about cartridges greased with cow and pig fat, offensive to Hindus and Muslims alike, but the discontent had deep roots. The next day the rebels entered Delhi and proclaimed the aged Mughal Bahadur Shah II emperor.

The rebellion spread across northern India and was put down with enormous violence by both sides. As a result, in 1858 Britain dissolved the Company and took direct rule over India, which would last until 1947.

title: The Berlin Blockade ends
headline: In 1949, the USSR lifted the siege of West Berlin after almost a year of Allied airlift.
story:
On May 12, 1949, the Soviet Union reopened the roads and railways to West Berlin, which it had blockaded in June 1948 to force the Western powers out of the city, deep inside the Soviet zone.

Instead of withdrawing, the United States and Britain organized a colossal airlift: for almost eleven months, planes landed every few minutes with coal, food and medicine for more than two million people. The blockade, a Soviet failure, accelerated the division of Germany into two states, which was formalized that same year.

title: The apparitions of Fátima
headline: In 1917, three Portuguese shepherd children said they had seen the Virgin; the site is now a major pilgrimage center.
story:
On May 13, 1917, three children herding near the village of Fátima, in Portugal, said that a "luminous lady" had appeared to them and asked them to return on the 13th of the following months. The visits were repeated and drew growing crowds.

On October 13, before tens of thousands of people, many witnesses described a strange solar phenomenon, the "miracle of the sun". The Catholic Church recognized the apparitions in 1930. Two of the three visionaries died soon after in the influenza epidemic of 1918–1920; the sanctuary of Fátima now receives millions of pilgrims a year.

title: Jenner tests the first vaccine
headline: In 1796, Edward Jenner inoculated a boy with cowpox to protect him from smallpox.
story:
On May 14, 1796, the English country doctor Edward Jenner took pus from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid and introduced it through two small cuts into the arm of James Phipps, an eight-year-old boy. Weeks later he inoculated him with smallpox and the boy did not fall ill.

Jenner was building on the popular observation that people who milked cows rarely caught the dreaded smallpox. The word "vaccine" comes precisely from 'vacca', cow. His method spread around the world and, almost two centuries later, in 1980, smallpox became the first and only human disease to be eradicated.

title: Kepler and the third law of planetary motion
headline: In 1618, Johannes Kepler found the mathematical relationship between a planet's distance from the Sun and its period.
story:
On May 15, 1618, according to his own notes, Johannes Kepler found the formula he had been seeking for years: the square of the time a planet takes to orbit the Sun is proportional to the cube of its mean distance. It is the third of his laws of planetary motion.

Together with the first two — elliptical orbits and varying speed — this law finally described the Copernican solar system precisely and set the stage for Newton, decades later, to explain all of it with a single cause: gravity.

title: China's Cultural Revolution begins
headline: In 1966, a Communist Party circular launched a decade of political chaos that cost more than a million lives.
story:
On May 16, 1966, the leadership of the Communist Party of China approved a circular, driven by Mao Zedong, calling for the purge of "bourgeois elements" infiltrated into the party, the government, the army and culture. It was the starting shot of the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution.

Millions of young people organized into Red Guards who humiliated and beat teachers, officials and "class enemies", destroyed temples and books, and plunged the country into factional strife. Schools and universities closed for years. It is estimated that between one and two million people died before the process was declared over in 1976, with Mao's death.

title: The Supreme Court bans school segregation
headline: In 1954, the ruling 'Brown v. Board of Education' declared race-separated schools unconstitutional.
story:
On May 17, 1954, the US Supreme Court ruled unanimously in 'Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka' that separating students by race in public schools violated the Constitution, because "separate facilities are inherently unequal".

The decision overturned a doctrine of almost sixty years and gave a decisive boost to the civil rights movement. Its actual enforcement, however, took decades and met fierce resistance in many Southern states.

title: The eruption of Mount St. Helens
headline: In 1980, a volcano in Washington State blew out its north flank in the deadliest and most destructive volcanic eruption in US history.
story:
On May 18, 1980, after weeks of earthquakes and a visible bulging of the mountain, a quake triggered the largest landslide ever recorded: the entire north face of Mount St. Helens collapsed and suddenly uncorked the pressurized magma. The lateral blast leveled 600 km² of forest in minutes.

Fifty-seven people died. An ash column rose 24 km and darkened cities hundreds of kilometers away. The summit lost 400 meters of height. It was a lesson in volcanology observed like no other until then.

title: The execution of Anne Boleyn
headline: In 1536, Henry VIII's second wife was beheaded at the Tower of London on charges of adultery and treason.
story:
On May 19, 1536, Anne Boleyn was beheaded in the courtyard of the Tower of London. Henry VIII had broken with Rome and founded the Church of England in order to marry her; three years later, without the male heir he craved and with a new favorite at court, he had her tried on charges of adultery and incest that almost no historian considers true.

An expert swordsman was brought from Calais to use a sword rather than an axe. The daughter Anne did give Henry, Elizabeth, would reign for 44 years and lead England to its age of greatest splendor.

title: Christopher Columbus dies
headline: In 1506, the navigator who opened Europe's route to America died in Valladolid, forgotten and litigating over his titles.
story:
On May 20, 1506, Christopher Columbus died in Valladolid at the age of 54, surrounded by his family and a few loyal companions. He had made four voyages across the Atlantic since 1492, but he died convinced he had reached the coasts of Asia, not a new continent.

His last years were bitter: the Crown had stripped him of the governorship of the Indies for his disastrous administration, and he was suing to recover the titles and revenues he had been promised. His remains later traveled to Seville, Santo Domingo and Havana, and today Seville Cathedral claims to hold them, though the matter is still disputed.

title: Lindbergh crosses the Atlantic alone
headline: In 1927, Charles Lindbergh landed in Paris after 33 hours of non-stop flight from New York.
story:
On May 21, 1927, at 10:22 p.m., the 'Spirit of St. Louis' touched down at Le Bourget airfield in Paris, before a crowd of more than 100,000 people. It was flown by Charles Lindbergh, a young airmail pilot who had left New York 33 and a half hours earlier, alone, with no radio and fighting off sleep.

Others had already crossed the Atlantic by plane, but never solo and non-stop between New York and Paris. Lindbergh became overnight the most famous man in the world and boosted the public's confidence in commercial aviation.

title: The most powerful earthquake ever recorded
headline: In 1960, a magnitude 9.5 quake shook southern Chile and sent tsunamis across the Pacific.
story:
On May 22, 1960, at 3:11 p.m., an earthquake of approximately magnitude 9.5 — the largest ever measured by instruments — ruptured about 1,000 km of the coast of southern Chile, near Valdivia. The shaking lasted several minutes and sank entire areas of land beneath the sea.

Between 1,000 and 6,000 people died, depending on the source. The tsunami it generated not only razed the Chilean coast: fifteen hours later it killed dozens of people in Hawaii and, almost a day later, just as many in Japan, 17,000 km away. The event spurred the creation of tsunami warning networks across the Pacific Ocean.

title: The Defenestration of Prague
headline: In 1618, nobles threw two imperial governors out of a window and ignited the Thirty Years' War.
story:
On May 23, 1618, a group of Protestant nobles of Bohemia, enraged by the policy of the Catholic emperor, burst into Prague Castle and threw two imperial regents and a secretary out of a window, from about 20 meters up. All three survived — they landed on a heap of manure, according to the most repeated version — but the gesture was a declaration of war.

The conflict that followed, the Thirty Years' War, devastated Central Europe until 1648 and caused millions of deaths, many from hunger and plague. The Peace of Westphalia that ended it laid the foundations of the modern system of sovereign states.

title: The first telegram in history
headline: In 1844, Samuel Morse sent a message between Washington and Baltimore over a copper wire.
story:
On May 24, 1844, from the Supreme Court chamber in Washington, Samuel Morse tapped out on his device a verse from the Bible — "What hath God wrought" — and the message appeared printed in dots and dashes 60 km away, in Baltimore, in an instant.

It was the first public use of the electric telegraph on a real line. Within a few years, cables crossed continents and, in 1866, the bottom of the Atlantic. For the first time, information traveled faster than people: it changed commerce, the press, diplomacy and war.

title: The May Revolution in Buenos Aires
headline: In 1810, the capital of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata removed the viceroy and formed its first local government.
story:
On May 25, 1810, after a week of assemblies in Buenos Aires, an open town council deposed the Spanish viceroy and named a First Junta of local government. The pretext was that, with King Ferdinand VII a prisoner of Napoleon, authority reverted to the people; the underlying reason was the Creole elites' desire for autonomy.

Independence was not yet declared — that would come in 1816 — but the May Revolution is the starting point of the process that gave rise to Argentina and stirred all of Spanish America. May 25 is Argentina's national day.

title: The Dow Jones index is born
headline: In 1896, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was published for the first time, with twelve companies and a value of 40.94 points.
story:
On May 26, 1896, the journalist Charles Dow began publishing in his financial bulletin an average of the share prices of twelve large American industrial companies — railroads, sugar, tobacco, gas — intended as a quick thermometer of the stock market.

That index, the Dow Jones Industrial Average, became Wall Street's most cited benchmark. Of those twelve original companies, none is in the index today; only General Electric held on, with interruptions, until 2018.

title: The Golden Gate Bridge opens
headline: In 1937, San Francisco unveiled its red suspension bridge, the longest in the world for almost three decades.
story:
On May 27, 1937, about 200,000 people walked across the Golden Gate Bridge on its pedestrian opening day; it opened to traffic the next day. With 1,280 meters between towers, it was the longest suspension bridge in the world until 1964.

It was built in a little over four years across a strait with strong currents and frequent fog. Its color, "international orange", was chosen to stand out against the sea and the mist. It is one of the most recognizable symbols of the United States.

title: The Spanish Armada sets sail
headline: In 1588, the great fleet Philip II sent against England left Lisbon on its way to disaster.
story:
On May 28, 1588, about 130 ships with close to 30,000 men set sail from Lisbon for the English Channel. Philip II's plan was to escort the army of Flanders to England to overthrow Elizabeth I and stop English support for the Dutch rebels and for piracy against the Indies.

The campaign failed: the fighting in the Channel, a fireship attack off Calais and, above all, the storms on the return voyage around the British Isles sank or crippled much of the fleet. Fewer than half the ships came back. The myth of the "Invincible Armada" and its defeat shaped the imagination of English ascent and Spanish decline.

title: The fall of Constantinople
headline: In 1453, the Ottomans took Constantinople and ended more than a thousand years of Byzantine Empire.
story:
On May 29, 1453, after 53 days of siege, the troops of the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II successfully stormed the walls of Constantinople. The last emperor, Constantine XI, died fighting. With the city fell the Eastern Roman Empire, direct heir of ancient Rome.

Mehmed turned the cathedral of Hagia Sophia into a mosque and made the city, later called Istanbul, the capital of an empire that would dominate the eastern Mediterranean for centuries. The conquest is often marked as the end of the Middle Ages and a spur for Europe to seek new sea routes to Asia.

title: The first Indianapolis 500
headline: In 1911, the most famous car race in the United States was run for the first time.
story:
On May 30, 1911, the first Indianapolis 500 got underway, on an oval paved with 3.2 million bricks — hence its nickname, "the Brickyard". Forty cars covered 200 laps — 800 kilometers — at an average of about 120 km/h. The winner was Ray Harroun, in a single-seater to which he had fitted a rearview mirror, a novelty that let him race without a riding mechanic.

The race, held every May, became one of the three great fixtures of world motorsport, alongside the 24 Hours of Le Mans and the Monaco Grand Prix.

title: The Johnstown Flood
headline: In 1889, the failure of a dam sent a giant wave over a Pennsylvania town and killed more than 2,000 people.
story:
On May 31, 1889, after days of heavy rain, the South Fork Dam gave way, in the mountains of Pennsylvania, poorly maintained by a recreational club of wealthy people who used it for their private lake. Some 20 million tons of water rushed 22 km down the valley and struck the steel town of Johnstown as a wall several meters high.

2,209 people died. Many victims were trapped against a railroad bridge, where the debris caught fire. The catastrophe generated a huge relief campaign — one of the first major operations of the American Red Cross — and a debate over the liability of the dam's owners that ended without any convictions.

title: CNN goes on air
headline: In 1980, the first television channel devoted to 24-hour news began broadcasting.
story:
On June 1, 1980, the businessman Ted Turner launched the Cable News Network, CNN, from Atlanta. The idea of a channel that did nothing but news, around the clock, sounded absurd; critics nicknamed it the "Chicken Noodle Network".

The Gulf War of 1991, broadcast live from Baghdad, established the model: governments, stock markets and newsrooms around the world began following events in real time. The "CNN effect" — the pressure of immediate images on political decisions — entered the vocabulary, and the 24-hour format was copied in dozens of countries.

title: The coronation of Elizabeth II
headline: In 1953, the coronation of the British queen was the first great world event seen on television.
story:
On June 2, 1953, Elizabeth II was crowned at Westminster Abbey in a ceremony of almost three hours steeped in medieval symbols. At public request, and despite the doubts of the government and the palace, television cameras were allowed in for the first time.

About 20 million people watched in the United Kingdom alone, many on sets bought or rented for the occasion, and tens of millions more around the world. It is often cited as the moment television became a mass medium. Elizabeth II reigned for 70 years, until 2022.

title: The first spacewalk by an American
headline: In 1965, Ed White left the Gemini 4 capsule and floated above the Earth for 21 minutes.
story:
On June 3, 1965, during the Gemini 4 mission, the astronaut Ed White opened the hatch and went out into the vacuum held by a golden tether, pushing himself along with a small compressed-gas gun. It was the first American spacewalk, almost three months after the Soviet Alexei Leonov's.

White enjoyed the experience so much — "it's the saddest moment of my life", he said on being ordered back in — that the maneuver stretched to 21 minutes. These outings would become routine for assembling space stations and repairing satellites such as Hubble.

title: The Tiananmen crackdown
headline: In 1989, the Chinese army crushed weeks of peaceful protests in the center of Beijing.
story:
On the night of June 3–4, 1989, columns of tanks and soldiers moved into Tiananmen Square in Beijing to clear by force the students and workers who had been camped there for six weeks demanding democratic reforms and less corruption. There was gunfire against the crowd on the approach avenues.

The death toll was never known for certain: estimates range from several hundred to more than a thousand. The next day, the image of a lone man standing before a line of tanks traveled the world. In China, the subject is still completely censored.

title: The first UN summit on the environment
headline: In 1972, the Stockholm conference put the environment on the world agenda; it is World Environment Day.
story:
On June 5, 1972, the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment opened in Stockholm, the first major international meeting devoted to the deterioration of the planet: pollution, acid rain, loss of forests, the depletion of resources.

Out of it came a declaration of principles and the seed of the UN Environment Programme. The General Assembly designated June 5 as World Environment Day, now marked in almost every country and used as an anchor date for campaigns and climate commitments.

title: D-Day
headline: In 1944, the Allies landed in Normandy in the largest amphibious operation in history.
story:
In the early hours of June 6, 1944, some 156,000 American, British and Canadian soldiers crossed the English Channel in almost 7,000 ships and landed on five beaches of the Normandy coast, preceded by paratroopers dropped at night. On Omaha Beach, German resistance caused thousands of casualties in a few hours.

By the end of the day, the Allies had established beachheads. It was the start of the liberation of Western Europe: in less than a year, Nazi Germany capitulated. The landing was prepared with years of deception so that the Germans would expect the attack elsewhere.

title: The Treaty of Tordesillas
headline: In 1494, Spain and Portugal divided the undiscovered world with a line drawn across the Atlantic.
story:
On June 7, 1494, in the Castilian town of Tordesillas, the Catholic Monarchs and the king of Portugal signed an agreement to divide the lands "discovered and to be discovered" outside Europe. An imaginary line running north to south, 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands, left whatever lay to the east for Portugal and whatever lay to the west for Castile.

That line explains why Brazil speaks Portuguese and the rest of South America Spanish: the eastern tip of the continent fell within the Portuguese zone. Other European countries never recognized the division, but the treaty shaped Iberian expansion for centuries.

title: '1984' is published
headline: In 1949, George Orwell's novel appeared and gave the world Big Brother and Newspeak.
story:
On June 8, 1949, 'Nineteen Eighty-Four', George Orwell's last novel, was published in London. Orwell was ill with tuberculosis and only months from death. It describes a totalitarian state that watches every gesture of its citizens, rewrites the past and manipulates language to make dissent unthinkable.

From the book came expressions now in common use: "Big Brother", "doublethink", "Newspeak", "Room 101", "thought police". It is read as much as a warning about dictatorships as about surveillance and propaganda in democracies.

title: The suicide of Nero
headline: In AD 68, the death of Nero ended the dynasty that had ruled Rome since Augustus.
story:
On June 9, AD 68, cornered by a revolt of provincial governors and abandoned by his guard and the Senate, which had declared him a public enemy, the emperor Nero took his own life on the outskirts of Rome with the help of a secretary. He is credited with the line "what an artist dies in me!".

Nero was 30 and had been in power for fourteen years. With him the Julio-Claudian dynasty, begun by Augustus, was extinguished. His death opened the "Year of the Four Emperors", a period of civil war that ended only when the general Vespasian founded a new dynasty.

title: The Paris Natural History Museum is founded
headline: In 1793, at the height of the Revolution, the Convention turned the King's Garden into a great public science museum.
story:
On June 10, 1793, a decree of the National Convention turned the old King's Garden — the monarchy's botanical garden and natural history cabinet — into the National Museum of Natural History, now an institution of the Republic. It was run by twelve professor-administrators, each heading one branch: zoology, botany, mineralogy, chemistry, comparative anatomy…

The decree gave it three missions it still keeps: research, teaching and the care of collections. Lamarck, Cuvier and the Geoffroy Saint-Hilaires held its chairs, and much of the nineteenth-century debate on the evolution of species came out of its galleries and laboratories. It was one of the first great science museums built for the specialist and the ordinary visitor alike.

title: Henry VIII marries Catherine of Aragon
headline: In 1509, the new king of England married the daughter of the Catholic Monarchs; the end of that marriage changed history.
story:
On June 11, 1509, shortly after coming to the throne, Henry VIII of England married Catherine of Aragon, daughter of Isabella and Ferdinand and widow of his older brother. The marriage lasted 24 years and produced one surviving daughter, the future Mary I.

With no male heir, Henry sought to annul the union in order to marry Anne Boleyn. The pope's refusal led him to break with Rome, declare himself head of the Church of England and set off the English Reformation, with the dissolution of the monasteries and decades of religious conflict.

title: Anne Frank starts her diary
headline: In 1942, a Jewish girl in Amsterdam received for her birthday the notebook in which she would write one of the world's most-read books.
story:
On June 12, 1942, Anne Frank turned 13, and among her gifts was a red-checked notebook. She began using it as a diary. Less than a month later, her family went into hiding in a secret annex of an office building in Amsterdam to escape Nazi persecution.

She wrote there for two years, until someone betrayed them in August 1944. Anne died at the Bergen-Belsen camp in early 1945. Her father, the only survivor of the family, published the diary in 1947. Translated into more than seventy languages, it has given a face and a voice to millions of victims of the Holocaust.

title: The Pentagon Papers
headline: In 1971, 'The New York Times' began publishing a secret report that exposed the official lies about Vietnam.
story:
On June 13, 1971, 'The New York Times' published the first extracts of an internal, classified Department of Defense study on the Vietnam War. The documents, leaked by the analyst Daniel Ellsberg, showed that successive administrations had expanded the war in secret and had misled Congress and public opinion for years.

The Nixon administration got a judge to halt publication, but the 'Washington Post' continued the series and, within two weeks, the Supreme Court ruled in favor of the press: there was no basis for prior restraint. The case strengthened press freedom and further eroded trust in the US government.

title: The first non-stop flight across the Atlantic
headline: In 1919, Alcock and Brown crossed the ocean by plane, eight years before Lindbergh.
story:
On June 14, 1919, the Britons John Alcock and Arthur Brown took off from Newfoundland, Canada, in a converted Vickers Vimy bomber and, after nearly 16 hours of flight through fog, ice and mechanical trouble, landed nose-down in an Irish bog. They had crossed the Atlantic non-stop for the first time.

Brown had to climb out onto the wing several times in mid-flight to clear ice from the instruments. They won a prize of £10,000 from the 'Daily Mail'. The feat was overshadowed by Lindbergh's in 1927, solo and on a longer, more publicized route.

title: Magna Carta
headline: In 1215, English barons forced King John to accept written limits on his power.
story:
On June 15, 1215, in a meadow on the banks of the Thames called Runnymede, King John of England sealed Magna Carta, a document imposed on him by rebel barons fed up with abusive taxes and arbitrary rule. Among its clauses: no one could be imprisoned or stripped of their possessions "except by the lawful judgment of their equals or by the law of the land".

The king broke it at once and the pope annulled it, but it was reissued several times in the following decades. Over the centuries it became a symbol that even power is subject to the law, and a reference for English and American constitutionalism.

title: Tereshkova, the first woman in space
headline: In 1963, the Soviet Valentina Tereshkova orbited the Earth 48 times in three days.
story:
On June 16, 1963, the spacecraft Vostok 6 put Valentina Tereshkova into orbit, a 26-year-old textile worker and amateur parachutist chosen from hundreds of candidates. She spent almost three days in space and circled the planet 48 times, more than all the American astronauts combined up to that point.

The Soviet Union used the flight as a propaganda coup about the equality of women, but it did not send another into space until 1982. The second woman in orbit, and the first American, was Sally Ride in 1983.

title: The Watergate break-in
headline: In 1972, five men were arrested breaking into the Democratic Party headquarters; two years later Nixon fell.
story:
In the early hours of June 17, 1972, police arrested five men who had broken in to steal documents and plant bugs at the Democratic National Committee headquarters, in the Watergate building in Washington. At first it looked like a minor incident.

The investigation by two 'Washington Post' journalists, with the help of an anonymous source called "Deep Throat", revealed that the espionage came from President Richard Nixon's circle and that the White House had mounted a cover-up. Cornered by the recordings he himself made in the Oval Office, Nixon resigned in August 1974, the only US president to have done so.

title: The Battle of Waterloo
headline: In 1815, Napoleon's defeat near Brussels ended his return to power and a quarter century of wars.
story:
On June 18, 1815, near the Belgian village of Waterloo, Napoleon's army faced the British and allied troops of the Duke of Wellington. For hours the French failed to break the enemy lines; in the late afternoon Blücher's Prussian army arrived and decided the battle.

Napoleon had returned from exile three months earlier and regained the throne of France. After Waterloo he abdicated again and was exiled to Saint Helena. The Napoleonic Wars, which had ravaged Europe since 1803, were over. "Waterloo" became a synonym for final defeat.

title: Juneteenth: freedom reaches Texas
headline: In 1865, Union troops announced in Galveston that enslaved people were free.
story:
On June 19, 1865, a Union general read out in Galveston, Texas, an order informing the population that all enslaved people were free. The Emancipation Proclamation was already two and a half years old, but in Texas, far from the front, it had barely been enforced.

That date, a blend of "June" and "nineteenth", is known as Juneteenth, and African American communities have celebrated it ever since as the real end of slavery. In 2021 it became a US federal holiday.

title: The Tennis Court Oath
headline: In 1789, the deputies of the Third Estate swore not to disband until they had given France a constitution.
story:
On June 20, 1789, the representatives of the Third Estate — the common people — arrived at their meeting hall in Versailles and found it locked by order of the king. They moved to a nearby indoor tennis court and there, almost all of them standing, swore not to disband until they had written a constitution for the kingdom.

It was an open challenge to the absolute authority of Louis XVI. A few weeks later the Bastille would fall. The Tennis Court Oath is considered one of the founding acts of the French Revolution and of modern representative government.

title: The scuttling of the German fleet at Scapa Flow
headline: In 1919, German crews sank their own interned battle fleet in a British base so the Allies could not take it.
story:
On June 21, 1919, at the British naval base of Scapa Flow, off the north of Scotland, the German rear admiral Ludwig von Reuter gave the order to sink the 74 ships of the High Seas Fleet, interned there since the armistice while the Treaty of Versailles was being negotiated. Von Reuter feared the Allies would divide the ships among themselves and believed, from the out-of-date newspapers he received, that the talks had collapsed.

The crews opened the seacocks and hatches and, within a few hours, 52 vessels — among them ten battleships — went to the bottom. It was the greatest loss of warships in a single day in history. The wrecks still lie on the seabed of the firth; some were later raised for scrap.

title: The invasion of the Soviet Union
headline: In 1941, Nazi Germany launched Operation Barbarossa, the largest land attack in history.
story:
On June 22, 1941, without a declaration of war, some 3.5 million Axis soldiers crossed the Soviet border on a 2,900 km front, with thousands of tanks and aircraft. Hitler was thus breaking the non-aggression pact signed with Stalin in 1939 and seeking "living space" and the destruction of communism.

In the first months the advance was overwhelming, but the German army failed to take Moscow before winter and became stuck in a war of attrition. The Eastern Front was the bloodiest of the Second World War: it is where the vast majority of German soldiers died, along with some 27 million Soviet citizens.

title: The United Kingdom votes for Brexit
headline: In 2016, a referendum decided by a narrow 52% that the United Kingdom would leave the European Union.
story:
On June 23, 2016, Britons voted in a referendum on whether to stay in the European Union or leave it. The Leave option won with 51.9% against 48.1%, with sharp contrasts: England and Wales voted mostly to leave; Scotland and Northern Ireland, to stay.

Prime Minister David Cameron, who had called the vote and campaigned to remain, resigned the next day. After years of negotiations and political crises, the United Kingdom formally left the EU on January 31, 2020. It was the first country to leave the bloc, and it revived the debate about the unity of the United Kingdom itself.

title: Solferino and the idea of the Red Cross
headline: In 1859, a battle in northern Italy horrified a witness who then founded the Red Cross.
story:
On June 24, 1859, near Solferino, the French and Austrian armies fought a battle that left some 40,000 dead and wounded in a single day. The Swiss Henri Dunant happened to be passing through on business and was horrified by the thousands of wounded left without care.

Dunant organized improvised relief with the local people and then wrote a book proposing the creation of societies of neutral volunteers to help the war wounded. From that idea came the International Committee of the Red Cross in 1863 and, in 1864, the first Geneva Convention. Dunant received the first Nobel Peace Prize.

title: The Korean War begins
headline: In 1950, North Korea crossed the 38th parallel and invaded the south, in the first major conflict of the Cold War.
story:
On June 25, 1950, the North Korean army, backed by the USSR, crossed the 38th parallel and invaded South Korea, nearly conquering all of it within weeks. The United Nations authorized a US-led intervention that pushed the North Koreans back to the border with China; China then entered the war and drove south again.

The front stabilized near the starting point. In 1953 an armistice — not a peace treaty — was signed, leaving the peninsula divided by a demilitarized strip. Between two and three million people died, most of them civilians.

title: The first draft of the human genome
headline: In 2000, it was announced that the human "instruction book" had been read almost in full.
story:
On June 26, 2000, at the White House and by video link with London, the leaders of the Human Genome Project — an international public consortium — and of the company Celera jointly announced that they had a draft of the complete sequence of human DNA: some 3 billion "letters".

The race between the two teams had sped up the work and forced the agreement. The final sequence was published in 2003. Knowing the genome gave no magic answers, but it transformed biology, cancer research and the study of rare diseases, and brought the cost of reading DNA down from billions to a few hundred euros.

title: The first nuclear plant connected to the grid
headline: In 1954, the Soviet plant at Obninsk began supplying nuclear electricity to homes.
story:
On June 27, 1954, in the town of Obninsk, near Moscow, a small 5-megawatt reactor went into operation, supplying electricity to the civilian grid. It was the first nuclear plant in the world to generate power for domestic and industrial use, not just for experiments or weapons.

It was tiny compared with today's plants, but it opened a path that many countries in the following decades saw as the future. Accidents such as Three Mile Island, Chernobyl and Fukushima, and the problem of waste, later slowed that expansion. Obninsk ran until 2002 and is now a museum.

title: The assassination in Sarajevo
headline: In 1914, the murder of the Austro-Hungarian heir in Sarajevo set off the First World War.
story:
On June 28, 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, and his wife Sophie were visiting Sarajevo. After a first bomb attack failed, the couple's car took a wrong turn and stopped right in front of Gavrilo Princip, a young Bosnian Serb nationalist, who shot them dead.

Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and declared war on it. In a chain reaction, through the web of alliances, Russia, Germany, France and Britain entered the conflict. In four years, the First World War left some 17 million dead and redrew the map of Europe.

title: The Globe theatre burns
headline: In 1613, a stage cannon set fire to Shakespeare's theatre during a performance of 'Henry VIII'.
story:
On June 29, 1613, during a performance of 'Henry VIII' at the Globe theatre in London, a prop cannon was fired to mark the king's entrance. A spark caught the thatched roof and the wooden building burned to the ground in an hour.

There were no casualties; the only anecdote that survives is of a spectator whose breeches began to smolder and who put out the fire with a bottle of beer. The Globe was rebuilt the following year. In 1997 a modern replica opened nearby, where Shakespeare is still performed in the open air.

title: The Tunguska event
headline: In 1908, a colossal explosion over Siberia flattened 80 million trees without leaving a crater.
story:
On the morning of June 30, 1908, over an uninhabited stretch of forest in the basin of the Tunguska River, in Siberia, an enormous explosion razed some 2,000 km² of trees, knocking them down in a circle from a central point. The energy is estimated at the equivalent of hundreds of Hiroshima bombs; the shockwave circled the planet and in Europe there were abnormally bright nights.

The most accepted hypothesis is that an asteroid or comet several tens of meters across exploded in the air, about 5–10 km up, without reaching the ground, which is why there is no crater. It is the largest known impact in recent history and a reminder of why the sky is watched.

title: The first day of the Somme
headline: In 1916, the British army suffered about 57,000 casualties in a single day, the bloodiest in its history.
story:
On July 1, 1916, after a week of bombardment that failed to destroy the German defenses, the British infantry climbed out of the trenches on the river Somme, in northern France, carrying 30 kilos of equipment and advancing at a slow walk under orders. The German machine guns cut them down: about 19,000 dead and 57,000 total casualties in a few hours.

The battle dragged on until November and advanced barely ten kilometers at a cost of more than a million casualties on both sides. The Somme became a symbol of industrial warfare and of the gap between the commanders and the reality of the front.

title: The Civil Rights Act of 1964
headline: In 1964, the United States outlawed racial segregation in public places, employment and schools.
story:
On July 2, 1964, President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act, which made discrimination on the basis of race, color, religion, sex or national origin illegal in employment, education and establishments open to the public. He had pushed it through despite the longest filibuster in Senate history.

It capped a decade of mobilization — boycotts, sit-ins, marches — and the pressure of the movement led by Martin Luther King. On signing it, Johnson remarked that his party had just lost the South for a generation. The Voting Rights Act followed the next year.

title: The third day of Gettysburg
headline: In 1863, Pickett's Charge failed in Pennsylvania and marked the turning point of the American Civil War.
story:
On July 3, 1863, the third day of the Battle of Gettysburg, the Confederate general Robert E. Lee sent some 12,500 men across open ground against the center of the Union lines. "Pickett's Charge" advanced more than a kilometer under artillery fire and was shattered: more than half the attackers fell.

Lee ordered the retreat toward Virginia. Gettysburg, with about 50,000 casualties in three days, was the bloodiest battle of the war and the moment the Confederacy lost the initiative. Months later, Lincoln would deliver his famous address there.

title: The US Declaration of Independence
headline: In 1776, the Continental Congress approved the text that broke the thirteen colonies' ties with Britain.
story:
On July 4, 1776, in Philadelphia, the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence, drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson. It proclaimed that "all men are created equal" and entitled to "life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness", and listed the grievances against King George III.

The war was already a year old and would last until 1783. The phrase about equality coexisted with slavery, which the new nation kept for almost another century. July 4 is the US national holiday.

title: Newton publishes the 'Principia'
headline: In 1687, the work appeared that established the laws of motion and universal gravitation.
story:
On July 5, 1687, the Royal Society of London published Isaac Newton's 'Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy', funded largely by the astronomer Edmond Halley. In it, Newton set out his three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation: the same force that makes an apple fall keeps the Moon in orbit.

With a handful of equations one could describe the tides, the orbits of the planets and the path of a projectile. The 'Principia' is one of the most influential books in the history of science and founded physics as it was taught for the following two centuries.

title: The first rabies vaccine
headline: In 1885, Louis Pasteur saved a boy bitten by a rabid dog with a still-experimental vaccine.
story:
On July 6, 1885, Louis Pasteur, who was a chemist and not a doctor, agreed to treat Joseph Meister, a nine-year-old Alsatian boy bitten fourteen times by a rabid dog. Rabies, once it set in, was fatal without exception. Pasteur injected him over ten days with increasing doses of infected, weakened rabbit spinal cord.

The boy did not fall ill. It was the first time an already contracted infection had been stopped with a vaccine. The news traveled the world, and the donations that followed made it possible to found the Pasteur Institute in Paris in 1888. Meister worked as an adult as a gatekeeper at that institute.

title: The 7/7 attacks in London
headline: In 2005, four suicide bombers set off explosions on the London Underground and a bus, killing 52 people.
story:
On the morning of July 7, 2005, at rush hour, three bombs exploded almost simultaneously on London Underground trains, and a fourth, shortly afterwards, on a double-decker bus in Tavistock Square. Fifty-two people were killed, in addition to the four bombers, and more than 700 were injured.

The attackers were British, three of them the sons of Pakistani immigrants, radicalized and linked to al-Qaeda. It was the deadliest attack the United Kingdom had suffered, and it came a day after London celebrated winning the right to host the 2012 Olympic Games.

title: Vasco da Gama sets out for India
headline: In 1497, a Portuguese fleet sailed from Lisbon to find the sea route to Asia around Africa.
story:
On July 8, 1497, four ships under Vasco da Gama left Lisbon with the aim of reaching India by sea, around the African continent. After ten months of sailing, having rounded the Cape of Good Hope and worked their way up the east coast of Africa, they reached Calicut, in southern India, in May 1498.

Portugal now had a direct route to the spice trade that did not depend on Arab middlemen or overland routes. Within a few decades it built an empire of bases and fortresses from Africa to China and Japan.

title: Argentina declares its independence
headline: In 1816, the Congress of Tucumán proclaimed the independence of the United Provinces from Spain.
story:
On July 9, 1816, the deputies gathered in the city of San Miguel de Tucumán declared the independence of the United Provinces of South America, which had begun their self-government with the May Revolution of 1810. They did so at a difficult moment: Spain had recovered much of the Americas and royalist troops were pressing from the north.

Consolidation took years and was achieved above all thanks to the campaign of José de San Martín, who crossed the Andes to liberate Chile and Peru. July 9 is Argentina's national holiday.

title: The Battle of Britain begins
headline: In 1940, the Luftwaffe launched an air offensive to subdue Britain and prepare an invasion.
story:
On July 10, 1940, with France already defeated, the German air force began systematically attacking British convoys and ports, the first step toward gaining command of the air over the English Channel. Without that command, the planned invasion, Operation Sea Lion, was impossible.

For almost four months, the RAF's Spitfire and Hurricane fighters, guided by a radar network, held off a larger air force. In September, Hitler postponed the invasion indefinitely. It was the first major German defeat of the war and the first campaign decided in the air alone.

title: The Srebrenica massacre
headline: In 1995, Bosnian Serb forces murdered about 8,000 Muslim men and boys in a UN "protected" area.
story:
On July 11, 1995, Bosnian Serb troops under General Ratko Mladić entered Srebrenica, an enclave in eastern Bosnia declared a "safe area" by the United Nations and guarded by a Dutch contingent that offered no resistance. Over the following days they separated the men and boys from the women and executed them en masse, burying them in mass graves.

About 8,000 were killed. International courts have classified it as genocide, the only one recognized as such in Europe since the Second World War. Mladić and the political leader Radovan Karadžić were sentenced to life imprisonment.

title: France win their first football World Cup
headline: In 1998, the host nation beat Brazil 3-0 in the World Cup final played in Saint-Denis.
story:
On July 12, 1998, before more than 75,000 spectators at the newly built Stade de France on the outskirts of Paris, France beat Brazil 3-0 to become world champions for the first time. Zinedine Zidane headed in two goals in the first half and Emmanuel Petit added a third in stoppage time.

Brazil, the holders, reached the final amid never-clarified rumours about the health of their star, Ronaldo. The win set off a huge celebration on the Champs-Élysées and was read as a symbol of a diverse France, its squad drawn from many backgrounds. Four years later, France would go out in the first round.

title: The Live Aid concert
headline: In 1985, two simultaneous mega-concerts in London and Philadelphia raised funds against the famine in Ethiopia.
story:
On July 13, 1985, Wembley Stadium in London and JFK Stadium in Philadelphia hosted a 16-hour benefit festival organized by the musician Bob Geldof after the impact of the images of the famine in Ethiopia. Queen, U2, David Bowie, Led Zeppelin, Madonna and dozens more artists performed.

It was broadcast to more than a hundred countries and watched by close to 1.9 billion people, one of the largest audiences in history. It raised more than £100 million and cemented the model of the global charity concert, though there was much later debate about the effectiveness of that aid.

title: The storming of the Bastille
headline: In 1789, a Parisian crowd stormed the fortress-prison of the Bastille and ignited the French Revolution.
story:
On July 14, 1789, fearing that the king would use the army against the National Assembly, thousands of Parisians sought weapons and gunpowder and headed for the Bastille, an old fortress that served as a prison and arsenal and symbolized absolute power. After hours of siege and a hundred dead, the garrison surrendered and the governor was lynched.

Inside there were only seven prisoners, but the gesture had enormous value: it showed that royal power could be defied by the street. July 14 is the national holiday of France.

title: The Crusaders take Jerusalem
headline: In 1099, the First Crusade conquered Jerusalem in an assault followed by a massacre of its inhabitants.
story:
On July 15, 1099, after a month-long siege and with wooden towers pushed up against the walls, the armies of the First Crusade entered Jerusalem. Chroniclers, both Christian and Muslim, describe an indiscriminate massacre of the city's Muslim and Jewish population that lasted for days.

The Crusaders founded a Latin kingdom there that would last, with ups and downs, for almost two centuries. The First Crusade had set out from Europe in 1096 at the call of Pope Urban II and was the only one to fully achieve its objective.

title: The Trinity test: the first atomic bomb
headline: In 1945, the United States detonated the first nuclear device in history in the New Mexico desert.
story:
At 5:29 a.m. on July 16, 1945, at a site called Jornada del Muerto, near Alamogordo, New Mexico, "Trinity" exploded, the first atomic bomb, the result of the Manhattan Project. The blast, equivalent to about 20,000 tons of TNT, raised a fireball visible for hundreds of kilometers and fused the sand into a greenish glass.

The scientific director, Robert Oppenheimer, later recalled a line from Hindu scripture: "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds." Three weeks later, atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

title: The Spanish Civil War begins
headline: In 1936, a military coup against the Second Republic half-failed and set off three years of war.
story:
On July 17, 1936, the garrisons of the Protectorate of Morocco rose against the government of the Popular Front. The next day the coup spread to the mainland. It neither fully succeeded — it failed in Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia and the Basque Country — nor was defeated, and Spain was split in two.

The war lasted until April 1939, caused hundreds of thousands of deaths and a repression that continued into the postwar years. It also became a rehearsal for the Second World War: Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy backed Franco; the USSR and the International Brigades backed the Republic.

title: The Great Fire of Rome
headline: In AD 64, a fire devastated the capital of the Empire for nine days.
story:
On the night of July 18–19, AD 64, a fire broke out beside the Circus Maximus and, driven by the wind, ravaged Rome for about nine days. Of the city's fourteen districts, three were completely destroyed and another seven badly damaged.

A rumor spread that the emperor Nero himself had ordered the fire in order to rebuild the city to his taste and build his palace, the Domus Aurea. Nero deflected the accusations onto the small Christian community, which suffered the first documented persecution. Rome was rebuilt with wider streets and fire regulations.

title: The Seneca Falls Convention
headline: In 1848, the first women's rights convention in history was held in New York State.
story:
On July 19, 1848, some 300 people gathered in a chapel in the town of Seneca Falls, in the state of New York, convened by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott. They approved a "Declaration of Sentiments" modeled on the Declaration of Independence: "all men and women are created equal".

Among its demands — education, property, divorce, legal equality — the most controversial, approved by a narrow margin, was the right to vote. It is considered the founding act of the American suffrage movement, which would not win the vote for women nationwide until 1920.

title: A human being sets foot on the Moon
headline: In 1969, the Apollo 11 mission landed a module on the Moon and Neil Armstrong took the first step.
story:
On July 20, 1969, the lunar module Eagle of the Apollo 11 mission touched down in the Sea of Tranquility after a descent with computer alarms and almost no fuel left. Six and a half hours later, Neil Armstrong came down the ladder and stepped onto the surface with the words "one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind". Buzz Aldrin followed.

Some 600 million people watched on television. It was the high point of the space race with the Soviet Union. Between 1969 and 1972, twelve people walked on the Moon; no one has been back since.

title: The Scopes "Monkey Trial"
headline: In 1925, a Tennessee teacher was convicted of teaching evolution in a public school.
story:
On July 21, 1925, the trial ended in Dayton, Tennessee, of John Scopes, a young teacher accused of breaking a state law that forbade teaching that human beings descended from other animals. The case, partly staged as publicity to draw tourism to the town, became a national duel between science and religious fundamentalism, followed by radio across the country.

Scopes was found guilty and fined $100, a penalty later overturned on a technicality. The debate over teaching evolution in American classrooms has remained alive to this day.

title: The 2011 Norway attacks
headline: In 2011, an extremist killed 77 people with a bomb in Oslo and a shooting at a youth camp.
story:
On July 22, 2011, Anders Behring Breivik, a 32-year-old Norwegian with a far-right ideology, set off a van bomb next to the government headquarters in Oslo, killing eight people. Shortly afterwards, disguised as a police officer, he reached the island of Utøya, where the Labour Party was holding a youth camp, and fired for more than an hour: he killed 69 people, most of them teenagers.

It was the deadliest attack in Norway since the Second World War. Breivik was sentenced to the country's maximum penalty, 21 years, extendable for as long as he remains a danger.

title: The Egyptian Revolution of 1952
headline: In 1952, a group of officers overthrew King Farouk and opened the way to the Nasser era.
story:
In the early hours of July 23, 1952, the Free Officers Movement, led by Muhammad Naguib and Gamal Abdel Nasser, took command of the Egyptian army and of the key points of Cairo almost without a shot. Three days later, King Farouk abdicated and left for exile on his yacht.

Egypt proclaimed itself a republic in 1953. Nasser, who took real power, nationalized the Suez Canal in 1956 and became the leading figure of Arab nationalism. July 23 is Egypt's national holiday.

title: The rediscovery of Machu Picchu
headline: In 1911, the explorer Hiram Bingham reached the Inca city hidden in the mountains of Peru.
story:
On July 24, 1911, guided by local farmers who knew the place and cultivated it, the American professor Hiram Bingham reached Machu Picchu, a 15th-century Inca city built on a mountain spur at 2,400 meters, among jungle and cliffs. The Spanish conquistadors had never found it, and it had been covered in vegetation for centuries.

Bingham made it known to the world with articles and photographs in 'National Geographic' magazine. Today it is the most visited monument in South America and one of the symbols of the pre-Columbian past.

title: The first baby by in vitro fertilization is born
headline: In 1978, the birth of Louise Brown in England opened the era of assisted reproduction.
story:
On July 25, 1978, Louise Joy Brown was born in Oldham, England, the first person conceived outside the human body. The physiologist Robert Edwards and the gynecologist Patrick Steptoe had managed to fertilize an egg from her mother with sperm from her father in the laboratory and transfer the embryo to the womb.

The announcement caused intense ethical and religious debate and headlines about "test-tube babies". Since then, more than ten million people have been born through in vitro fertilization. Edwards received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2010.

title: The attack on the Moncada Barracks
headline: In 1953, a failed attack by Fidel Castro on a barracks gave its name to the movement that would carry out the Cuban Revolution.
story:
On July 26, 1953, a group of about 135 young people led by the lawyer Fidel Castro attacked the Moncada Barracks, in Santiago de Cuba, with the idea of seizing weapons and sparking an uprising against the dictator Fulgencio Batista. The attack failed: many of the assailants were killed, some after being tortured, and Castro was captured and put on trial.

At the trial he delivered his plea "History will absolve me". Amnestied in 1955, he went into exile in Mexico, prepared an expedition, and in 1959 his 26th of July Movement overthrew Batista.

title: The armistice of the Korean War
headline: In 1953, the ceasefire was signed that froze the Korean War, still without a peace treaty.
story:
On July 27, 1953, in the village of Panmunjom, on the front line, representatives of North Korea, China and the UN command signed an armistice after two years of negotiations that ran alongside the fighting. It established a ceasefire and a demilitarized zone four kilometers wide along the line, very close to the 38th parallel from which the war had started.

South Korea never signed the document. As no peace treaty was ever reached, the two Koreas remain technically at war, with one of the most militarized borders on the planet.

title: The First World War breaks out
headline: In 1914, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia a month after the Sarajevo assassination.
story:
On July 28, 1914, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, which it held responsible for the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Within days, the system of alliances dragged in the great powers: Russia mobilized in support of Serbia; Germany declared war on Russia and France and invaded Belgium; Britain then entered the conflict.

What many expected to be a short war lasted more than four years, left some 17 million dead, brought down four empires and sowed the conditions for the Second World War.

title: NASA is created
headline: In 1958, the United States founded a civilian space agency in response to the Soviet Sputnik.
story:
On July 29, 1958, President Eisenhower signed the National Aeronautics and Space Act, which created NASA out of an old aeronautical research body. The agency began operating on October 1. The political aim was clear: to recover the prestige lost after the launch of Sputnik and the first Soviet satellite.

Within a decade, NASA went from having no reliable rockets to carrying people to the Moon. Since then it has operated the shuttles, the International Space Station and probes that have explored every planet in the Solar System.

title: The first World Cup final
headline: In 1930, Uruguay beat Argentina in Montevideo in the final of the first FIFA World Cup.
story:
On July 30, 1930, before some 68,000 spectators at the Estadio Centenario in Montevideo, Uruguay's national team beat Argentina's 4–2 and became the first world champions. Uruguay, the host country and double Olympic champion, had paid for the tournament; only thirteen teams took part, four of them European after a long sea voyage.

The World Cup would become, over the years, the biggest sporting event on the planet alongside the Olympic Games, followed by billions of people every four years.

title: The Weimar Constitution
headline: In 1919, Germany adopted the constitution of its first democratic republic, born of defeat.
story:
On July 31, 1919, the National Assembly meeting in the city of Weimar approved the constitution of the new German republic, which had emerged after the fall of the Kaiser at the end of the First World War. It was very advanced: universal suffrage, including for women, social rights, referendums.

It also had weaknesses: an electoral system that fragmented the parliament and an article, Article 48, that allowed the president to govern by decree in emergencies. That mechanism, used heavily in the crisis years, made it easier for Hitler to dismantle democracy from within in 1933.

title: The Warsaw Uprising
headline: In 1944, the Polish resistance rose against the German occupation and fought alone for 63 days.
story:
On August 1, 1944, with the Red Army at the gates of Warsaw, the Polish Home Army launched an insurrection to liberate the capital before the Soviets arrived, and so take political control of the country. They expected to hold out for a few days; they lasted 63.

Soviet help never came: Stalin halted his advance on the far bank of the river. The Germans crushed the revolt and, on Hitler's orders, systematically razed the city. About 200,000 Poles died, most of them civilians, and Warsaw was reduced to rubble.

title: Iraq invades Kuwait
headline: In 1990, Saddam Hussein's troops occupied the emirate of Kuwait in a day and set off the Gulf War.
story:
On August 2, 1990, the Iraqi army crossed the border and invaded Kuwait, a small, rich neighbor it accused of stealing oil and of denying it access to the sea. Within hours it occupied the whole country, and weeks later annexed it as "province 19".

The international community reacted harshly. A coalition of 35 countries led by the United States, with UN backing, launched Operation Desert Storm in January 1991: six weeks of bombing and a hundred hours of ground offensive drove Iraq out. Saddam stayed in power for another twelve years.

title: Columbus sets sail into the unknown
headline: In 1492, three ships left the port of Palos in search of a western route to Asia.
story:
On August 3, 1492, the Santa María, the Pinta and the Niña set sail from the port of Palos de la Frontera (Huelva) under Christopher Columbus, with the permission and funding of the Catholic Monarchs. Columbus calculated, wrongly, that by sailing west he would reach Asia in a few weeks.

After a stop in the Canary Islands and more than a month in open sea, with the crew on the verge of mutiny, they sighted land on October 12: an island in the Caribbean. Columbus died believing he had reached Asia. The voyage put two worlds that had ignored each other into permanent contact.

title: Britain enters the Great War
headline: In 1914, the German invasion of Belgium led Britain to declare war and turned the conflict into a world war.
story:
On August 4, 1914, German troops crossed the border of Belgium, a neutral country, to attack France from the north according to the Schlieffen Plan. The United Kingdom, guarantor of that neutrality under an 1839 treaty, gave Germany an ultimatum that expired at midnight and declared war on it.

With the British Empire in, the war ceased to be a European affair. Foreign Secretary Edward Grey summed up the moment: "The lamps are going out all over Europe; we shall not see them lit again in our lifetime."

title: The first treaty to curb nuclear testing
headline: In 1963, the United States, the USSR and Britain banned nuclear tests in the atmosphere, at sea and in space.
story:
On August 5, 1963, after the previous year's Cuban missile crisis, the first three nuclear powers signed the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty in Moscow. It prohibited test explosions in the atmosphere, underwater and in space; it allowed only underground ones.

The immediate aim was to curb the radioactive fallout that hundreds of open-air tests were spreading across the planet. It was the first arms-control agreement of the Cold War and the basis for later, more ambitious treaties.

title: The atomic bomb on Hiroshima
headline: In 1945, a single American plane destroyed the Japanese city of Hiroshima with a nuclear weapon.
story:
At 8:15 a.m. on August 6, 1945, the bomber 'Enola Gay' dropped the bomb "Little Boy" on Hiroshima. It exploded 600 meters up with a force equivalent to about 15,000 tons of TNT. Between 70,000 and 80,000 people died instantly; many more died later from injuries and radiation, reaching about 140,000 by the end of the year.

It was the first time a nuclear weapon had been used against a population. Three days later another was dropped on Nagasaki, and Japan surrendered. The debate over whether the bombings were necessary is still open.

title: The attacks on US embassies in Africa
headline: In 1998, two nearly simultaneous car bombs in Kenya and Tanzania killed 224 people and introduced al-Qaeda.
story:
On August 7, 1998, minutes apart, car bombs exploded outside the US embassies in Nairobi (Kenya) and Dar es Salaam (Tanzania). Two hundred and twenty-four people died, the vast majority Africans passing on the street or working in neighboring buildings, and more than 4,000 were injured.

Osama bin Laden's network claimed the attacks. The United States responded by bombing targets in Sudan and Afghanistan and put Bin Laden on its most-wanted list. It was the warning of a threat that would erupt at full scale on September 11, 2001.

title: Nixon announces his resignation
