headline: In 1974, cornered by the Watergate scandal, Richard Nixon became the first US president to resign.
story:
On the night of August 8, 1974, Richard Nixon appeared on television to announce that he would leave the presidency at noon the next day. Days earlier, the Supreme Court had forced him to hand over recordings that proved he had taken part in the cover-up of the 1972 break-in at the Democratic headquarters, and his own party had withdrawn its support in Congress.

Vice President Gerald Ford was sworn in and, a month later, granted him a full pardon. The Watergate affair left a lasting distrust of politics and strengthened the role of the press as a check on power.

title: The atomic bomb on Nagasaki
headline: In 1945, the second nuclear attack in three days hastened Japan's surrender and the end of the Second World War.
story:
At 11:02 a.m. on August 9, 1945, an American bomber dropped the plutonium bomb "Fat Man" on Nagasaki. The intended target was another city, Kokura, which was covered by cloud. Nagasaki's mountainous terrain partly contained the blast, but about 40,000 people died immediately and some 70,000 by the end of the year.

That same day, the Soviet Union had declared war on Japan and invaded Manchuria. On August 15, Emperor Hirohito announced the surrender by radio, the first time the Japanese people had heard his voice.

title: Magellan's expedition sets sail
headline: In 1519, five ships left Seville on a voyage that would become the first circumnavigation of the world.
story:
On August 10, 1519, five ships under the Portuguese Ferdinand Magellan, in the service of the Crown of Castile, set out from Seville down the Guadalquivir. The aim was to reach the Spice Islands by sailing west, seeking a passage around the south of the Americas.

Magellan found the strait that bears his name, crossed the Pacific and died in the Philippines in 1521. Only one ship, the Victoria, under Juan Sebastián Elcano, completed the return to Seville in September 1522: 18 men of the original 240. They had made, not entirely on purpose, the first voyage around the planet.

title: The Watts riots
headline: In 1965, six days of unrest in a Black neighborhood of Los Angeles left 34 dead and destroyed entire blocks.
story:
On August 11, 1965, the arrest of a young Black man for drunk driving in the Watts neighborhood of Los Angeles escalated into a clash with police that lasted six days. There were fires, looting and shootings over an area of about 120 km²; the National Guard was called in.

Thirty-four people died and the damage was enormous. It happened a few days after the Voting Rights Act was passed, and it showed that laws alone did not erase poverty, unemployment and police abuse in the urban ghettos of the North and West of the country.

title: The end of the Spanish-American War
headline: In 1898, an armistice sealed Spain's defeat; it lost Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Philippines and Guam.
story:
On August 12, 1898, Spain and the United States signed a peace protocol in Washington ending a little over three months of war. Spain agreed to give up Cuba and to cede Puerto Rico and Guam; the fate of the Philippines would be decided in the final negotiation, the Treaty of Paris in December, which also handed them over in exchange for compensation.

In four months, Spain went from colonial power to a country with no overseas empire. That "Disaster of '98" caused a moral crisis and a current of intellectuals, the Generation of '98, who reflected on the country's decline.

title: Construction of the Berlin Wall begins
headline: In 1961, East Germany closed the border between the two halves of Berlin overnight.
story:
In the early hours of August 13, 1961, soldiers and workers from East Germany began putting up barbed wire and concrete blocks along the 43 km of border between East and West Berlin. Within days the barrier was completely sealed, cutting through streets, subway lines and families.

East Germany was losing population at an unsustainable rate: almost three million people had fled to the West through Berlin since 1949. The Wall stopped the drain, but it became the world's symbol of the division of Europe. At least 140 people died trying to cross it.

title: Japan surrenders and the Second World War ends
headline: In 1945, after the atomic bombs and the entry of the USSR, Japan accepted unconditional surrender.
story:
On August 14, 1945 (the 15th in Japan because of the time difference), the Japanese government told the Allies it accepted surrender. The next day, Emperor Hirohito announced it by radio to a population that had never heard his voice, in language so formal that many barely understood the message.

So ended the deadliest conflict in history, with between 70 and 85 million dead worldwide since 1939. The formal signing took place on September 2 aboard the battleship Missouri, in Tokyo Bay.

title: The independence and partition of India
headline: In 1947, the end of British rule created two states, India and Pakistan, and one of the largest forced migrations in history.
story:
At midnight on August 15, 1947, India ceased to be a British colony. Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru spoke of a "tryst with destiny". But independence came with partition: the territory was divided along religious lines into a Hindu-majority India and a Muslim-majority Pakistan (which had been born the day before).

Some 15 million people crossed the new borders within a few months, and massacres broke out between communities, leaving between several hundred thousand and two million dead. Gandhi, opposed to the division, did not attend the celebrations.

title: The Peterloo Massacre
headline: In 1819, cavalry charged a peaceful pro-suffrage gathering in Manchester and killed about fifteen people.
story:
On August 16, 1819, some 60,000 people gathered on open ground in Manchester, St Peter's Field, to demand reform of the electoral system, which left the new industrial cities without representation. The magistrates ordered the speakers arrested, and the cavalry rode into the crowd with sabers drawn.

Around 18 people died and hundreds were injured. The reformist press dubbed it "Peterloo", in ironic reference to Waterloo. Far from stopping the movement, the massacre strengthened the demand for reform, which would come in 1832 and, more broadly, in the decades that followed.

title: Indonesia proclaims its independence
headline: In 1945, two days after Japan's surrender, Sukarno declared the world's largest archipelago independent.
story:
On August 17, 1945, in Jakarta, the nationalist leaders Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta read a brief proclamation of Indonesian independence, taking advantage of the power vacuum after the capitulation of Japan, which had occupied the Dutch East Indies during the war.

The Netherlands tried to reclaim the colony, and four years of war and negotiations followed, with growing international pressure. In 1949 they recognized Indonesian sovereignty. Today Indonesia is the fourth most populous country on the planet and the one with the largest Muslim population.

title: American women win the vote
headline: In 1920, the ratification of the 19th Amendment barred denying the vote on the basis of sex across the United States.
story:
On August 18, 1920, the state of Tennessee became the 36th to ratify the Nineteenth Amendment to the Constitution, reaching the required majority. The decision came down to a single vote in the state chamber: a young legislator changed his position after receiving a letter from his mother.

The amendment capped more than 70 years of suffrage campaigning since Seneca Falls. In practice, however, many Black women in the South remained unable to vote because of segregationist laws until the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

title: The August coup in the USSR
headline: In 1991, a group of Soviet leaders tried to stop the reforms with a coup that failed in three days and hastened the end of the USSR.
story:
On August 19, 1991, a self-styled State Committee on the State of Emergency, made up of senior figures from the party, the army and the KGB, announced that it was taking power and placed President Mikhail Gorbachev, who was on holiday in Crimea, under house arrest. They sent tanks into the streets of Moscow.

Resistance formed around the Russian president, Boris Yeltsin, who climbed onto a tank outside the parliament. The army split, the population took to the streets, and within three days the plotters surrendered. The attempt destroyed the authority of the party and of Gorbachev himself: in December, the Soviet Union ceased to exist.

title: The invasion of Czechoslovakia
headline: In 1968, Warsaw Pact tanks crushed the "Prague Spring" and its democratizing reforms.
story:
On the night of August 20–21, 1968, some 200,000 soldiers and 2,000 tanks from the Soviet Union and four Warsaw Pact allies entered Czechoslovakia to end the process of opening that the communist leader Alexander Dubček had driven under the slogan "socialism with a human face".

There was massive but peaceful civil resistance; about a hundred people died. The reforms were rolled back and "normalization" was imposed. The invasion disillusioned many Western communists and stood as a symbol of the limits Moscow imposed on its satellites.

title: The theft of the Mona Lisa
headline: In 1911, a Louvre employee carried the 'Mona Lisa' out under his clothes and made it, unintentionally, the most famous painting in the world.
story:
On August 21, 1911, a Monday when the Louvre was closed, the Italian Vincenzo Peruggia, who had worked fitting protective glass to the paintings, took the 'Mona Lisa' down, hid it under his smock and walked out through a service door. The museum did not notice it was missing until the next day.

For two years the work moved through headlines around the world while the police questioned even Picasso. Peruggia was arrested in 1913 trying to sell it in Florence; he said he wanted to "return" it to Italy. The theft made the portrait famous, until then just one among the Louvre's masterpieces.

title: The Battle of Bosworth
headline: In 1485, the death of Richard III on the battlefield ended the Plantagenet dynasty and put the Tudors on the throne.
story:
On August 22, 1485, near Bosworth, in central England, the army of King Richard III faced that of Henry Tudor, a noble with a weak claim to the throne who had landed from France. In the middle of the fighting, part of Richard's troops switched sides. The king charged personally at Henry and was cut down.

He was the last English king to fall in battle and the last of the House of York. Henry was crowned Henry VII and founded the Tudor dynasty, which would reign for more than a century. Richard III's remains were found in 2012 under a parking lot in Leicester.

title: The pact between Hitler and Stalin
headline: In 1939, Nazi Germany and the USSR signed a non-aggression pact that secretly divided Eastern Europe.
story:
On August 23, 1939, the foreign ministers of Germany and the Soviet Union, Ribbentrop and Molotov, signed a non-aggression pact in Moscow. It stunned the world: the two regimes had presented themselves as irreconcilable enemies.

A secret protocol, denied for decades by Moscow, divided Poland, the Baltic states and other territories into spheres of influence. With its rear secured, Germany invaded Poland nine days later and the Second World War began. The USSR occupied its share a little later. The pact was broken when Hitler attacked Stalin in 1941.

title: The St Bartholomew's Day Massacre
headline: In 1572, a wave of killings of Protestants in Paris and other French cities left thousands dead and reignited the wars of religion.
story:
In the early hours of August 24, 1572, St Bartholomew's Day, the massacre of the Huguenots — the French Protestants — began in Paris. Many had come to the capital for the wedding of the king of Navarre to Margaret of Valois, sister of King Charles IX. After the attempted murder of a Huguenot leader days earlier, the court ordered its chiefs killed; the violence spilled over and the Catholic crowd joined a house-by-house hunt.

Over the following weeks the killing spread to a dozen cities. Estimates of the dead range from several thousand to tens of thousands. The pope greeted the news with a Te Deum; for Protestants across Europe, St Bartholomew's became the symbol of Catholic treachery and hardened the conflict for a generation.

title: The liberation of Paris
headline: In 1944, the German garrison of Paris surrendered and the French capital returned to Allied hands.
story:
On August 25, 1944, after several days of a Resistance uprising in the streets and the arrival of General Leclerc's French 2nd Armored Division and American troops, the German commander of Paris, Dietrich von Choltitz, signed the surrender. He had disobeyed Hitler's order to raze the city.

The next day, General de Gaulle marched down the Champs-Élysées amid crowds. The liberation of Paris had enormous symbolic value: two months after the Normandy landings, Free France recovered its capital.

title: The Declaration of the Rights of Man
headline: In 1789, the French Assembly proclaimed that men are born free and equal in rights.
story:
On August 26, 1789, the French National Constituent Assembly approved the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, a text of 17 articles drafted with the help of Lafayette and Jefferson. It asserted liberty, equality before the law, property, the presumption of innocence, freedom of opinion and of the press, and the sovereignty of the nation.

It became a reference for liberal constitutions around the world and a direct precursor of the Universal Declaration of 1948. Its reach was limited in its time — it excluded women and the enslaved people of the colonies — but it set out an ideal.

title: The eruption of Krakatoa
headline: In 1883, a volcano in Indonesia exploded with a force heard almost 5,000 km away, killing about 36,000 people.
story:
On August 27, 1883, the volcano Krakatoa, in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra, capped days of activity with four colossal explosions. The largest was heard in Australia and on the island of Rodrigues, 4,800 km away, and is considered the loudest sound in recorded history. The volcano's island was almost destroyed.

The tsunamis it generated, up to 30 meters high, razed hundreds of coastal towns: some 36,000 victims. The ash in the atmosphere lowered the global temperature by close to a degree for several years and turned sunsets red across half the world.

title: "I Have a Dream"
headline: In 1963, Martin Luther King delivered his most famous speech before 250,000 people in Washington.
story:
On August 28, 1963, some 250,000 people — white and Black — marched to the Lincoln Memorial in Washington to demand jobs and civil rights. At the end of the day, Martin Luther King improvised, urged on by the singer Mahalia Jackson, the passage that begins "I have a dream that my four children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the color of their skin".

The march helped the Civil Rights Act pass the following year. The speech is one of the most quoted in history. King received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964 and was assassinated in 1968.

title: The USSR tests its first atomic bomb
headline: In 1949, the Soviet Union detonated a nuclear weapon years earlier than the West believed, and the arms race truly began.
story:
On August 29, 1949, the Soviet Union exploded its first atomic bomb, called RDS-1, at a test site in Kazakhstan. The design closely resembled that of the Nagasaki bomb, thanks in part to information passed by spies inside the Manhattan Project.

The United States, which expected to keep its nuclear monopoly for another decade, detected the explosion from the radioactivity in the atmosphere. The "balance of terror" between the two superpowers shaped the Cold War for 40 years and led to the stockpiling of tens of thousands of nuclear warheads.

title: The attempt on Lenin's life
headline: In 1918, shots fired at the Bolshevik leader served as the trigger for the Red Terror.
story:
On August 30, 1918, as he left a rally at a Moscow factory, Vladimir Lenin was shot twice by Fanny Kaplan, a revolutionary militant who accused him of betraying the revolution. Lenin survived with lasting effects. That same day, the head of Petrograd's political police had been assassinated.

The Bolshevik government responded with the "Red Terror": mass executions of real or supposed opponents, the taking of hostages and the creation of camps. Kaplan was shot without trial a few days later. Systematic repression became a routine instrument of the new state.

title: The death of Diana, Princess of Wales
headline: In 1997, Princess Diana died in a car crash in Paris while being chased by photographers.
story:
In the early hours of August 31, 1997, the car carrying Diana, Princess of Wales, and her partner, Dodi Al-Fayed, crashed into a pillar of the Pont de l'Alma tunnel in Paris while speeding away from paparazzi. Diana, Al-Fayed and the driver, who had been drinking, were killed.

The death of the princess, 36, separated from the heir to the British throne and very popular for her humanitarian work, caused a wave of worldwide mourning and a crisis for the monarchy over its response, seen as cold. It also sharpened the debate about the limits of tabloid journalism.

title: Germany invades Poland
headline: In 1939, the German attack on Poland began the Second World War.
story:
At 4:45 a.m. on September 1, 1939, without a declaration of war, Nazi Germany launched a combined offensive of aircraft, armor and infantry against Poland, the "lightning war". The battleship Schleswig-Holstein opened fire on a Polish garrison in Danzig.

Two days later, Britain and France, Poland's allies, declared war on Germany. On September 17, the Soviet Union invaded Poland from the east as it had secretly agreed with Hitler. In six weeks Poland was divided and occupied. The deadliest conflict in history had begun.

title: The Great Fire of London
headline: In 1666, a fire that started in a bakery razed the City of London over four days.
story:
On September 2, 1666, a fire broke out before dawn in a bakery on Pudding Lane. Driven by a strong wind and fed by crowded wooden houses, it spread out of control for four days and destroyed some 13,200 homes, 87 churches and the old St Paul's Cathedral. It is estimated to have left about 70,000 people homeless, most of the City's population.

Remarkably, the recorded death toll was very small. The rebuilding brought wider streets, brick houses and Christopher Wren's new St Paul's Cathedral.

title: The Treaty of Paris recognizes the United States
headline: In 1783, Britain recognized the independence of its former thirteen colonies and ended the war.
story:
On September 3, 1783, in Paris, representatives of Britain and the United States signed the treaty ending the war of independence. London recognized the thirteen colonies as "free, sovereign and independent states" and ceded to them a vast territory as far as the Mississippi River.

France and Spain, which had backed the rebels, signed separate agreements; Spain recovered Menorca and Florida. The United States was thus born as a recognized country, though it would take years to give itself a stable constitution and federal government.

title: The end of the Western Roman Empire
headline: In AD 476, a Germanic chief deposed the last emperor of Rome and appointed no other.
story:
On September 4, AD 476, the Germanic leader Odoacer, at the head of mercenary troops serving Rome, deposed at Ravenna Romulus Augustulus, a teenager who was emperor of the West in name only. Rather than proclaiming a successor, Odoacer made himself king of Italy and sent the imperial regalia back to Constantinople.

The Eastern Empire continued for a thousand more years as the Byzantine Empire, but in the West there was no longer an emperor. Historians take that date as the conventional end of antiquity and the beginning of the Middle Ages, though the process of collapse had lasted a century.

title: The Munich Olympics massacre
headline: In 1972, a Palestinian commando kidnapped and killed eleven athletes of the Israeli team during the Olympic Games.
story:
In the early hours of September 5, 1972, eight members of the group Black September entered the Olympic Village in Munich, killed two members of the Israeli team and took nine others hostage, demanding the release of Palestinian prisoners.

After a day of negotiations, a police rescue attempt at Fürstenfeldbruck airfield ended in a gunfight: the nine hostages, five terrorists and a police officer were killed. The Games paused for a day and then continued. Israel responded with a years-long campaign to track down and kill those involved.

title: The first voyage around the world
headline: In 1522, the ship Victoria returned to Spain after circumnavigating the planet for the first time.
story:
On September 6, 1522, the ship Victoria anchored at Sanlúcar de Barrameda with 18 exhausted crew aboard, under Juan Sebastián Elcano. It was the only survivor of the five ships that had left Seville three years earlier with Ferdinand Magellan, who had died in the Philippines.

They had covered more than 60,000 km, crossed for the first time the strait south of the Americas and the Pacific Ocean, and shown in practice that the Earth is round and can be sailed around. On arriving they also discovered that they had "lost" a day by always sailing westward.

title: The independence of Brazil
headline: In 1822, Prince Pedro proclaimed the independence of Brazil on the banks of the river Ipiranga.
story:
On September 7, 1822, the prince regent Pedro of Braganza received near the Ipiranga stream, on the outskirts of São Paulo, dispatches from Lisbon in which the Portuguese Cortes demanded that he return to Europe and annulled the autonomy of the Kingdom of Brazil. By tradition, Pedro turned to his escort and gave the "cry of Ipiranga": "Independence or death."

Brazil was thus born as an independent monarchy, a rare case in an Americas that was filling up with republics. Pedro had himself acclaimed emperor a few weeks later. September 7 is Brazil's national holiday.

title: Michelangelo's David is unveiled
headline: In 1504, Florence placed before the seat of government the marble statue that became the symbol of the city.
story:
On September 8, 1504, after several days of transport, Michelangelo's David was installed in the Piazza della Signoria in Florence: more than five meters of marble carved from a block that other sculptors had abandoned as flawed. The artist was 29 and worked on it for more than two years.

The figure of the young biblical shepherd before facing Goliath, tense and defiant, was read as an emblem of the Florentine republic against its powerful enemies. In 1873 it was moved to the Galleria dell'Accademia for protection; in the square there is a copy.

title: Mao Zedong dies
headline: In 1976, the death of the leader who founded communist China opened the door to a radical turn for the country.
story:
On September 9, 1976, Mao Zedong died in Beijing at the age of 82, having led China since the communist victory of 1949. His legacy was contradictory: he unified and modernized the country and restored its international weight, but his great campaigns — the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution — caused famines and chaos with tens of millions of deaths.

Within weeks, his successors arrested the "Gang of Four", the most radical faction. Within a few years, Deng Xiaoping drove through market reforms that transformed the Chinese economy and lifted hundreds of millions of people out of poverty.

title: The Large Hadron Collider starts up
headline: In 2008, the largest machine ever built came online, a 27 km ring beneath the French-Swiss border.
story:
On September 10, 2008, at the European laboratory CERN, near Geneva, a beam of protons circulated for the first time through the Large Hadron Collider, a circular tunnel 27 kilometers long at 100 meters underground. In it, particles are made to collide at nearly the speed of light to recreate conditions similar to those of the early universe.

An electrical fault kept it shut down for a year. In 2012, its detectors confirmed the existence of the Higgs boson, the particle that explains why matter has mass, predicted theoretically almost fifty years earlier.

title: The September 11 attacks
headline: In 2001, al-Qaeda hijackers crashed four planes in the United States and killed almost 3,000 people.
story:
On the morning of September 11, 2001, nineteen al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four commercial airliners. Two crashed into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York, which collapsed; a third into the Pentagon; the fourth came down in a field in Pennsylvania when the passengers tried to regain control. 2,977 people were killed.

It was the deadliest attack in history. The United States responded by invading Afghanistan, where Osama bin Laden was sheltering, and in 2003 Iraq. The "war on terror" shaped the following two decades: new security laws, airport checks and prolonged conflicts.

title: The Battle of Vienna
headline: In 1683, a Christian army broke the Ottoman siege of Vienna and halted the Turkish advance into central Europe.
story:
On September 12, 1683, after two months of Ottoman siege of Vienna, a relief army made up of troops of the Holy Roman Empire and of Poland-Lithuania came down from the nearby hills and attacked the Turkish camp. The charge of the Polish heavy cavalry, led by King John III Sobieski, decided the battle.

The Ottoman Empire, which had reached the gates of Vienna for the second time in a century and a half, began from there a long retreat in the Balkans. The date is remembered as the moment the Ottoman expansion toward the heart of Europe was stopped.

title: The Battle of the Plains of Abraham
headline: In 1759, the British victory at Quebec decided that northern North America would be British and not French.
story:
On September 13, 1759, after scaling a cliff by night beside the city of Quebec, a British army under General James Wolfe surprised the French troops of the Marquis de Montcalm on a plateau called the Plains of Abraham. The battle lasted less than an hour. Both generals died.

Quebec capitulated days later, and all of New France passed to British hands with the Treaty of Paris in 1763. The outcome shaped Canada — with its French-speaking minority — and, by removing the French threat, emboldened the southern British colonies to stand up to London years later.

title: Napoleon enters Moscow
headline: In 1812, the Grande Armée occupied a burning, almost empty Moscow; it was the beginning of its destruction.
story:
On September 14, 1812, Napoleon entered Moscow after the bloody Battle of Borodino. He expected Tsar Alexander I to sue for peace. Instead, the city burned for days — set alight by its own inhabitants as they withdrew — and the tsar did not negotiate.

With winter closing in and no supplies, Napoleon ordered the retreat in October. Cold, hunger and the harassment of Cossacks and peasants annihilated the Grande Armée: of more than 400,000 men who had entered Russia, barely a few tens of thousands returned. It was the blow that began the end of the Napoleonic Empire.

title: The Nuremberg Laws
headline: In 1935, Nazi Germany stripped Jews of citizenship and banned their marriages to "Aryans".
story:
On September 15, 1935, during the annual Nazi Party congress in Nuremberg, the Reichstag passed two laws: the Reich Citizenship Law, which reduced Jews to "subjects" with no political rights, and the Law for the Protection of German Blood, which forbade marriages and relationships between Jews and non-Jews.

Later decrees defined who was "Jewish" according to grandparents. The Nuremberg Laws gave legal form to the persecution and were a decisive step on the road that, six years later, led to extermination.

title: The Cry of Dolores
headline: In 1810, the priest Miguel Hidalgo called for arms against Spanish rule and set off Mexico's independence.
story:
In the early hours of September 16, 1810, the priest Miguel Hidalgo rang the bells of his parish in the town of Dolores and urged the people to rise against misgovernment and the Spaniards. That "Cry of Dolores" gathered within a few days a peasant army of tens of thousands.

Hidalgo was captured and shot in 1811, but the struggle continued under other leaders until independence was achieved in 1821. Every September 15 at night, the president of Mexico repeats the cry from the balcony of the National Palace.

title: The Constitution of the United States is signed
headline: In 1787, 39 delegates signed in Philadelphia the oldest written constitution still in force.
story:
On September 17, 1787, after almost four months of closed-door debate in Philadelphia, the delegates to the Convention signed the text of the United States Constitution. It replaced a weak confederal system with a federal government of three branches that check one another and a mechanism for amendment.

It took effect in 1789 after being ratified by the states, with a commitment to add a bill of rights straight away. It has been amended only 27 times and has served as a model for dozens of countries, though in its origin it coexisted with slavery and a very restricted suffrage.

title: The Mukden Incident
headline: In 1931, Japan used a faked railway sabotage as a pretext to invade Manchuria.
story:
On the night of September 18, 1931, Japanese army officers set off a small charge beside a railway line that Japan controlled near Mukden, in northeastern China, and blamed the sabotage on Chinese soldiers. On that pretext, Japanese troops occupied all of Manchuria within months and created the puppet state of Manchukuo.

The League of Nations condemned the aggression, but did not stop it; Japan simply left the organization. The incident is regarded as the first step of the Japanese militarist expansion that would lead to war with China and to the Second World War in the Pacific.

title: New Zealand grants women the vote
headline: In 1893, New Zealand became the first country in the world with national women's suffrage.
story:
On September 19, 1893, the governor of New Zealand signed a new electoral law recognizing the right of all adult women, including Māori women, to vote in national elections. It was the first time a country had done so across its whole territory.

It had been achieved by a suffrage movement that presented parliament with petitions carrying almost 32,000 signatures, a huge number for the population of the time. New Zealand women could not, however, stand for parliament until 1919. The example spread to Australia and the Nordic countries in the following years.

title: Italy takes Rome and completes its unification
headline: In 1870, Italian troops entered Rome through the breach at Porta Pia and made it the capital.
story:
On September 20, 1870, taking advantage of the fact that France had withdrawn the garrison protecting the pope because of the Franco-Prussian War, the army of the young Kingdom of Italy opened a breach in the wall of Rome next to the Porta Pia and entered the city after a few hours of fighting.

The Papal States disappeared, and Rome became the capital of Italy. Pope Pius IX declared himself a "prisoner in the Vatican", and the Holy See did not recognize the Italian state until the Lateran Pacts of 1929. With the taking of Rome, the process of Italian unification begun decades earlier was complete.

title: France abolishes the monarchy
headline: In 1792, the Convention abolished the crown and the next day proclaimed the First French Republic.
story:
On September 21, 1792, in its first session, the newly elected National Convention unanimously decreed the abolition of the monarchy in France. King Louis XVI had already been under arrest since August. The next day the Republic was proclaimed, and a new calendar began to be counted from that "Year I".

Months later, the Convention tried and guillotined the king. The First Republic passed through the Terror, the Directory, and ended in 1804 when Napoleon crowned himself emperor, but the republican idea became anchored in French politics.

title: The war between Iran and Iraq begins
headline: In 1980, Iraq invaded Iran in a conflict that lasted eight years and caused close to a million deaths.
story:
On September 22, 1980, Saddam Hussein's Iraq launched a full-scale invasion of Iran, weakened by the previous year's Islamic revolution. Saddam wanted to annex an oil-rich province and to stop the revolutionary contagion, and expected a quick victory.

The war bogged down into a static front reminiscent of the trenches of 1914–1918, with waves of infantry, missile attacks on cities and the massive use of chemical weapons by Iraq. It ended in 1988 with a ceasefire and no clear victor, the borders almost unchanged, after between 500,000 and a million deaths.

title: The discovery of Neptune
headline: In 1846, a new planet was found right where calculations had predicted, with no need to search the sky for it.
story:
On September 23, 1846, the astronomer Johann Galle, at the Berlin Observatory, pointed his telescope at the position the French mathematician Urbain Le Verrier had sent him by letter and, that same night, identified an unknown planet: Neptune. It was less than a degree from the calculated point.

Le Verrier had deduced its existence and orbit from the anomalies in the motion of Uranus. It was a spectacular triumph of Newtonian mechanics: a planet found "at the tip of the pen" before it was found with the telescope. The Briton John Couch Adams had reached similar conclusions independently.

title: The Little Rock Nine
headline: In 1957, President Eisenhower sent in the army so that nine Black students could enter a high school in Arkansas.
story:
On September 24, 1957, troops of the 101st Airborne Division arrived in Little Rock, Arkansas, to escort nine Black students into Central High School. The state governor had used the National Guard to block their entry, defying the 1954 Supreme Court ruling against school segregation.

Eisenhower federalized the National Guard and sent in the army. For the entire school year, the nine students attended class amid insults and assaults, protected by soldiers. It was one of the first times federal power was imposed by force on a state in defense of civil rights.

title: Balboa sights the Pacific Ocean
headline: In 1513, Núñez de Balboa became the first European to see the Pacific from the Americas.
story:
On September 25, 1513, after weeks of cutting through the jungle of the Isthmus of Panama with a handful of men and Indigenous guides, the conquistador Vasco Núñez de Balboa climbed a hill and saw to the south an immense stretch of water. Days later he waded into it with his sword and claimed it, along with "all its coasts", for the Crown of Castile. He called it the "South Sea".

The discovery showed that the Americas were a continent separated from Asia by another ocean, later named the Pacific by Magellan. Balboa was beheaded in 1519, accused of treason by a rival.

title: The man who prevented a nuclear war
headline: In 1983, a Soviet officer disobeyed protocol on receiving a false alert of a US nuclear attack.
story:
In the early hours of September 26, 1983, the Soviet early-warning system alerted Lieutenant Colonel Stanislav Petrov, on duty in a bunker near Moscow, that the United States had launched five intercontinental missiles. Protocol called for informing the command immediately for a nuclear response.

Petrov reasoned that a real attack would involve hundreds of missiles, not five, and decided to report it as a system malfunction. He was right: the satellites had confused sunlight reflected off clouds with launches. It happened in one of the tensest weeks of the Cold War. His decision, secret for years, may have prevented a catastrophe.

title: Champollion deciphers the hieroglyphs
headline: In 1822, a young Frenchman announced that he had finally read the writing of ancient Egypt.
story:
On September 27, 1822, Jean-François Champollion presented to the Academy of Inscriptions in Paris his "Letter to M. Dacier", setting out the system for reading Egyptian hieroglyphs. He had spent years studying the Rosetta Stone, a slab with the same decree in three scripts, and comparing the names of pharaohs such as Ptolemy and Cleopatra.

His key: hieroglyphs were not only symbols but also signs that represented sounds. The discovery opened three thousand years of texts to reading — treatises, contracts, poetry, king lists — and founded Egyptology as a science.

title: Fleming discovers penicillin
headline: In 1928, a mold that appeared by accident on a laboratory dish opened the era of antibiotics.
story:
On September 28, 1928, returning from holiday to his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital in London, the bacteriologist Alexander Fleming noticed that one of his dishes with staphylococcus cultures had been contaminated with a mold, and that around that mold the bacteria had died. The fungus was 'Penicillium notatum'.

Fleming published the finding but could not isolate the active substance. It was a team at Oxford, led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, who managed to produce and test it as a medicine from 1940. Penicillin, available in bulk during the Second World War, saved millions of lives.

title: The Munich Agreement
headline: In 1938, France and Britain handed Hitler part of Czechoslovakia to avoid war.
story:
On September 29, 1938, the heads of government of Germany, Italy, France and Britain met in Munich — without inviting Czechoslovakia — and agreed to cede to Germany the Sudetenland, the Czech region with a German-speaking population and the country's main defenses.

British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain returned to London waving the paper and proclaiming "peace for our time". Less than a year later, Germany occupied the rest of Czechoslovakia and then invaded Poland. "Munich" became a synonym for the futility of giving in to a dictator.

title: 'The Magic Flute' premieres
headline: In 1791, Mozart conducted the premiere of his last opera nine weeks before his death.
story:
On September 30, 1791, in a popular theater on the outskirts of Vienna, 'The Magic Flute' premiered, with music by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart and a libretto by Emanuel Schikaneder, who also played the bird-catcher Papageno. It mixed fairy tale, comedy, Masonic symbolism and arias of enormous difficulty.

It was an immediate success with the public, not just the court. Mozart, struggling with money and health, could enjoy it for only a few weeks: he died on December 5 at the age of 35, leaving his Requiem unfinished. 'The Magic Flute' is today one of the most performed operas in the world.

title: The People's Republic of China is born
headline: In 1949, Mao Zedong proclaimed the new communist state from Beijing after winning the civil war.
story:
On October 1, 1949, before a crowd in Tiananmen Square in Beijing, Mao Zedong announced the founding of the People's Republic of China. The Communist Party had won the civil war against the Nationalist government of Chiang Kai-shek, who took refuge on the island of Taiwan with what was left of his army.

So began communist rule over a country of hundreds of millions of people. After decades of convulsive campaigns and market reforms since 1978, China has become the second-largest economy in the world. October 1 is its national holiday.

title: Saladin retakes Jerusalem
headline: In 1187, the sultan Saladin took Jerusalem from the Crusaders, 88 years after they had conquered it.
story:
On October 2, 1187, after a short siege, the sultan Saladin entered Jerusalem. Months earlier he had annihilated the army of the Crusader kingdom at the Battle of Hattin. Unlike the Christian massacre of 1099, Saladin allowed the inhabitants to leave on payment of a ransom and freed many who could not pay it.

The loss of the holy city shocked Europe and set off the Third Crusade, with kings such as Richard the Lionheart, who recovered part of the coast but not Jerusalem. Saladin was remembered, in the West as well, as a model of the chivalrous ruler.

title: The reunification of Germany
headline: In 1990, less than a year after the Wall fell, East Germany joined the Federal Republic and Germany was one state again.
story:
At midnight on October 3, 1990, the German Democratic Republic ceased to exist and its five states joined the Federal Republic of Germany. A single flag was raised outside the Reichstag in Berlin before hundreds of thousands of people.

Reunification was rapid: the Wall had fallen in November 1989, and within a few months the economic union, an internal treaty and the approval of the four victorious powers of 1945 were negotiated. Integrating the East, with its obsolete economy, took decades and trillions of euros. October 3 is Germany's national holiday.

title: Sputnik opens the space age
headline: In 1957, the Soviet Union put the first artificial satellite into orbit and stunned the world.
story:
On October 4, 1957, a Soviet rocket placed Sputnik 1 into orbit, an aluminum sphere 58 centimeters across and weighing 84 kilos, with four antennas that emitted a simple "beep" pickable by radio amateurs across the planet. It circled the Earth every 96 minutes.

The psychological impact was enormous: if the Soviets could put something in orbit, they could also launch missiles at any point on the globe. The United States accelerated its space program, created NASA and overhauled science teaching. The space race had begun.

title: The Women's March on Versailles
headline: In 1789, thousands of Parisian women marched to Versailles and forced the king to move to Paris.
story:
On October 5, 1789, faced with scarcity and the price of bread, several thousand women from the markets of Paris set out in the rain toward Versailles, 20 kilometers away, followed by the National Guard. They demanded bread and that the king sign the revolutionary decrees.

After a tense night and a few deaths, the crowd got Louis XVI and his family to leave Versailles and move to the Tuileries Palace, in the center of Paris, under the watch of the people. The monarchy lost its gilded refuge and was left at the mercy of the revolutionary city.

title: The Yom Kippur War begins
headline: In 1973, Egypt and Syria attacked Israel by surprise on the holiest day of the Jewish calendar.
story:
On October 6, 1973, coinciding with Yom Kippur, Egypt and Syria launched a coordinated attack to recover the territories lost to Israel in 1967: Egypt crossed the Suez Canal and Syria attacked the Golan Heights. Israel, caught off guard, suffered serious setbacks in the first days before counterattacking and regaining the initiative with an airlift of American matériel.

The war ended in three weeks with a ceasefire negotiated by the superpowers. The Arab oil-exporting countries responded to Western support for Israel with an embargo that sent prices soaring and caused the economic crisis of 1973.

title: The United States invades Afghanistan
headline: In 2001, the US and its allies attacked Afghanistan to overthrow the Taliban and pursue al-Qaeda.
story:
On October 7, 2001, less than a month after the 9/11 attacks, the United States and Britain began bombing Afghanistan, whose Taliban regime was sheltering Osama bin Laden and the leadership of al-Qaeda. With air support and special forces, the Afghan militia of the Northern Alliance took Kabul in November.

Overthrowing the Taliban was quick; stabilizing the country, impossible. The war dragged on for twenty years, the longest in US history. In 2021, after the American withdrawal, the Taliban regained power within a few weeks.

title: The Great Chicago Fire
headline: In 1871, a fire razed downtown Chicago, left 100,000 people homeless and transformed the city.
story:
On the night of October 8, 1871, a fire broke out in a barn on the southwest side of Chicago. Legend blames a cow that supposedly kicked over a lantern, though it was never proven. After a dry summer, with wooden houses and sidewalks and a strong wind, the fire crossed the river and razed the heart of the city over two days.

About 300 people died and more than 17,000 buildings burned over an area of 9 km². The rebuilding, in steel and concrete and with fire regulations, made Chicago the cradle of the skyscraper and a laboratory of modern architecture.

title: The execution of Che Guevara
headline: In 1967, the Argentine guerrilla was shot in Bolivia a day after being captured by the army.
story:
On October 8, 1967, Bolivian troops backed by CIA advisers captured Ernesto "Che" Guevara, wounded, in a ravine in southeastern Bolivia, where he was trying to build a guerrilla foothold. The next day, October 9, he was executed in the schoolhouse of the village of La Higuera on government orders.

Guevara, an Argentine doctor and one of the figures of the Cuban Revolution, had given up his posts in Cuba to carry the revolution to other continents. After his death, the photo of his corpse and, above all, a portrait taken years earlier made him a global icon of rebellion.

title: The Xinhai Revolution in China
headline: In 1911, a military mutiny in Wuchang began the revolution that ended 2,000 years of empire in China.
story:
On October 10, 1911, soldiers of a garrison at Wuchang, in central China, mutinied against the Qing dynasty. The uprising, precipitated by the accidental discovery of a conspiracy, spread from province to province within a few weeks.

In February 1912 the child emperor Puyi abdicated and the Republic of China was proclaimed, with Sun Yat-sen as its first president. More than two millennia of imperial rule were ending. The republic, however, soon sank into warlord conflict. October 10 is a national holiday in Taiwan.

title: The Second Vatican Council opens
headline: In 1962, the Catholic Church began the greatest renewal of its liturgy and doctrine in centuries.
story:
On October 11, 1962, Pope John XXIII opened the Second Vatican Council in St Peter's Basilica, with more than 2,000 bishops from around the world. The aim, he said, was an "aggiornamento", a bringing up to date of the Church in the face of the modern world.

Over three years, the council approved profound changes: Mass in the vernacular rather than Latin, greater lay participation, openness to dialogue with other religions and to religious freedom. It shaped the Catholic Church of recent decades and is still a reference point in debate between more reformist and more traditionalist sectors.

title: Columbus reaches the Americas
headline: In 1492, Columbus's expedition made landfall on a Caribbean island and permanently joined two worlds.
story:
In the early hours of October 12, 1492, a lookout on the Pinta shouted "land!" after 33 days of crossing from the Canary Islands. At dawn they landed on a small island in the Bahamas, called Guanahani by its inhabitants, which Columbus named San Salvador and claimed for Castile.

Columbus died convinced he had reached Asia. The contact between Europe and the Americas began an immense exchange of people, crops, animals and diseases, the conquest and colonization of a continent and the demographic collapse of its peoples. In Spain, October 12 is the national holiday.

title: The fall of the Templars
headline: In 1307, on a Friday the 13th, the king of France ordered the simultaneous arrest of all the Knights Templar in the kingdom.
story:
At dawn on Friday, October 13, 1307, officers of King Philip IV of France opened sealed orders and simultaneously arrested hundreds of members of the Order of the Temple, a powerful military and financial organization born of the Crusades. They were accused of heresy, blasphemy and obscene practices; many confessed under torture.

The king, deeply in debt to the order, seized its property. The pope dissolved the Temple in 1312, and the last grand master, Jacques de Molay, died at the stake in 1314. The episode fed centuries of legend and is one of the roots of the superstition of "Friday the 13th".

title: The Battle of Hastings
headline: In 1066, the victory of William of Normandy changed forever the language, nobility and state of England.
story:
On October 14, 1066, near Hastings, in southern England, the army of Duke William of Normandy defeated that of King Harold II, killed in the fighting — according to tradition, by an arrow in the eye. The Saxons, who days earlier had repelled a Norwegian invasion in the north, arrived exhausted after a forced march.

William "the Conqueror" was crowned king at Christmas. The Norman conquest replaced the English aristocracy with a Franco-Norman one, transformed the language with thousands of French words, and created a centralized state whose survey, the Domesday Book, was compiled in 1086.

title: The Gregorian calendar begins
headline: In 1582, Catholic countries jumped from October 4 to October 15 to correct the calendar's drift.
story:
The Julian calendar, in force since 46 BC, counted the year slightly too long, and over 16 centuries a drift of 10 days had built up relative to the seasons. To correct it, Pope Gregory XIII ordered that, in Catholic territories, Thursday, October 4, 1582, be followed directly by Friday, October 15. Those ten days never existed.

He also changed the leap-year rule. Protestant and Orthodox countries took centuries to adopt it — Britain in 1752, Russia in 1918 — which explains mismatches of dates in history. It is the civil calendar of almost the whole world.

title: Pope John Paul II is elected
headline: In 1978, the Polish cardinal Karol Wojtyła was elected pope, the first non-Italian in 455 years.
story:
On October 16, 1978, after the very brief pontificate of John Paul I, the conclave elected as pope the cardinal of Kraków, Karol Wojtyła, 58. He took the name John Paul II and broke a centuries-old tradition: he was the first non-Italian pontiff since 1523 and the first Slav in history.

His pontificate lasted almost 27 years. He traveled to more than a hundred countries, became a media figure and played a prominent role in the fall of communism in his native Poland and in Eastern Europe. He also held firm doctrinal positions that earned him criticism within and outside the Church.

title: The oil embargo of 1973
headline: In 1973, the Arab countries cut off crude oil to the West and caused the first great oil crisis.
story:
On October 17, 1973, the Arab oil-exporting countries announced a progressive cut in production and an embargo on the United States and other allies of Israel in the Yom Kippur War, which had begun days earlier. Within a few months, the price of a barrel quadrupled.

Western economies, which had grown for decades on cheap energy, went into recession with high inflation, something thought impossible. There were gasoline rationing and car-free Sundays. The crisis spurred energy saving, the search for alternatives and a greater awareness of dependence on oil.

title: Louis XIV revokes the Edict of Nantes
headline: In 1685, France outlawed Protestantism and drove hundreds of thousands of people into exile.
story:
On October 18, 1685, Louis XIV signed the Edict of Fontainebleau, revoking the Edict of Nantes of 1598. That earlier edict had granted the French Protestants, the Huguenots, freedom of worship and certain guarantees after the wars of religion. Now their churches and schools were closed, their services banned, and they were forbidden to emigrate, while being persecuted if they stayed.

Between 200,000 and 300,000 Huguenots fled despite the ban, mainly to the Netherlands, England, Switzerland and Prussia, taking with them trades, capital and knowledge. It was a drain on the French economy and a boost to those of the receiving countries.

title: The surrender at Yorktown
headline: In 1781, the capitulation of the British army in Virginia decided the independence of the United States.
story:
On October 19, 1781, at Yorktown, Virginia, the British general Charles Cornwallis surrendered some 8,000 men after a three-week siege. A Franco-American army under Washington and Rochambeau had surrounded him by land, while the French fleet prevented reinforcements or evacuation by sea.

The news destroyed the will to fight in the British Parliament. Although minor fighting continued, there were no more major campaigns. Two years later, the Treaty of Paris recognized the independence of the thirteen colonies.

title: The Long March ends
headline: In 1935, the Chinese communists completed a retreat of 9,000 km that saved the party and elevated Mao.
story:
In October 1935, after a year on the march, the remnants of the Chinese Red Army reached the arid province of Shaanxi, in the northwest of the country. They had set out a year earlier from the south, about 86,000 strong, fleeing the Nationalist army's encirclement. They covered more than 9,000 kilometers crossing rivers, mountain ranges and marshes under constant attack; fewer than 10,000 survived.

The Long March came close to wiping out the Communist Party, but it became its founding myth and consolidated the leadership of Mao Zedong. From Yan'an, the party rebuilt itself and, fourteen years later, won the civil war.

title: The Battle of Trafalgar
headline: In 1805, Nelson's fleet destroyed the Franco-Spanish fleet off Cádiz and secured British command of the seas.
story:
On October 21, 1805, off Cape Trafalgar, near Cádiz, 27 British ships under Admiral Horatio Nelson attacked 33 French and Spanish ships, breaking their line in two columns. Within hours, the allied fleet was destroyed: it lost 22 ships and thousands of men; the British, none.

Nelson died from a shot in the middle of the battle, becoming a national hero at once. Trafalgar dashed any plan of Napoleon's to invade England and gave the Royal Navy a naval supremacy it held for a century.

title: The Cuban Missile Crisis breaks out
headline: In 1962, Kennedy revealed on television that the USSR was installing nuclear missiles in Cuba and announced a naval blockade.
story:
On the night of October 22, 1962, President John F. Kennedy addressed Americans to report that spy planes had photographed Soviet nuclear missile bases under construction in Cuba, a few minutes' flight from the cities of the southern US. He announced a naval "quarantine" of the island and demanded the withdrawal of the weapons.

For thirteen days, the world lived on the brink of nuclear war. In the end, the USSR withdrew the missiles in exchange for a US commitment not to invade Cuba and, secretly, to remove missiles from Turkey. It was the most dangerous moment of the Cold War.

title: The Hungarian Revolution of 1956
headline: In 1956, a popular uprising in Hungary against the communist regime was crushed by Soviet tanks.
story:
On October 23, 1956, a student demonstration in Budapest in support of the Polish reforms turned into a general uprising. The political police fired on the crowd, militias formed, the statue of Stalin came down, and the reformist Imre Nagy took over the government, announcing the end of one-party rule and withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact.

On November 4, the Red Army moved in force and crushed the revolt: about 2,500 Hungarians dead and 200,000 in exile. Nagy was secretly executed in 1958. The West condemned the repression but did not intervene, also busy with the Suez crisis.

title: The United Nations is born
headline: In 1945, the UN Charter took effect with the goal of "saving succeeding generations from the scourge of war".
story:
On October 24, 1945, the Charter of the United Nations took effect after being ratified by China, France, the USSR, Britain, the United States and most of the other signatories. It replaced the failed interwar League of Nations.

The UN created a General Assembly of all states and a fifteen-member Security Council, five of them permanent and holding a veto. It has promoted decolonization, peacekeeping missions, humanitarian aid and human rights treaties, though the veto has blocked its action in many crises. October 24 is United Nations Day.

title: The Battle of Agincourt
headline: In 1415, an exhausted, outnumbered English army destroyed the French cavalry in the mud of Agincourt.
story:
On October 25, 1415, during the Hundred Years' War, the army of King Henry V of England, exhausted and outnumbered, faced the French nobility near Agincourt, in northern France. A field turned to mud by rain, a narrow front between woods and, above all, the English longbowmen turned the French charge into a massacre.

Thousands of French knights died; English casualties were minimal. The victory strengthened the English position in France for a generation and was fixed as a national feat, above all thanks to the play Shakespeare devoted to it two centuries later.

title: The Football Association is founded
headline: In 1863, London clubs agreed on common rules and created football as it is played today.
story:
On October 26, 1863, representatives of eleven clubs and schools met at the Freemasons' Tavern in London to fix a single set of rules for a game that until then changed from place to place. From those sessions came the Football Association and, weeks later, the first "Laws of the Game".

The great split was banning carrying the ball with the hands and tripping; the supporters of those practices broke away and years later codified rugby. Association football spread with British trade and industry and is today the most played and watched sport in the world.

title: The "Black Saturday" of the Cuban crisis
headline: In 1962, on the most dangerous day of the missile crisis, a spy plane was shot down over Cuba.
story:
On October 27, 1962, at the height of the missile crisis, a Soviet missile shot down an American U-2 spy plane over Cuba and killed its pilot. That same day, Soviet submarines harassed by the US Navy came close to using nuclear-armed torpedoes; on one of them, the officer Vasili Arkhipov refused to authorize the launch.

With tension at its peak, that night the deal was struck between Kennedy and Khrushchev that resolved the crisis the next day. Historians consider October 27, 1962, the moment the world came closest to a nuclear war.

title: The March on Rome
headline: In 1922, pressure from the Fascists led the king of Italy to hand the government to Benito Mussolini.
story:
On October 28, 1922, tens of thousands of Fascist militants converged on Rome in a threatening march. The army could easily have stopped it, but King Victor Emmanuel III refused to sign a state of siege and, the next day, asked Benito Mussolini to form a government. The Fascist leader arrived in the capital by train.

In less than three years, Mussolini turned Italy into a one-party dictatorship. The March on Rome was the model that inspired Hitler and stood as an example of how an anti-democratic movement can take power with the appearance of legality.

title: Wall Street's "Black Tuesday"
headline: In 1929, the collapse of the New York stock market marked the start of the Great Depression.
story:
On October 29, 1929, "Black Tuesday", 16 million shares were sold on the New York Stock Exchange in a day of panic. It capped a week of falls that wiped out billions of dollars and the gains of years of speculative euphoria, much of it bought with borrowed money.

The crash sank banks and companies and dragged the United States and much of the world into the Great Depression: mass unemployment, deflation and poverty for a decade. The crisis fed the rise of authoritarian movements in Europe and led to a rethinking of the role of the state in the economy.

title: The Tsar Bomba
headline: In 1961, the USSR detonated over the Arctic the largest explosion ever caused by human beings.
story:
On October 30, 1961, a Soviet bomber dropped over the Novaya Zemlya archipelago, in the Arctic, the "Tsar Bomba", a thermonuclear device of about 50 megatons, some 3,000 times the Hiroshima bomb. The fireball was several kilometers across and the shockwave circled the Earth three times; the flash was seen 1,000 km away.

Its theoretical yield had been halved to give the aircraft a chance to escape. It was above all a show of force in the middle of the Cold War. Nothing more powerful has ever been tested or built; it was too big to be a practical weapon.

title: Luther and the 95 Theses
headline: In 1517, a German monk made public 95 objections to the sale of indulgences and opened the Protestant Reformation.
story:
On October 31, 1517, according to tradition, the Augustinian friar Martin Luther nailed to the door of the castle church in Wittenberg a document with 95 theses in Latin against the sale of indulgences, with which the Church promised to reduce the punishment for sins in exchange for money.

Thanks to the printing press, the theses spread across Germany within weeks. What began as an academic debate ended in schism: Luther was excommunicated in 1521 and his movement gave rise to the Protestant churches. Western Christianity was divided and Europe endured more than a century of religious wars.

title: The Lisbon earthquake
headline: In 1755, a quake, a tsunami and a fire destroyed Lisbon and shook European thought.
story:
On the morning of November 1, 1755, All Saints' Day, with the churches full, an earthquake with an estimated magnitude of around 8.5 shook Lisbon for several minutes. Half an hour later, a tsunami several meters high razed the harbor and the center, and then a fire burned for five days. Tens of thousands of people died.

The minister Pombal rebuilt the city with a grid layout and pioneering earthquake-resistant buildings. The catastrophe, which struck on a holy day, fueled a philosophical debate about divine goodness and evil; Voltaire used it in his 'Candide'.

title: The Balfour Declaration
headline: In 1917, the British government expressed its support for a Jewish "national home" in Palestine.
story:
On November 2, 1917, the British foreign secretary, Arthur Balfour, sent a letter to the leader of the Jewish community, Lord Rothschild, in which the government declared that it viewed "with favour" the establishment of a "national home for the Jewish people" in Palestine, without prejudice to the rights of the other communities.

Palestine was then under Ottoman rule; shortly afterward it passed to British control. The declaration, made to win support in the middle of the war, is a key precursor of political Zionism, of the creation of Israel in 1948 and of the conflict that continues.

title: Laika, the first living creature in orbit
headline: In 1957, a stray dog from Moscow became the first animal to orbit the Earth, on a one-way trip.
story:
On November 3, 1957, barely a month after Sputnik 1, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 2 with Laika aboard, a dog picked up from the streets of Moscow. The aim was to test whether a living being could survive the launch and weightlessness.

The capsule had no return system: Laika was doomed from the start. She died a few hours after liftoff from overheating, though the USSR maintained for years that she had lived several days. Her flight showed that an organism could withstand orbital flight and opened the way to human astronauts.

title: The Iran hostage crisis
headline: In 1979, Iranian students stormed the US embassy in Tehran and held 52 people for 444 days.
story:
On November 4, 1979, months after the revolution that overthrew the shah, a group of Islamist students occupied the American embassy in Tehran and took its staff hostage. They demanded the handover of the shah, exiled and ill in the United States, to be put on trial.

The crisis lasted 444 days. A military rescue attempt in 1980 failed with eight dead in the desert. The hostages were released on the very day in 1981 that Ronald Reagan replaced Jimmy Carter, whose presidency was sunk by the episode. The United States and Iran have not restored relations since.

title: The Gunpowder Plot
headline: In 1605, a group of English Catholics came close to blowing up Parliament with the king inside.
story:
On the night of November 4–5, 1605, Guy Fawkes was arrested guarding 36 barrels of gunpowder hidden in a cellar beneath the House of Lords. A group of Catholics, persecuted by the law, planned to blow up Parliament during the opening session, with King James I and much of the country's elite present.

Betrayed by an anonymous letter, the conspirators were captured or killed and executed. Since then, every November 5 the United Kingdom marks "Bonfire Night" with bonfires and fireworks, and the Guy Fawkes mask has become a global symbol of protest.

title: Lincoln is elected president
headline: In 1860, the victory of an anti-slavery candidate hastened the secession of the South and the Civil War.
story:
On November 6, 1860, Abraham Lincoln, of the young Republican Party, won the US presidency without gaining a single vote in most Southern states, where he was not even on the ballot. Lincoln did not propose abolishing slavery where it already existed, but he did propose preventing its spread to the new territories.

The slave states saw this as an existential threat. Before he took office in March, seven had seceded from the Union and formed the Confederate States. In April the war began, the bloodiest in the country's history.

title: The October Revolution
headline: In 1917, Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in Petrograd and founded the first communist state.
story:
On the night of November 7, 1917 (October 25 in the Russian calendar), the Bolsheviks, with the Red Guard and sailors from Kronstadt, occupied the key points of the Russian capital, Petrograd, and stormed the Winter Palace, seat of the provisional government that had emerged from the fall of the tsar in February.

The next day, the congress of soviets approved decrees on peace and the distribution of land and appointed a government headed by Lenin. A three-year civil war followed. From that coup came the Soviet Union, which existed until 1991 and shaped the 20th century.

title: The discovery of X-rays
headline: In 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen detected an invisible radiation able to pass through the body and photograph the bones.
story:
On November 8, 1895, the German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen, experimenting with cathode-ray tubes in a darkened room, saw a fluorescent screen glowing a meter and a half away, out of reach of those rays. An unknown radiation — he called it "X-rays" — was coming out of the tube and passing through cardboard.

He soon found that it also passed through flesh, but not through bone or metal: he made an X-ray of his wife's hand, with her ring clearly visible. Within weeks, hospitals around the world were using X-rays to see fractures and bullets. Röntgen received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.

title: The fall of the Berlin Wall
headline: In 1989, a confused announcement on television opened the Wall, and thousands of Berliners crossed to the West that same night.
story:
On the night of November 9, 1989, a spokesman for the East German government read a new travel regulation at a press conference and, asked when it took effect, answered hesitantly: "As far as I know… immediately." The agencies reported that East Germany was opening the border.

Thousands of people crowded the crossings of the Wall. With no clear orders and overwhelmed, the guards ended up raising the barriers. East and West Berliners climbed onto the Wall by the Brandenburg Gate and began chipping at it. Less than a year later, the two Germanys reunified; the Cold War was coming undone.

title: "Dr. Livingstone, I presume?"
headline: In 1871, the journalist Stanley found in the heart of Africa the explorer no one had heard from in years.
story:
On November 10, 1871, at Ujiji, on the shore of Lake Tanganyika, the Welshman Henry Morton Stanley, sent by a New York newspaper, found David Livingstone, the famous Scottish missionary and explorer thought to be dead after years without news. Stanley greeted him, by his own account, with the words "Dr. Livingstone, I presume?".

Livingstone, ill, refused to leave and died in Africa in 1873. Stanley's report was a worldwide success. The adventure revived European interest in the interior of the continent and was one of the preludes to the colonial partition of Africa in the following decades.

title: The armistice that ended the First World War
headline: In 1918, at 11 a.m. on the 11th, the guns fell silent on the Western Front.
story:
On November 11, 1918, at 5 a.m., in a railway carriage stopped in the forest of Compiègne, Germany signed the armistice with the Allies. The ceasefire took effect at 11:00: "the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month". Some soldiers died that very morning, in the final hours.

Germany had to withdraw from occupied territories, hand over weapons and accept the occupation of the left bank of the Rhine. The definitive peace treaty, Versailles, came in 1919 with very harsh terms. November 11 is a day of remembrance for the fallen in many countries.

title: The birth of the World Wide Web
headline: In 1990, two CERN researchers presented the project that turned the internet into something for everyone.
story:
On November 12, 1990, at the European laboratory CERN, Tim Berners-Lee and Robert Cailliau presented a formal proposal for a "hypertext" system that would let documents be linked and read over the internet through a browser. Berners-Lee had already written the first server, the first browser and the HTML language.

The internet had existed since the 1970s, but it was the preserve of universities and experts. The Web added a simple layer — pages, links, addresses — that anyone could use. CERN released it patent-free in 1993. Within a few years it transformed commerce, media, politics and everyday life.

title: The Paris attacks of 2015
headline: In 2015, coordinated Islamic State attacks on a concert hall, café terraces and a stadium killed 130 people.
story:
On the night of November 13, 2015, several jihadist commandos acted at once in Paris: they blew themselves up near the Stade de France during a match, shot up the terraces of bars and restaurants, and stormed the Bataclan hall during a rock concert, where they massacred the audience. One hundred and thirty people died and more than 400 were injured.

The Islamic State, based in Syria and Iraq, claimed the killings. France declared a state of emergency, intensified the bombing in Syria and tightened border controls. It was the deadliest attack on French soil since the Second World War.

title: First spacecraft to orbit another planet
headline: In 1971, the Mariner 9 probe entered orbit around Mars and mapped it almost in full.
story:
On November 14, 1971, the US probe Mariner 9 fired its engines and let itself be captured by the gravity of Mars, becoming the first human object to orbit a planet other than Earth, ahead of two Soviet probes that arrived days later.

At first, a global dust storm covered the entire planet; NASA waited for it to clear. Then, for almost a year, Mariner 9 photographed 85% of the surface and revealed giant volcanoes such as Olympus Mons, the Valles Marineris canyon and dry channels that suggested water in the past.

title: Brazil becomes a republic
headline: In 1889, a military coup deposed Emperor Pedro II and proclaimed the Republic after nearly 70 years of monarchy.
story:
On November 15, 1889, a group of soldiers led by Marshal Deodoro da Fonseca deposed Emperor Pedro II in Rio de Janeiro. He had reigned since 1831. There was almost no resistance. The emperor and his family left for exile in Europe two days later.

Brazil, which had abolished slavery only a year earlier — the last country in the Americas to do so — was transformed into a federal republic. The new regime, dominated for decades by the coffee and cattle oligarchies, kept the date as a national holiday: the Day of the Proclamation of the Republic.

title: Pizarro captures the Inca Atahualpa
headline: In 1532, about 170 Spaniards seized the Inca emperor at Cajamarca and hastened the fall of his empire.
story:
On November 16, 1532, in the square of Cajamarca, in the northern Andes of Peru, Francisco Pizarro ambushed Atahualpa, ruler of an Inca empire of millions of people fresh out of a civil war. With fewer than 170 men, horses, arquebuses and cannon, the Spaniards caused a massacre and captured the Inca.

Atahualpa offered to fill a room with gold and silver in exchange for his freedom. He kept his word, but the Spaniards executed him anyway in 1533. The fall of the Inca, combined with epidemics and alliances with subject peoples, allowed a handful of conquistadors to dominate the largest state in the Americas.

title: The Suez Canal opens
headline: In 1869, a 160 km canal joined the Mediterranean and the Red Sea and halved the route from Europe to Asia.
story:
On November 17, 1869, the Suez Canal, in Egypt, opened to traffic after ten years of work directed by the Frenchman Ferdinand de Lesseps and carried out by hundreds of thousands of Egyptian workers in very harsh conditions. It connected the Mediterranean with the Red Sea without locks.

Ships no longer had to sail around Africa: the distance between London and Bombay was shortened by about 7,000 km. The canal became a vital artery of world trade and a contested strategic point: Britain controlled it for decades, and its nationalization by Egypt in 1956 caused an international crisis.

title: The Jonestown tragedy
headline: In 1978, more than 900 members of an American cult died in the jungle of Guyana in a mass murder-suicide.
story:
On November 18, 1978, at an isolated settlement in Guyana called Jonestown, the preacher Jim Jones ordered the roughly one thousand followers of his cult, the Peoples Temple, to drink a beverage laced with cyanide. Beforehand, his men had murdered on a nearby airstrip Congressman Leo Ryan, who was investigating complaints from relatives, and four other people.

918 people died, a third of them children, who were forced to swallow the poison. It was the largest deliberate loss of American civilian lives until 9/11. The expression "drink the Kool-Aid" comes from it.

title: The Gettysburg Address
headline: In 1863, Lincoln summed up the meaning of the Civil War and of democracy in two minutes and 272 words.
story:
On November 19, 1863, at the dedication of a cemetery for those fallen at the Battle of Gettysburg, President Abraham Lincoln gave a very short speech, after the main orator, who had spoken for two hours. Lincoln tied the war to the ideal of the Declaration of Independence — "all men are created equal" — and asked that "government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth".

Some newspapers dismissed it; over time it became one of the founding texts of American political identity and a classic definition of democracy.

title: The death of Franco
headline: In 1975, the dictator's death after nearly 40 years in power opened the transition to democracy in Spain.
story:
On November 20, 1975, after weeks of agony, Francisco Franco died in Madrid. He had ruled Spain as a dictator since the end of the Civil War in 1939. He had designated as his successor "with the title of king" Juan Carlos de Borbón, who was sworn in two days later.

Contrary to what many feared, the dictatorship did not perpetuate itself and the country did not explode. In less than three years the parties were legalized, free elections were held and a democratic constitution was approved by referendum. That process is known as the Spanish Transition.

title: The first human flight
headline: In 1783, two men rose above Paris in a hot-air balloon built by the Montgolfier brothers.
story:
On November 21, 1783, Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes lifted off from a garden in Paris in a balloon of cloth and paper inflated with hot air, built by the Montgolfier brothers, papermakers. They flew for about 25 minutes, covered 9 km over the city and landed while stoking the fire with pitchforks to avoid coming down on the rooftops.

It was the first time human beings had risen from the ground and traveled through the air. Ten days later, another balloon, this one of hydrogen, made an even longer flight. "Balloon mania" gripped Europe.

title: The assassination of John F. Kennedy
headline: In 1963, the president of the United States was shot in an open car in Dallas.
story:
On November 22, 1963, around 12:30, as his motorcade drove through downtown Dallas, Texas, in a convertible, President John F. Kennedy was hit by two shots, one of them in the head, and died shortly afterward at the hospital. That afternoon police arrested Lee Harvey Oswald, a former Marine, who was himself murdered two days later on camera.

An official commission concluded that Oswald acted alone, but the doubts, the gaps and the Cold War atmosphere fed countless conspiracy theories. The assassination, broadcast and analyzed endlessly, marked a generation.

title: The Irpinia earthquake
headline: In 1980, a quake devastated southern Italy, leaving close to 3,000 dead and a heavily criticized relief effort.
story:
On the afternoon of November 23, 1980, an earthquake of magnitude 6.9 shook the Irpinia region, in the interior of Campania, east of Naples. Entire mountain villages, with old stone houses, were razed. About 2,900 people died, some 8,800 were injured and close to 250,000 were left homeless.

The rescue arrived late and in disarray; the Italian president publicly denounced the slowness of the state. The reconstruction, with enormous public funds, later became a case study of corruption and mafia infiltration in public works.

title: 'On the Origin of Species' is published
headline: In 1859, Darwin's book on evolution by natural selection went on sale and sold out on the first day.
story:
On November 24, 1859, 'On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection', by Charles Darwin, went on sale in London. The initial print run, about 1,250 copies, sold out among booksellers the same day. Darwin had spent twenty years gathering evidence and only decided to publish on learning that Alfred Russel Wallace had reached similar ideas.

The book argued that all species descend from common ancestors and change through the differential reproduction of the best-adapted. It raised a fierce debate, scientific and religious, but it prevailed: it is the foundation of modern biology.

title: The Anti-Comintern Pact
headline: In 1936, Germany and Japan signed an agreement against the Communist International that was the seed of the Axis.
story:
On November 25, 1936, Nazi Germany and the Empire of Japan signed the Anti-Comintern Pact in Berlin, an agreement aimed on the surface against the Communist International directed from Moscow, but in fact against the Soviet Union. A secret protocol provided for consultations and neutrality in the event of war with the USSR.

Italy joined in 1937, and other countries later. The pact drew together the three powers that in 1940 would form the Rome-Berlin-Tokyo Axis. It was thrown into doubt in 1939, when Hitler signed a non-aggression pact with Stalin without warning Tokyo.

title: The Mumbai attacks of 2008
headline: In 2008, ten Pakistani terrorists spread terror for three days in India's largest city.
story:
On the night of November 26, 2008, ten armed men of the group Lashkar-e-Taiba, who had come by boat from Pakistan, attacked several points in southern Mumbai: the central train station, two luxury hotels, a hospital, a café and a Jewish center.
