The siege of the Taj Mahal and Oberoi hotels lasted three days.

About 175 people died and more than 300 were injured. Nine terrorists were killed; the only one captured alive was executed in 2012. The attacks stretched relations between India and Pakistan, two nuclear powers, to the limit.

title: Nobel signs the will that created his prizes
headline: In 1895, the inventor of dynamite set it down in writing that his fortune should fund annual prizes for the good of humanity.
story:
On November 27, 1895, at the Swedish-Norwegian Club in Paris, Alfred Nobel signed his last will. He left most of an enormous fortune, amassed with dynamite and other explosives, to a fund whose interest would be distributed each year among those who had most benefited humanity in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace.

The family contested the will and there were several years of litigation. The first Nobel Prizes were awarded in 1901. It is said that Nobel decided to create them after reading, by mistake, his own obituary, which called him "the merchant of death".

title: The Tehran Conference
headline: In 1943, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin met for the first time and planned the Normandy landings.
story:
On November 28, 1943, the first summit of the "Big Three" began in Tehran, the capital of Iran: the American Franklin D. Roosevelt, the Briton Winston Churchill and the Soviet Joseph Stalin. Over four days they agreed to open a second front in France in the spring of 1944 — the future D-Day — to ease the pressure on the Eastern Front.

They also sketched out the division of postwar Europe and the westward shift of Poland's borders. Tehran marked the moment when the Allied coalition truly coordinated its strategy to win the war.

title: The UN votes for the partition of Palestine
headline: In 1947, the General Assembly approved dividing the territory into a Jewish state and an Arab one.
story:
On November 29, 1947, the UN General Assembly approved, by 33 votes in favor, 13 against and 10 abstentions, Resolution 181, which recommended ending the British mandate over Palestine and creating there two states, one Jewish and one Arab, with Jerusalem under international administration.

The Zionist leadership accepted it; the Arab countries and the Palestinians rejected it as unjust to the territory's Arab majority. The resolution was never applied as written: when Israel was proclaimed in May 1948, the first Arab-Israeli war broke out, and the conflict continues.

title: The Winter War begins
headline: In 1939, the USSR invaded Finland, which held out for months far better than expected.
story:
On November 30, 1939, three months after dividing Eastern Europe with Nazi Germany, the Soviet Union attacked Finland after unsuccessfully demanding territory and bases from it. It counted on a quick victory thanks to its enormous numerical superiority.

The Finnish army, with troops on skis, guerrilla tactics in the frozen forest and a skillful use of the terrain, inflicted disastrous losses on the Soviets during the harsh winter. Even so, exhausted, Finland had to cede 10% of its territory in March 1940. The Red Army's poor showing encouraged Hitler to attack it a year later.

title: Rosa Parks refuses to give up her seat
headline: In 1955, a Black seamstress refused to rise from her seat on an Alabama bus and set off a historic boycott.
story:
On December 1, 1955, in Montgomery, Alabama, Rosa Parks was riding home from work on a bus when the driver ordered her to give up her seat to a white passenger, as the segregation law required. Parks refused and was arrested.

Her arrest was the spark for a boycott of the city's buses that lasted 381 days, organized by the Black community with a young pastor, Martin Luther King, as its spokesman. In 1956, the Supreme Court declared segregation on public transport unconstitutional. Parks went down in history as "the mother of the civil rights movement".

title: The first nuclear chain reaction
headline: In 1942, under the stands of a Chicago stadium, human beings controlled nuclear fission for the first time.
story:
On December 2, 1942, a team led by the physicist Enrico Fermi started up, in a squash court under the stands of the University of Chicago football field, the first nuclear reactor in history, "Chicago Pile-1": a six-meter pile of graphite and uranium blocks. At 3:25 p.m. it reached a self-sustaining, controlled chain reaction that lasted 28 minutes.

The coded message to Washington was: "The Italian navigator has landed in the New World." The experiment, part of the Manhattan Project, showed that both the atomic bomb and civilian nuclear power were possible.

title: The Bhopal disaster
headline: In 1984, a leak of toxic gas from a pesticide plant in India killed thousands of people as they slept.
story:
In the early hours of December 3, 1984, a leak of about 40 tons of methyl isocyanate at a plant of the American company Union Carbide, in Bhopal, India, formed a toxic cloud that spread over the poor neighborhoods nearby. Thousands of people died that night, suffocated or blinded; it is estimated that the catastrophe has caused between 15,000 and 25,000 deaths in total.

More than half a million people were left with lasting effects. The compensation was far below what was demanded, the site is still contaminated, and almost no one was convicted. It is the worst industrial accident in history.

title: British India bans 'sati'
headline: In 1829, the practice of burning a widow alive on her husband's funeral pyre was outlawed.
story:
On December 4, 1829, the governor-general of British India, Lord William Bentinck, signed a law making 'sati' or 'suttee' a crime, the custom by which some widows, sometimes pressured by family or community, immolated themselves on their husband's pyre. It was practiced above all in Bengal.

The ban was the result of a campaign by Indian reformers, especially Ram Mohan Roy, allied with missionaries and British officials. It was one of the first major interventions by colonial power in local religious customs and a precedent for later debates about tradition and rights.

title: Mozart dies
headline: In 1791, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart died in Vienna at the age of 35, leaving his Requiem unfinished.
story:
On December 5, 1791, around one in the morning, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart died in Vienna after several weeks of fever and swelling. He was 35. He had been a child prodigy and, as an adult, one of the most complete composers in history: operas such as 'The Marriage of Figaro' and 'Don Giovanni', symphonies, concertos, chamber music.

He was working on a commissioned Requiem when he fell ill; he left it half-finished and a pupil completed it. The legend of poisoning by his rival Salieri has no evidence. He was buried in a common grave, in keeping with the Viennese custom of the time for the middle classes.

title: The Irish Free State is born
headline: In 1922, most of Ireland ceased to be under direct British rule after centuries of struggle.
story:
On December 6, 1922, the Anglo-Irish Treaty took effect and the Irish Free State was established, a self-governing dominion within the British Empire that grouped 26 of the island's 32 counties. The six counties of the northeast, with a Protestant and unionist majority, chose to stay in the United Kingdom: Northern Ireland was born.

The agreement, which required an oath of loyalty to the crown and accepted partition, split the independence movement and caused a year-long civil war. In 1937 the Free State became Ireland, and in 1949 a full republic. Partition still shapes the island's politics.

title: The attack on Pearl Harbor
headline: In 1941, Japan made a surprise bombing of the US fleet in Hawaii and brought the United States into the war.
story:
On the morning of December 7, 1941, without a prior declaration of war, more than 350 Japanese planes launched from aircraft carriers attacked the naval base at Pearl Harbor, in Hawaii. In about two hours they sank or damaged 18 ships — among them eight battleships — destroyed nearly 200 aircraft and killed about 2,400 people.

Japan sought to neutralize the Pacific Fleet in order to conquer Southeast Asia without interference. It achieved the opposite: the next day, the United States declared war on Japan, and Germany and Italy declared war on the US. The conflict became truly global.

title: The murder of John Lennon
headline: In 1980, the former Beatle was shot by a fan outside his home in New York.
story:
On the night of December 8, 1980, John Lennon was returning with Yoko Ono to his building, the Dakota, next to Central Park, when Mark David Chapman, a young man to whom he had signed an autograph hours earlier, shot him four times in the back. Lennon, 40, died shortly afterward at the hospital.

A former member of the Beatles, author of anthems such as 'Imagine' and a peace activist, Lennon was in the middle of a musical comeback with a newly released album. His death caused mass vigils around the world. Chapman, who said he had done it for fame, is still in prison.

title: The Genocide Convention
headline: In 1948, the UN defined genocide as an international crime, the day before adopting the Declaration of Human Rights.
story:
On December 9, 1948, the UN General Assembly adopted the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. It defined genocide as acts committed "with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group" and obliged states to prevent and punish it.

The driving force behind the term and the treaty was the Polish jurist Raphael Lemkin, who had lost most of his family in the Holocaust. The Convention has served as the basis for international tribunals on Rwanda, the former Yugoslavia and other cases.

title: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
headline: In 1948, the UN proclaimed in Paris a list of rights common to "all members of the human family".
story:
On December 10, 1948, at the Palais de Chaillot in Paris, the UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, with 48 votes in favor, none against and 8 abstentions. Its 30 articles set out liberty, equality, the prohibition of torture and slavery, due process, freedom of expression and religion, and social rights such as education and work.

It is not a binding treaty, but it has inspired dozens of constitutions and binding conventions. Its drafting was led by a commission chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt. December 10 is Human Rights Day.

title: The Kyoto Protocol
headline: In 1997, the first treaty was signed that required rich countries to cut their greenhouse gas emissions.
story:
On December 11, 1997, after a marathon summit in Kyoto, Japan, 38 industrialized countries committed to reducing their greenhouse gas emissions by an average of 5% from 1990 levels in the period 2008–2012. It was the first climate agreement with binding targets.

The United States, the largest emitter of the time, never ratified it, and emerging countries such as China had no obligations. Its real effect on global emissions was limited, but it established a framework — inventories, verification, carbon markets — that led to the Paris Agreement of 2015.

title: The first transatlantic radio signal
headline: In 1901, Marconi received in Canada a signal sent from England and showed that radio could cross the ocean.
story:
On December 12, 1901, at Signal Hill, near St John's, Newfoundland, Canada, Guglielmo Marconi and his assistants, with an antenna held up by a kite, said they had picked up three dots in Morse — the letter "S" — transmitted from a station in Cornwall, 3,500 km away.

Many scientists doubted it: it was thought that radio waves, traveling in a straight line, could not clear the curvature of the Earth. In fact they bounce off the ionosphere. The experiment, disputed but soon confirmed, opened the era of long-distance wireless communication. Marconi shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1909.

title: The Nanjing Massacre
headline: In 1937, the Japanese army took the Chinese capital and committed one of the worst atrocities of the century over several weeks.
story:
On December 13, 1937, Japanese troops entered Nanjing, then the capital of China. Over the following six weeks an orgy of violence broke out: mass executions of prisoners and civilians, fires, looting and tens of thousands of rapes. Estimates of the dead range from 40,000 to more than 300,000.

A small group of foreigners created a "safety zone" that saved hundreds of thousands of people. Japan played down the events for decades, and they are still a source of tension with China. In Spanish the city was known as Nankín; today it is transcribed Nanjing.

title: Amundsen reaches the South Pole
headline: In 1911, a Norwegian expedition reached the South Pole for the first time, a month before its British rival.
story:
On December 14, 1911, five Norwegians led by Roald Amundsen planted their flag at the geographic South Pole after a journey of some 1,400 km from the Antarctic coast. They had used dog sledges, skis and meticulous planning of supply depots.

His rival, the Briton Robert Falcon Scott, reached the Pole on January 17, 1912, and found the Norwegian tent. Scott and his four companions died of cold and hunger on the way back. The contrast between the two expeditions is still studied as an example of preparation and decision-making.

title: The United States Bill of Rights
headline: In 1791, the first ten amendments to the Constitution took effect, shielding individual liberties.
story:
On December 15, 1791, with Virginia's ratification, the first ten amendments to the United States Constitution took effect, known as the Bill of Rights. Several states had accepted the 1787 Constitution only on the promise that they would be added.

They guarantee freedom of religion, speech, press and assembly; the right to bear arms; protection against arbitrary searches; due process and trial by jury; and reserve to the states and the people the powers not delegated to the federal government. They have been the ground for some of the country's great legal debates.

title: The Boston Tea Party
headline: In 1773, disguised colonists threw a cargo of British tea into the sea to protest against taxes.
story:
On the night of December 16, 1773, a group of Boston colonists, some disguised as Mohawk Indians, boarded three East India Company ships and dumped 342 chests of tea, about 45 tons, into the harbor. They were protesting against the monopoly and against the idea of paying taxes to a Parliament in which they had no representation.

London responded with punitive laws that closed the port and cut back Massachusetts's self-government. Far from isolating Boston, those measures united the colonies. Less than two years later, the war of independence began.

title: The Wright brothers' first flight
headline: In 1903, a heavier-than-air machine flew under power and control for the first time, for 12 seconds.
story:
On December 17, 1903, on a beach at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville Wright flew the 'Flyer' for 12 seconds and 37 meters, the first time a powered, heavier-than-air machine took off, sustained itself and landed under the pilot's control. That day they made four flights; the longest, 59 seconds.

The Wright brothers, owners of a bicycle shop in Ohio, had solved the key problem: not propulsion, but control on all three axes through the warping of the wings. Within a decade, aviation went from curiosity to weapon of war and means of transport.

title: The United States abolishes slavery
headline: In 1865, the Thirteenth Amendment took effect and banned slavery throughout the country.
story:
On December 18, 1865, the Secretary of State certified that the Thirteenth Amendment to the Constitution had been ratified by three-quarters of the states. Its text is brief: "Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime, shall exist within the United States."

The Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 had freed only the enslaved people in the rebel states and could be revoked. The amendment made abolition total and permanent. It affected some four million people. The exception for crime has been criticized for its later use against the Black population.

title: Humanity's last trip to the Moon
headline: In 1972, the return of Apollo 17 closed the lunar program; no one has set foot on the Moon since.
story:
On December 19, 1972, the Apollo 17 capsule splashed down in the Pacific, ending the last crewed mission to the Moon. Days earlier, the astronauts Eugene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt — the first scientist to walk on another world — had spent three days exploring the Taurus-Littrow valley with an electric vehicle and had collected 110 kilos of rocks.

As he climbed back into the module, Cernan said that humanity would return "not too far into the future". More than five decades have passed. Budget cuts canceled the following missions; current plans for a return point to the end of this decade.

title: South Carolina secedes from the Union
headline: In 1860, the first state to secede opened the way to the American Civil War.
story:
On December 20, 1860, weeks after the election of Abraham Lincoln, a convention in South Carolina voted unanimously to separate from the United States. In the document, the state made clear that the cause was the threat to slavery, the "institution" on which its plantation economy depended.

Over the following three months, six more states joined it and formed the Confederate States of America. The war broke out in April 1861, when Confederate troops bombarded the federal Fort Sumter, in the harbor of Charleston, South Carolina.

title: Apollo 8 and the "Earthrise"
headline: In 1968, three astronauts set out for the Moon, orbited it on Christmas Eve and brought back a photo that changed how we see the planet.
story:
On December 21, 1968, Apollo 8 lifted off, the first crewed spacecraft to leave Earth orbit and travel to the Moon. On Christmas Eve, its three astronauts made ten orbits of our satellite and read the opening of Genesis on television to the largest audience in history up to then.

On one of those orbits, Bill Anders photographed the Earth rising above the lunar horizon: a blue, fragile globe against the blackness. That image, "Earthrise", became an icon of the environmental movement and of a new awareness of the planet's fragility.

title: The Ceaușescu dictatorship falls in Romania
headline: In 1989, a revolt ended the Romanian communist regime, the only one in the region to fall violently.
story:
On December 22, 1989, after days of protests that began in the city of Timișoara and a crackdown with dozens of deaths, the Romanian dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu tried to give a speech from the balcony of the Central Committee in Bucharest, and the crowd jeered him live on television. Hours later he fled by helicopter.

Arrested with his wife Elena, a summary military court convicted them and had them shot on Christmas Day. It was the bloodiest outcome of the 1989 revolutions in Eastern Europe, which in the other countries were peaceful.

title: The invention of the transistor
headline: In 1947, three physicists at Bell Labs demonstrated the device that made all of modern electronics possible.
story:
On December 23, 1947, at Bell Labs in New Jersey, John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley demonstrated a small device of germanium with two gold contacts able to amplify and switch electric currents: the transistor. It did the work of the bulky, fragile vacuum tubes, but tiny, cheap, robust and low-power.

From it descend integrated circuits, computers, mobile phones and practically every electronic device. A modern chip holds tens of billions of transistors. The three inventors received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1956.

title: The Christmas truce
headline: In 1914, along several stretches of the Western Front, enemy soldiers stopped firing and greeted one another between the trenches.
story:
On Christmas Eve and Christmas Day 1914, at various points along the front in Belgium and northern France, German and British soldiers — sometimes French as well — stopped fighting on their own initiative. They sang carols, exchanged tobacco, food and buttons, buried their dead together and, in a few places, played football in no man's land.

The commanders, alarmed, forbade any repeat, and in the following Christmases there were strict orders and scheduled bombardments to prevent it. The truce of 1914 stood as a symbol of humanity in the middle of a war that would still last four years.

title: Charlemagne is crowned emperor
headline: In the year 800, the pope crowned the king of the Franks in Rome and revived the idea of an empire in the West.
story:
On Christmas Day in the year 800, during Mass in St Peter's Basilica in Rome, Pope Leo III placed a crown on the head of Charlemagne, king of the Franks and the Lombards, and proclaimed him "emperor of the Romans". According to his biographer, Charlemagne feigned surprise.

It was the first time in more than three centuries that there had been an emperor in Western Europe. The act strengthened the alliance between Frankish power and the papacy and sowed the dispute, for centuries, over who was above whom. From that title came the Holy Roman Empire, which lasted until 1806.

title: The Indian Ocean tsunami
headline: In 2004, an undersea earthquake off Sumatra generated waves that killed about 230,000 people in 14 countries.
story:
On the morning of December 26, 2004, an earthquake of magnitude close to 9.2 ruptured about 1,200 km of seafloor off the northwest coast of Sumatra, in Indonesia. The displacement of the ocean bed raised waves that spread at hundreds of km/h across the whole Indian Ocean.

Within hours, walls of water several meters high razed coasts in Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, Thailand and even Somalia, 8,000 km away. About 230,000 people died and millions were left homeless. The absence of a warning system in the region made the tragedy worse; one was installed afterward.

title: The USSR invades Afghanistan
headline: In 1979, Soviet troops entered Afghanistan to prop up a communist government and were trapped there for nine years.
story:
On December 27, 1979, Soviet special forces stormed the presidential palace in Kabul, killed the Afghan communist leader Hafizullah Amin and replaced him with a more compliant one, while tens of thousands of soldiers crossed the border. Moscow wanted to stabilize an allied regime threatened by an Islamist insurgency.

The war became the "Soviet Vietnam": nine years of fighting against mujahideen guerrillas armed by the United States, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, with more than a million Afghans dead. The USSR withdrew in 1989, weakened. Out of that conflict came the Taliban and al-Qaeda.

title: The first paying film screening
headline: In 1895, the Lumière brothers projected films to an audience that paid admission, in the basement of a Paris café.
story:
On December 28, 1895, at the Salon Indien of the Grand Café on the Boulevard des Capucines in Paris, the Lumière brothers projected ten short films of less than a minute each before some 33 spectators who had paid one franc. They watched workers leaving a factory, a train entering a station and a comic scene with a hose.

Others had shown moving images, but this is usually taken as the birth of cinema as public spectacle and business. Within a year, the 'cinématographe' was touring the world and several countries already had dedicated theaters.

title: The Wounded Knee Massacre
headline: In 1890, the US army killed about 250 Lakota, most of them unarmed, and ended the Indian wars.
story:
On December 29, 1890, beside Wounded Knee Creek, in South Dakota, a cavalry regiment was trying to disarm a group of Lakota under the chief Spotted Elk (Big Foot). A shot went off in a struggle and the soldiers opened fire with rifles and rapid-fire cannon on men, women and children who were fleeing.

About 250–300 Lakota and 25 soldiers died, several by friendly fire. The massacre ended the spiritual movement of the "Ghost Dance" and is considered the end of the wars between the army and the Indigenous peoples of the plains. In 1990, Congress expressed "deep regret".

title: The Soviet Union is founded
headline: In 1922, four republics signed the treaty that created the USSR, a state that would last almost 70 years.
story:
On December 30, 1922, after winning the civil war, the Bolsheviks formalized the union of Soviet Russia with the republics of Ukraine, Belarus and Transcaucasia into a single federal state: the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. Over time it would come to comprise fifteen republics.

In theory it was a voluntary federation; in practice, power was centralized in the Communist Party and in Moscow. The USSR became an industrial and military superpower, rival of the United States during the Cold War, and dissolved in December 1991.

title: The East India Company is born
headline: In 1600, Queen Elizabeth I granted a group of London merchants a monopoly on trade with Asia.
story:
On December 31, 1600, Queen Elizabeth I of England signed the charter granting the "Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies" a monopoly on English trade with all the territory east of the Cape of Good Hope. It began as a spice venture with a few ships.

Over the centuries it became a colossal power: it had its own army, minted coins and ended up governing almost all of India in its own name, until the British Crown took direct control in 1858. It is often cited as the first great multinational and as an example of the dangers of a company with the power of a state.
